Module 2

Enabling Organizational Strategy through Information Systems

Module 1 asked what an information system is. This one asks the harder question a manager actually gets paid to answer: which system, where, and why that one. A company can spend heavily on technology and end up merely faster at what it already did. The difference between spending and strategy is a way of thinking — about where the pressure in your industry comes from, where in your own operation value is created, and what a competitor would have to do to copy you.

How to use this page

  1. Read the short setup first. Every term is explained in ordinary language before an activity uses it, so nothing assumes a background you have not been given.
  2. Answer as you go. The activities sit inside the reading. When you answer a question, every option explains itself — including the three you did not pick, because knowing why a wrong answer is wrong is the part that transfers.
  3. Write real formulas and real queries. The last section is not a description of a spreadsheet and a database. You type into them and they run, on the page, against real rows — and they tell you plainly when something will not work.
  4. Retry anything. Restart one activity, one section, or the whole page. Your best result stays in this browser until you clear it; answers reset on reload so every attempt is fresh.

Section 2–1a

How an organization is arranged for deciding

Before anyone can say which information system a company needs, they have to say who is asking. A cashier, a store manager, and a chief executive all work for the same firm and all want information — but different information, on different clocks, for different reasons. This section maps the organization first, so every system has somewhere to sit.

Business processes: what a company actually does all day

Companies do not exist to own technology; they exist to do things, and the things they do have a name. Business processes are the activities an organization performs to reach its business goals, and they come in two kinds.

  • Core activities — the activities that transform inputs and produce outputs, because that transformation is the thing a customer eventually pays for: flour and labor become a loaf, and an order becomes a delivered package.
  • Supporting activities — the activities that enable the core activities to take place, because nobody bakes the loaf if payroll never runs, the oven is never repaired, and no baker was ever hired.

A broad range of information is needed to support those processes, which is why structure comes first: it shows which type of system supports which process, and how much value each one delivers.

Three levels, three different questions

Every organization is composed of different decision-making levels. The usual drawing is a pyramid: a wide operational level at the bottom, a narrower managerial level in the middle, and a narrow executive level at the top.

The shape matters less than what follows from it. Each level has different responsibilities and, therefore, different informational needs — which is why each level is commonly supported by a different type of information system.

The operational level: running the day

At the operational level of a firm, the routine, day-to-day business processes and the interactions with customers occur. This is the checkout lane, the loading dock, the order screen. The chapter’s figure states three facts about it.

  • Who — foremen and supervisors, the managers closest to the work, who make day-to-day decisions that are highly structured and recurring.
  • What the systems do — they automate routine and repetitive activities and events, such as processing sales transactions, and improve the efficiency of business processes at the customer interface.
  • Why — to improve organizational efficiency, meaning the extent to which goals are accomplished faster, at lower cost, or with relatively little time and effort.

The unit of work here is the transaction. A transaction is anything that occurs as part of a firm’s daily business of which it must keep a record: a sale rung up, an item received, a shift clocked. The clock is short too, since operational planning typically has a time frame of a few hours or days.

Because activities here are clearly delineated and well focused, optimizing them can offer quick returns on the investment, and the same systems help managers find the underlying causes of performance problems.

The managerial level: running a function

At the managerial level — also called the tactical level — functional managers such as marketing, finance, manufacturing, and human resource managers monitor and control operational-level activities and pass information up to higher levels. The chapter calls them midlevel managers.

  • Who — midlevel managers and functional managers, who typically focus on problems inside one business function such as marketing or finance.
  • What the systems do — they automate the monitoring and controlling of operational activities, so a manager can see what the level below is producing.
  • Why — to improve organizational effectiveness, meaning the extent to which goals or tasks are accomplished well, in service of the organization’s strategic objectives.

A managerial decision is usually contained within the business function, is moderately complex, and has a time horizon of a few days to a few months — a horizon with its own name, tactical planning. The chapter’s example is a marketing manager at Nike allocating the advertising budget for the next business quarter.

Managers here watch a few numbers rather than every transaction. The metrics deemed most critical to assessing progress toward a certain goal are called key performance indicators, or KPIs, and they are displayed on digital dashboards.

The chapter’s illustration is a production manager at Nike whose business intelligence system supplies analytics and forecasts on multiple product lines, inventory levels, and overall production capacity. The manager builds several hypothetical production schedules, then runs predictive analyses on each to compare inventory levels and potential sales profitability.

The executive level: running the company

At the executive level — also called the strategic level — managers face the long-term questions: which products to produce, which countries to compete in, and what strategy to follow. The people here are the president and chief executive officer, the chief information officer, vice presidents, and possibly the board.

  • Who — executive-level managers, who must weigh the ramifications of any decision for the overall organization rather than for one department.
  • What the systems do — they supply aggregate summaries of past organizational data and projections of the future, rather than individual records.
  • Why — to improve organizational strategy and planning, which is a longer and broader job than either efficiency or effectiveness.

Executive-level decisions deal with complex problems whose consequences are broad and long-term. Deciding to develop a new product, or discontinue an existing one, can have vast effects on the organization’s levels of employment and profitability. Three things follow for the systems.

  • Balancing KPIs — some indicators here focus on balancing performance across the organization, staggering product launches so spikes in demand do not hit the supply chain all at once.
  • Benchmarking KPIs — others benchmark the organization’s performance against its competitors, because a rising number means little until you know what rivals did.
  • Unstructured data — the systems must take in global economic factors, demographic changes, and changing customer tastes and preferences, none of which arrive as tidy rows of transactions.

Executives also engage in environmental scanning, assessing how new information systems could help the organization offer new products or services and support its strategy.

Reading the three levels side by side

Set out together, the differences stop looking like job titles and start reading like a design brief.

LevelWho works thereWhat the systems doWhyDecision typePlanning horizon
OperationalForemen and supervisorsAutomate routine and repetitive activities and eventsImprove organizational efficiencyStructuredA few hours or days
Managerial
tactical		Midlevel and functional managersAutomate the monitoring and controlling of operational activitiesImprove organizational effectivenessSemistructuredA few days to a few months
Executive
strategic		Executives: the CEO, CIO, vice presidents, possibly the boardProvide aggregate summaries of past data and projections of the futureImprove organizational strategy and planningUnstructuredLong-term

Efficiency is not effectiveness. Efficiency is the extent to which goals are accomplished faster, at lower cost, or with relatively little time and effort, and it belongs to the operational level. Effectiveness is the extent to which goals or tasks are accomplished well, and it belongs to the managerial level. A warehouse shipping the wrong item in record time is efficient, not effective.

The diagram redraws each level on its own, so you can recall who, what, why, and the decision type without the table in front of you.

The three decision-making levels, one at a time

Pick a level to see who works there, what its information systems do, why the organization wants them, and what kind of decision gets made.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Operational level — The widest part of the pyramid, where the day happens one recorded event at a time

Who (Foremen and supervisors) → What (Automate routine and repetitive activities and events) → Why (To improve organizational efficiency) → Decision type (Structured and recurring)

  • This is where the routine, day-to-day business processes and the interactions with customers occur, so the systems sit at the customer interface: registers, order screens, receiving scanners.
  • The unit of work is the transaction — anything that occurs as part of a firm’s daily business of which it must keep a record.
  • Decisions here are structured: the procedures to follow can be specified in advance, so they can be programmed directly into the system and made with little or no human intervention.
  • Operational planning typically has a time frame of a few hours or days, and because the activities are clearly delineated and well focused, optimizing them can offer quick returns on the investment.

Managerial level, also called tactical — The middle of the pyramid, where one business function is monitored and steered

Who (Midlevel managers and functional managers) → What (Automate the monitoring and controlling of operational activities) → Why (To improve organizational effectiveness) → Decision type (Semistructured)

  • Functional managers — marketing, finance, manufacturing, human resource managers — monitor and control the level below them and provide information to the levels above them.
  • Their aim is effectiveness, the extent to which goals or tasks are accomplished well, achieved by effectively utilizing and deploying organizational resources toward the strategic objectives.
  • Decisions here are semistructured: some procedures can be specified in advance, but not to the point of producing a specific recommendation, so judgment and expertise are still required.
  • The scope is usually contained within the business function, is moderately complex, and has a horizon of a few days to a few months, which the chapter calls tactical planning.

Executive level, also called strategic — The narrow top of the pyramid, where commitments are made for the whole organization

Who (Executives: CEO, CIO, vice presidents, possibly the board) → What (Aggregate summaries of past data and projections of the future) → Why (To improve organizational strategy and planning) → Decision type (Unstructured)

  • The questions are long-term: which products to produce, which countries to compete in, and what organizational strategy to follow.
  • Decisions here are unstructured, because few or no procedures can be specified in advance for problems that are relatively complex, nonroutine, and consequential for the overall organization.
  • KPIs at this level balance performance across the organization — staggering product launches so demand spikes do not hit the supply chain at once — and benchmark the firm against its competitors.
  • These systems must handle unstructured data such as global economic factors, demographic changes, and shifting customer tastes, and executives use environmental scanning to see how new systems could support strategy.

Test the three levels against a few situations before turning to the decisions.

Check yourself

Placing work at the right level

Four options, one best answer; read every explanation, including the ones for options you did not choose.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. A supervisor on a distribution floor needs to know whether tonight’s shift can clear the orders already sitting in the building. Which level is she working at, and what are its systems for?

  • A. The managerial level, because a supervisor is a manager and the question covers a whole shift rather than one order — Job titles are not levels. The chapter places foremen and supervisors at the operational level precisely because their decisions are day-to-day, highly structured, and recurring, whatever the word on the badge.
  • B. The operational level, where systems automate routine and repetitive activities and events in order to improve efficiency — correct. This is routine day-to-day work with a horizon of a few hours, and operational systems exist to automate routine and repetitive activities and events so that goals are accomplished faster, at lower cost, or with relatively little time and effort.
  • C. The executive level, because whether orders ship tonight affects whether customers stay with the firm at all — Executive-level decisions deal with complex problems whose ramifications are broad and long-term, such as which countries to compete in. Tonight’s backlog matters, but it is settled before the executives next meet.
  • D. The managerial level, because the systems there automate the monitoring and controlling of operational activities — The description of managerial systems is accurate, and it would fit a functional manager comparing this week’s throughput across several shifts. Here the supervisor is inside the shift doing the work, not standing above it monitoring a function.

2. A company reports that one process now finishes faster and at lower cost than it did last year. Which term names that result, and which level does the chapter associate it with?

  • A. Effectiveness, at the managerial level, since the goal is now being accomplished well — Effectiveness is the extent to which goals or tasks are accomplished well, and it is the managerial-level aim. Speed and cost alone say nothing about whether the right thing was produced.
  • B. Efficiency, at the managerial level, since midlevel managers deploy the organization’s resources — Half right is still wrong here. Efficiency is the correct term, but the chapter ties it to the operational level, where systems optimize clearly delineated processes and return the investment quickly.
  • C. Efficiency, at the operational level, since goals are accomplished faster, at lower cost, or with relatively little time and effort — correct. Efficiency is defined as the extent to which goals are accomplished faster, at lower cost, or with relatively little time and effort, and improving it is the stated purpose of operational-level systems.
  • D. Effectiveness, at the executive level, since a faster process supports the organization’s long-term strategy — Executive systems aim at strategy and planning through aggregate summaries and projections, not at the speed of a single process. Naming this effectiveness also misses that nothing was said about how well the work was done.

3. A marketing manager is deciding how to allocate the advertising budget for the next business quarter. How does the chapter describe the scope and time horizon of a decision like this one?

  • A. The scope is usually contained within one business function, is moderately complex, and runs a few days to a few months — correct. That is the chapter’s description of managerial decisions, and it is why this horizon of a few days to a few months carries the name tactical planning.
  • B. The scope reaches across the whole organization with long-term ramifications, since real money is being committed — Broad scope and long-term ramifications describe executive-level decisions, such as developing or discontinuing a product. A quarter of advertising spend is a large sum inside one function, not a commitment for the whole organization.
  • C. The scope is a single business function, but the horizon is a few hours or days, matching operational planning — The scope is right and the horizon is not. A few hours or days is operational planning, the pace of the register and the loading dock, whereas a business quarter is months away.
  • D. The scope covers several functions at once, which is exactly why the chapter calls this level tactical planning — Tactical planning is named for its time horizon, not for spanning functions, and midlevel managers typically focus on problems within one business function such as marketing or finance.

Structured, semistructured, and unstructured decisions

The levels differ in more than seniority. The decisions themselves have different shapes, and the shape determines how much of the decision a machine can take over.

  • Structured decisions — those in which the procedures to follow for a given situation can be specified in advance, so they can be programmed directly into operational information systems and made with little or no human intervention.
  • Semistructured decisions — those in which some procedures can be specified in advance, but not to the extent where a specific recommendation can be made, because the problems and solutions are not clear-cut and often require judgment and expertise.
  • Unstructured decisions — those in which few or no procedures can be specified in advance, because the problems are relatively complex and nonroutine and their consequences reach the whole organization.

The chapter’s smallest example is the clearest. An inventory system in a mall shoe store tracks stock and orders more when levels drop below a specified point, and the store’s operational managers simply confirm the order was needed. The rule existed before the situation did, so software can carry it.

The less a procedure can be written down in advance, the higher in the organization the decision travels, and the more the system shifts from deciding to informing.

Sort

How structured is this decision?

Place each decision in the category the chapter defines for it. Situations that are not the chapter’s own examples are practice situations, and each one states the conditions you need.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Structured — the procedures to follow can be specified in advance, so the system can carry the decision itself

  • An inventory system in a mall shoe store tracks stock and issues an order for more shoes whenever the count falls below a set level, and the operational managers in the store only confirm it — This is the chapter’s own example of a rule written before the situation arose, which is why it can be programmed directly into an operational system and run with almost no human intervention.
  • A payroll system multiplies the hours a system recorded by a stored pay rate to produce gross pay for each employee — The procedure is fixed in advance and the same every period, so it is highly structured and recurring — exactly the work operational systems automate.
  • A register records each completed sale so the firm keeps a record of its daily business — Recording a transaction is the definition of routine operational work, and no judgment enters it: the steps are identical for every customer.
  • In a practice situation, a supervisor assigns a returning part-time worker to a shift using a posted seniority rule that already covers this exact case — Because the rule was specified in advance and fits the situation without interpretation, the decision is structured even though a person happens to be the one applying it.

Semistructured — some procedures can be specified in advance, but not far enough to produce a specific recommendation

  • A marketing manager at Nike decides how to allocate the advertising budget for the next business quarter — The chapter gives this as managerial work: past results and forecasts narrow the choice, but no procedure returns the specific allocation, so judgment finishes the job.
  • A production manager uses a business intelligence system to build several hypothetical production schedules and then runs predictive analyses on each one — The system supplies analytics, forecasts, and comparisons, but it stops short of naming the schedule to use, which is precisely the semistructured boundary.
  • In a practice situation, a functional manager watching a dashboard of quarterly KPIs must choose which of two underperforming processes to repair first, with the metrics known but no rule ranking them — Measurement is specified in advance and the choice is not, so the manager brings judgment and expertise to a moderately complex problem inside one function.
  • In a practice situation, a midlevel manager decides how many temporary staff to bring into one department for a seasonal peak, using a forecast that narrows the range without naming a number — The scope stays inside a single business function on a horizon of a few weeks, and the forecast informs the decision rather than making it.

Unstructured — few or no procedures can be specified in advance, and the ramifications reach the whole organization

  • Top managers decide whether to develop a new product or discontinue an existing one, knowing employment levels and profitability may be affected for years — The chapter uses this decision to show ramifications that are vast and long-term, and no procedure written in advance can settle it.
  • Executives decide which countries the organization will compete in — This is one of the long-term strategic questions the chapter puts at the executive level, and it turns on complex, nonroutine judgments about the whole organization.
  • Executives weigh global economic factors, demographic changes, and shifting customer tastes in choosing what organizational strategy to follow — These are the unstructured data types the chapter says executive systems must consider, and no advance procedure converts them into a single answer.

Functional areas and the systems that serve them

Decision-making levels cut the organization horizontally. Functional areas cut it vertically. A functional area is a discrete area of an organization that focuses on a specific set of activities.

Two examples show how different those sets of activities can be. People in marketing focus on activities that promote the organization and its products in a way that attracts and retains customers, while people in accounting and finance manage and control its capital assets and financial resources.

Because the activities differ, the systems differ. Functional area information systems are designed to support the unique business processes of specific functional areas, and the chapter’s Table 2.1 names four of them.

Functional areaInformation systemSample applications
Accounting and financeSystems used for managing, controlling, and auditing the financial resources of the organizationAccounts payable; expense accounts; cash management; payroll processing
Human resourcesSystems used for managing, controlling, and auditing the human resources of the organizationRecruiting and hiring; education and training; benefits management; employee termination; workforce planning
MarketingSystems used for managing new product development, distribution, pricing, promotional effectiveness, and sales forecasting of the products and services offered by the organizationMarket research and analysis; new product development; promotion and advertising; pricing and sales analysis; product location analysis
Production and operationsSystems used for managing, controlling, and auditing the production and operations resources of the organizationInventory management; cost and quality tracking; materials and resource planning; job costing; resource utilization

The two cuts meet in one picture. The chapter’s Figure 2.6 puts five functional area systems along the base — accounting, financial, human resource, marketing, and operational — and stacks applications above them by how demanding the decision is.

  • Transaction processing and basic reporting — payroll processing in accounting, cash management in finance, an employee skill inventory in human resources, pricing and sales analysis in marketing, and manufacturing resource utilization in operations.
  • Tactical and managerial control — order processing in accounting, financial forecasting in finance, compensation analysis in human resources, sales force automation in marketing, and inventory management in operations.
  • More complex planning and coordination — portfolio management and ratio analysis in finance, personnel forecasting in human resources, advertising and promotion planning in marketing, and manufacturing resource planning in operations.

Read the two cuts together and you get a grid: the function names the column and the level names the row. Naming both narrows a vague request such as “we need better reporting” down to a single cell.

Ask which function owns the process and which level makes the call; those two answers describe the system before a single vendor is contacted.

Accounting and finance
Systems used for managing, controlling, and auditing the financial resources of the organization Accounts payable, expense accounts, cash management, and payroll processing are the sample applications, and all four track where money sits and where it moves.
Human resources
Systems used for managing, controlling, and auditing the human resources of the organization Recruiting and hiring, education and training, benefits management, employee termination, and workforce planning cover a person’s whole span with the organization.
Marketing
Systems used for managing new product development, distribution, pricing, promotional effectiveness, and sales forecasting This function focuses on activities that promote the organization and its products in a way that attracts and retains customers, which is why forecasting and pricing sit here.
Production and operations
Systems used for managing, controlling, and auditing the production and operations resources of the organization Inventory management, cost and quality tracking, materials and resource planning, job costing, and resource utilization all concern making the thing rather than selling it.
Financial information systems
Cash management, then financial forecasting, then portfolio management and ratio analysis One functional system reaches across all three application layers, from a basic transaction record up to complex planning and coordination.
Human resource information systems
An employee skill inventory, then compensation analysis, then personnel forecasting The same function is served at three heights: recording who has which skill, controlling pay, and planning the workforce the organization will need.
Marketing information systems
Pricing and sales analysis, then sales force automation, then advertising and promotion planning Analysis of what sold supports tactical control of the sales force, which in turn feeds the longer planning of campaigns.
Operational information systems
Manufacturing resource utilization, then inventory management, then manufacturing resource planning Measuring how resources were used supports managing stock, and both feed the complex coordination of manufacturing resource planning.

Check yourself

Indicators, executives, and functions

Three questions on the vocabulary this section introduced; the explanations say what each wrong option genuinely describes.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. What are key performance indicators, and where does the chapter say they are displayed?

  • A. The complete set of transactions a firm records each day, displayed inside a transaction processing system — That describes raw transaction data, which is the record of everything that happened rather than the few numbers chosen to show progress. Indicators exist because nobody can watch every transaction.
  • B. The metrics deemed most critical to assessing progress toward a certain goal, displayed on digital dashboards — correct. KPIs are the metrics deemed most critical to assessing progress toward a certain goal, and they are displayed on digital dashboards for managers who need the state of things at a glance.
  • C. Targets set once a year by executives for every function, displayed in an annual report prepared for the board — KPIs are watched continuously rather than published once a year, and both managers and executives use them. This would be closer to a description of annual financial reporting.
  • D. The procedures specified in advance for a recurring decision, displayed to supervisors as they do the work — Procedures specified in advance define a structured decision, not an indicator. A rule tells you what to do; an indicator tells you how the goal is going.

2. How does the chapter describe the information executives need from their systems?

  • A. Detailed records of individual transactions, so that nothing is lost between the register and the boardroom — Individual transaction records are the output of operational systems. Executives receive them summarized, because the question at that level is the shape of the trend and not the content of one sale.
  • B. Summaries built from the organization’s own internal transaction data, because outside signals such as demographic change belong to the marketing function — The chapter says the opposite about the sources: executive-level systems need to consider various types of unstructured data, such as global economic factors, demographic changes, and changing customer tastes and preferences, none of which start inside the firm.
  • C. Reports confined to one business function at a time, because each executive is responsible for a single function — That is the managerial level, where a midlevel manager typically focuses on problems within a specific business function. Executives must consider the ramifications of a decision for the overall organization.
  • D. Aggregate summaries of past organizational data and projections of the future, with KPIs that balance performance and benchmark competitors — correct. Executive systems supply aggregate summaries of trends and projections of the future, with KPIs that balance performance across the organization and benchmark it against competitors.

3. What is a functional area, and what makes a functional area information system different from an information system in general?

  • A. A functional area is one of the decision-making levels, and its systems serve everyone standing on that rung — Levels and functions are the two different cuts through an organization. Operational, managerial, and executive are the levels; marketing, human resources, and the rest are the functions.
  • B. A functional area is a discrete area focused on a specific set of activities, and its systems support that area’s unique business processes — correct. A functional area is a discrete area of an organization that focuses on a specific set of activities, and functional area information systems are designed to support the unique business processes of specific functional areas.
  • C. A functional area is a physical site such as a store or a plant, and its systems are installed and operated locally — Location is not what defines a function. A single marketing function can operate from several sites, and a single site usually contains people from several functional areas.
  • D. A functional area is a single business process such as order fulfillment, and its systems automate the steps of that one process — Business processes are the activities an organization performs to reach its goals, and a functional area is the standing part of the organization that owns a whole set of them: marketing runs market research, pricing, and promotion, not one process.

Section 2–1b

Automating, learning, and strategizing

Three companies can buy identical software for completely different reasons. One wants the same work done faster. One wants to learn whether the work is worth doing at all. One wants to change what it competes on. The chapter treats these as a ladder, where each rung adds more value than the one below.

Deployed across an organization’s decision-making levels and functional areas, an information system can add value in three general ways: by enabling automating activities, by enabling learning, and by enabling the execution of organizational strategy. These are not necessarily mutually exclusive, but the chapter holds that each is progressively more useful to the firm and adds more value to the business.

The shorthand worth memorizing is faster, better, smarter. These are ambitions rather than product categories: one system can be defended and measured on any of the three, and people make that choice, not the software.

Explore

Faster, better, smarter

Open each card and read all four panels; the fourth card sets the three against each other, which is where the distinction usually breaks down.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Automating · Doing things faster

  • The mindset in one line: Technology used to help complete a task within an organization faster, more cheaply, and perhaps with greater accuracy or consistency — in other words, to increase efficiency.
  • What it looks like in practice: Loan applications go into a computer database so the people deciding on them work faster, more easily, and with fewer errors, and customers can complete the application online instead of carrying paper home.
  • The payoff it produces: Time and cost fall. In the fully automated loan process a small loan can be finished in as little as 15 minutes, and moving off the manual process may enable the organization to deploy its employees more efficiently.
  • Where it stops: It changes what a process costs, never what the process is. If the underlying process is flawed, automating use of technology may mask the problem while multiplying its effects.

Organizational learning · Doing things better

  • The mindset in one line: The ability of an organization to use past behavior and data to improve its business processes, built on top of the automating mentality rather than in place of it.
  • What it looks like in practice: The loan processing system tracks types of application by date, month, or season, so a manager can see trends, plan timely staffing and training, and manage the funds used to fulfill the loans.
  • The payoff it produces: Effectiveness rises, meaning goals get accomplished well rather than merely quickly, because new data about the underlying process can be used to monitor, control, and change that process.
  • Where it stops: Learning tells you how well the current process is working. It does not by itself say what the organization ought to be competing on, which is a question decided a level higher up.

Supporting strategy · Doing things smarter

  • The mindset in one line: Going beyond automating and learning to find ways of using information systems to achieve the organization’s chosen strategy — by innovating, streamlining operations, optimizing the supply chain, or better understanding customers.
  • What it looks like in practice: Uber’s use of information systems for personalization, anticipation, and coordination sits at the heart of its organizational strategy, is fundamental to its business model, and is essential to the long-term survival of the organization.
  • The payoff it produces: Strategic value, meaning help in improving the business so that it can compete better — and the chapter is blunt that a system delivering none of that, even while saving money, is not likely to be funded.
  • Where it stops: It depends on the organization already having a strategy worth serving. Strategic planning happens at the executive level, and no system can supply the vision it is being built to carry out.

The three compared · Why the order matters

  • The mindset in one line: Three general ways an information system can provide value, which the chapter presents as progressively more useful to the firm and therefore as adding progressively more business value.
  • What it looks like in practice: One product can occupy all three at once: Uber automatically matches riders and drivers, learns preferences from past behavior, and builds its strategy on exactly those capabilities.
  • The payoff it produces: The chapter draws the comparison as three bars of business value added, where automating is the shortest bar, learning is taller, and strategizing is the tallest of the three.
  • Where it stops: They are not mutually exclusive, so the real question is never which single rung a proposal belongs to but how far up it reaches, since a strategic system almost always automates and learns as well.

Automating: doing things faster

Someone with an automating perspective thinks of technology as a way to complete a task inside an organization faster, more cheaply, and perhaps with greater accuracy or consistency. What they are buying is efficiency — the extent to which goals are accomplished faster, at lower cost, or with relatively little time and effort. The work itself is never questioned; only what it costs.

The chapter’s worked example is a bank screening loan applications. A person with an automating mentality makes three moves, and not one of them changes who decides or on what grounds.

  • Put the applications into a computer database — so the people deciding on the loans process them faster, more easily, and with fewer errors than they could from a stack of paper.
  • Let customers apply online — because an application completed from home arrives already entered, which removes the trip home and back from the schedule.
  • Redeploy the people the change frees — moving from a manual to an automated loan process may enable the organization to deploy employees more efficiently, which is where the further cost savings come from.

Automation is not confined to paperwork. With increasing digital density, almost every sector can gain efficiency: sensors monitoring machinery or product flows throughout production can tremendously improve a manufacturing company’s performance. Operational-level systems automate repetitive activities and also gather valuable data for higher decision-making levels, which is the hinge into the next rung.

The table takes one loan application through three versions of the same process. Read down a column to see one whole process; read across a row to watch a single activity change.

Sequence

The loan application process, activity by activity

Put the six primary activities into the order the loan table lists them, then read why each one sits where it does.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

The table you just read runs the same six activities through three different processes. Getting the sequence straight is what makes the time savings legible, because each activity can only be shortened by the technology that touches it.

  1. Complete and submit the loan application. Manually the customer takes the application home, completes it, and returns it in 1.5 days; in the fully automated process the customer fills it out from home via the web in 15 minutes. — Nothing else can start until an application exists, and this is the only activity where the work sits with the customer rather than the bank, which is why moving it to the web removes a day and a half at a stroke.
  2. Check the application for errors. An employee does this in batches over 2.5 days in both the manual and the technology-supported processes; the computer does it in 1 second as the form is being completed. — Errors are caught before the data travel any further into the bank. Batching is what makes this take days rather than minutes, because a form waits for the batch it belongs to rather than for a person.
  3. Input the data from the application into the information system. Paper handling takes about 1 hour in the manual process, an employee keys batches over 2.5 days in the technology-supported process, and no extra time is needed once the customer fills the form in online. — This is the activity that gets worse before it gets better: the middle column costs 2.5 days where the manual process cost an hour, because a half-computerized process still needs somebody to type everything in.
  4. Assess loan applications under $250,000 to determine whether to fund them. An employee does this completely by hand in 15 days, does it with the help of the computer in 1 hour, or the computer does it automatically in 1 second. — This is the largest single saving in the table, falling from 15 days to 1 second, and it is the one activity where an actual funding decision was handed over to a machine rather than merely assisted by one.
  5. The committee decides on any loan over $250,000, which takes 15 days in the manual, technology-supported, and fully automated processes alike. — The table lists this immediately after the smaller-loan assessment because the two are alternative paths chosen by the size of the loan, which is why every total is given as a range. This is also the only row technology never touches.
  6. The applicant is notified. Manually generated letters go out in batches over a week, computer-assisted letters take a day, and the fully automated system notifies the applicant by email in 1 second. — A loan process is not finished when the decision is made but when the customer knows the decision, which is why a week of letter writing belonged in the manual total all along.

What the totals actually show

The headline is a fall from weeks to minutes, but three quieter facts in that table teach more.

  • One row never moves — the committee deciding any loan over $250,000 takes 15 days in all three processes, because none of the three columns changed who makes that decision.
  • That row is the ceiling — the fully automated process runs from 15 minutes to 15 days depending on loan size, and 15 days is exactly the committee’s figure, so the slowest automated loan is slow for a human reason.
  • One step gets worse first — entering data takes about an hour in the manual process, where applications stay on paper, but 2.5 days in the technology-supported one, where an employee keys in the batches. Half-computerizing can create work where none existed.

Automation compresses the parts of a process a machine is permitted to touch and leaves everything else where it was, which is why the fully automated column reports a range instead of a number.

Check yourself

Reading an automation table honestly

Four options, one best answer; read every explanation, including the ones for the answers you did not choose.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. Which activity in the loan table takes the same amount of time in the manual, technology-supported, and fully automated processes, and why does that matter?

  • A. Checking the application for errors, because a person still has to read every form no matter how it arrives — Error checking is one of the activities that changes the most across the table: an employee does it in batches over 2.5 days in the first two processes, while the computer does it in 1 second as the form is being completed. This would be right only if a person still had to read each form.
  • B. The committee decision on loans over $250,000, at 15 days in all three, because none of the three processes changed who makes that decision — correct. That row reads 15 days in every column, so the ceiling on the fully automated process — anywhere from 15 minutes to 15 days — is set by a decision reserved for people rather than by any limit of the technology.
  • C. Notifying the applicant, because a decision still has to reach a human being at the other end — Notification changes in all three columns: letters generated manually in batches take a week, computer-assisted letters take a day, and the fully automated system emails the applicant in 1 second. The letter is precisely the part that disappeared.
  • D. Inputting the data into the information system, because entering an application takes as long as it takes — This activity does change, and unusually it moves in both directions: about an hour of paper handling in the manual process, 2.5 days of batch keying in the technology-supported process, and no extra time at all once the customer completes the form online.

2. Entering application data takes 2.5 days in the technology-supported process but only about an hour in the manual one. What is the accurate reading of that?

  • A. The columns must be reversed, since a process that gained a computer should not take longer at that step than the paper one did — It is reasonable to expect every row to improve, but the table reports what it reports: applications are kept in paper form with handling time in the manual process, and an employee keys batches for 2.5 days in the technology-supported one. Partly computerizing a process can create work where none existed.
  • B. In the manual process nothing is keyed in at all, since applications stay on paper, while the supported process needs somebody to key batches in — correct. The hour in the manual column is handling paper, not data entry. Once a system exists but the customer is not filling it in directly, somebody has to type every application into it, and that work is done in batches.
  • C. The technology-supported process is checking each application far more thoroughly than the paper one ever did, and it is that extra scrutiny rather than the keying which takes the extra time — Checking the application for errors is a separate row of the table and takes 2.5 days in both the manual and the technology-supported processes, so the extra time here is not extra scrutiny. It is data entry that simply did not exist before.
  • D. The two processes handle different sizes of loan, so their times for this activity cannot fairly be compared — Loan size splits the assessment activity and the committee activity, not data entry, and the three columns describe three versions of one process rather than three kinds of loan. Every row is meant to be read straight across.

3. A manager says: “Our new system lets each reviewer handle three times as many files a day at a lower cost per file. That is all I need to know.” Which mentality is that, and what does the chapter say it leaves out?

  • A. An automating mentality, and it leaves out whether the process being sped up is a sound one — correct. Automating aims at efficiency — accomplishing goals faster, at lower cost, or with relatively little time and effort — and the chapter warns that automating a flawed process with no learning built in can mask the problem while multiplying its effects.
  • B. A learning mentality, and it leaves out how much the system costs the bank to run — A learning mentality uses past behavior and data to improve the business process itself, and this manager has asked about neither. Cost is also the one thing he did mention, so it cannot be what is missing from his account.
  • C. A strategic mentality, and it leaves out the return the investment will produce — A strategic mentality asks how a system helps achieve the organization’s chosen strategy and produces competitive advantage. Throughput and cost per file are efficiency measures, which the chapter places on the lowest rung rather than the strategic one.
  • D. An automating mentality, and it leaves out how many employees the change will let the bank redeploy — The first half is right and the second half is not. Redeploying employees more efficiently is part of the automating case, since the chapter names it as where the further cost savings come from, so adding that number makes the efficiency story fuller rather than answering whether the process being sped up is sound.

Organizational learning: doing things better

Organizational learning is the ability of an organization to use past behavior and data to improve its business processes. It builds on the automating mentality rather than replacing it: by analyzing the data created when a process was automated, you develop an improved understanding of the work process itself.

Return to the loan department. A computer-based loan processing system can track types of loan application by date, month, or season, and that single capability changes what a manager can do.

  • Trends become visible — the manager can see more auto loan applications arriving in the fall, for instance, and plan the timely staffing and training of loan department personnel around that shape.
  • Money can be planned — the manager can more efficiently manage the funds used to fulfill the loans, because demand stops being a surprise arriving one application at a time.
  • Patterns in the decisions appear — the manager can study which types of people apply at which times of year, the patterns of the decisions made, and the subsequent performance of those loans.

The test for learning is not how much data a system holds. It is whether the system creates data about the underlying business process that can be used to monitor, control, and change that process. Speed was efficiency; this is effectiveness, the extent to which goals or tasks are accomplished well. Used this way, a loan processing system sits at the managerial level of the organization.

What automating alone can hide. If the underlying process is flawed, a learning use of technology may help you detect the problem and change it: a pattern among accepted loans can separate low-performing from high-performing ones and prompt a change to the acceptance criteria. Automate the same process with no learning built in, and you never uncover the data that would show the process is bad.

The chapter puts numbers on it. Suppose the criteria are poor: they approve someone with a high level of debt as long as no payment has been late recently.

  • Working by hand, a reviewer might get through four applications a day and, because of those criteria, inadvertently accept about two bad applications a week.
  • Automate that same faulty process with no learning built in, and the reviewer might handle 12 applications a day, resulting in up to six bad applications accepted per week on average.
  • The technology served only to magnify the existing business problem, so automating a loan process requires sound underlying business processes or the errors rapidly increase.

Learning also scales outward. Increasing digital density, together with the ability to learn from data gathered through many interactions, can increase personalization, anticipation, and coordination, and the chapter’s example is Uber.

  • Personalization — Uber uses a rider’s past behavior to learn about her preferences and provide personalized ride recommendations.
  • Anticipation — the app uses data about riders’ and drivers’ locations and a host of other factors to anticipate surges in demand and change pricing accordingly.
  • Coordination — that same data is then used to coordinate riders and drivers so that the matching of supply and demand is optimized.

Plain efficiency is on that list too: the app automatically matches riders with drivers. One product doing all four at once shows why the three ways of adding value are not mutually exclusive.

Supporting strategy: doing things smarter

Automating and improving processes both have real advantages, but in most cases the chapter argues that the best way to use an information system is to support the organization’s strategy. Organizational strategy is a firm’s plan to accomplish its mission and goals and to gain or sustain competitive advantage over rivals.

That plan is made at the executive level through strategic planning: senior managers form a vision of where the organization needs to head, convert it into measurable objectives and performance targets, and craft a strategy to reach them. Someone with a strategic mentality then looks for ways to use information systems to achieve that strategy, and the chapter names four.

  • Innovating, because a genuinely new offering changes what the company sells rather than what it costs.
  • Streamlining operations, so that the savings serve the chosen plan instead of being an end in themselves.
  • Optimizing the supply chain, since what a firm can promise a customer depends on what its suppliers deliver.
  • Understanding customers better, because deep knowledge of a customer is not something a rival can simply buy.

This person still wants the benefits of automating and learning, and also looks for some strategic, competitive advantage from the system. The funding rule follows. In today’s business environment, if a proposed information system will not clearly deliver strategic value — help improve the business so it can compete better — while also helping people work smarter and save money, it is not likely to be funded.

Uber shows the top rung too. Using information systems for personalization, anticipation, and coordination is at the heart of its organizational strategy, is fundamental to its business model, and is essential to the organization’s long-term survival. What counted as learning one rung down counts as strategy here.

Why the top rung matters more than it used to. Rather than solely improving an organization’s efficiency, information systems now enable technology- and data-driven business model disruption: incumbents see their ways of working challenged by technology startups that approach the business in fundamentally different ways, grabbing market share and ultimately making existing business models obsolete.

A firm parked on the automating rung is getting steadily cheaper at doing something a newcomer may be about to make unnecessary.

Decide

Which ambition does this proposal actually serve?

Work the four decisions in order, and after each one compare every outcome before moving on.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

A hypothetical practice situation. You manage the loan department at a community bank, and four proposals land on your desk. For each one the question is not whether it is a good idea, but which of the three ways of adding value it actually serves — because that decides what you measure and who has to approve it.

Decision 1. A vendor offers to replace the paper application with a web form customers complete at home, with the computer checking for errors as they type and the data flowing straight into the loan system with no separate keying.

  • Automating. It compresses activities the bank already performs, and the payoff is time and cost. — the stronger call. Right. Completing the application from home via the web, error checking as the form is filled in, and no separate data entry step are exactly the moves in the fully automated column of the loan table. Judge it on efficiency: faster, cheaper, fewer errors.
  • Organizational learning, because the applications will now sit in a database where they can be analyzed. — Storing data and learning from data are different things. Nothing in this proposal creates information about the underlying process — who applies when, or how the approved loans later perform — and nobody has been given a report. A database is a precondition for learning, not learning itself.
  • Supporting strategy, because customers will prefer a bank they can apply to from the sofa. — Convenience may well matter to customers, but nothing here ties it to a plan to gain or sustain advantage over rivals, and any competitor can buy a comparable web form. Labelling an efficiency project strategic is how a project ends up measured against the wrong target.

Decision 2. The same vendor offers a reporting add-on. It charts application types by date, month, and season, and tracks how the loans that were approved perform afterwards. It will not speed up a single approval by one minute.

  • Nothing worth funding, because a report does not process an application. — This is the mistake the chapter warns about most directly. Without learning it is more difficult to uncover a bad process underneath the system, so the bank would simply run the existing process faster. Reports are how a process gets examined at all.
  • Automating, because reporting is one more clerical task the computer takes over. — Efficiency is measured in time and cost, and this proposal saves neither by its own description. Judging it on approval speed would kill a proposal whose whole purpose is to tell you something you do not currently know.
  • Organizational learning, because it creates data about the process that can be used to change the process. — the stronger call. Right. The manager can now plan timely staffing and training, manage the funds used to fulfill loans, and study the patterns in the decisions made and the later performance of those loans. That is using past behavior and data to improve a business process.

Decision 3. Now the pressure. A consultant reports a finding in this hypothetical bank: the department approves applicants carrying a high level of debt as long as they have not been late on any payments recently, and those loans are performing badly. The vendor’s throughput system would take each reviewer from four applications a day to twelve.

  • Deploy the throughput system now and revisit the acceptance criteria later, once the backlog is cleared. — This is the chapter’s cautionary arithmetic. A reviewer working by hand under those criteria might accept two bad applications a week; automated to twelve applications a day, the same faulty process yields up to six bad ones a week. The technology serves only to magnify the existing business problem.
  • Fix the acceptance criteria first and install the reporting that would have exposed them, then raise throughput. — the stronger call. Right. Automating a loan process requires sound underlying business processes, and the learning layer is what surfaces the pattern — distinguishing low-performing from high-performing loans over their lives and changing the acceptance criteria accordingly.
  • Keep technology out of this department altogether, since automation is what produced the bad loans. — Automation did not write the criteria; it would only multiply their effect. Removing the technology leaves a flawed process in place and slow, and leaves nobody any way to see the pattern that would identify the flaw.

Decision 4. The executive committee will fund one write-up of the same project. Three drafts of the case sit in front of you.

  • “It will cut our processing cost per application.” — True, and on its own insufficient. This is a pure efficiency case, and the chapter states that a proposed system that does not clearly deliver strategic value as well is not likely to be funded in today’s business environment.
  • “It gives us same-day decisions on small loans, built on application and performance data we already hold, and it lowers cost per application while doing it.” — the stronger call. Right. That reaches strategic value — helping the business compete better — while also helping people work smarter and saving money in the process, which is the combination the chapter says a proposal needs to be likely to be funded.
  • “Every competitor is digitizing their loan process, so we cannot afford to be the last one.” — This argues for parity, never for advantage, and it hands the bank’s technology plan to its rivals. It also tells the committee nothing about what the system would do here or how anyone would know whether it worked.

Reading the ladder correctly

Three ambitions, three payoffs, and three different questions to ask about any proposal.

  1. Faster — ask what this work costs today and what it will cost afterwards, because the payoff is efficiency, measured in time and money.
  2. Better — ask what the system will teach you about the process itself, because the payoff is effectiveness, measured in decisions that turn out well.
  3. Smarter — ask what the system lets you do that a rival cannot, because the payoff is competitive advantage, measured against competitors rather than last year.

Most good systems reach all three rungs, so the useful question is not which one a proposal is but how far up it reaches — and a project that answers only the first is an efficiency story told in a room that funds strategy.

Check yourself

Learning, strategy, and the funding test

Three questions on the upper two rungs; the wrong answers are the ones people actually give in meetings.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. What makes an information system produce organizational learning rather than mere speed?

  • A. It stores considerably more data than the system it replaced, since learning is a matter of volume — Volume by itself changes nothing, because an automated process also generates data and the question is what the data are about and whether anyone analyzes them. A bigger database nobody examines teaches an organization exactly as much as a smaller one.
  • B. It creates data about the underlying business process that can be used to monitor, control, and change that process — correct. That is the chapter’s own test, and the loan example shows it working: trends by season, the patterns of the decisions that were made, and the later performance of those loans, all of which can change how applications are evaluated.
  • C. It removes human judgment from the process, so that the decisions come out consistent — Consistency is one of the benefits claimed for automating, not for learning, and the chapter’s learning example depends on a manager reading trends and acting on them. A system that removed the judgment would leave nothing to improve.
  • D. It operates at the executive level of the organization rather than the managerial level — The chapter places the learning-focused loan processing system at the managerial level, where midlevel managers monitor and control operational activity. Which level a system serves is a separate question from whether it produces learning.

2. In the chapter’s illustration, a reviewer working by hand under flawed acceptance criteria handles four applications a day and inadvertently accepts about two bad ones a week. The same faulty process is automated so that the reviewer handles twelve a day. What follows?

  • A. Up to six bad applications a week are accepted, because the technology serves only to magnify the existing business problem — correct. Three times the throughput under the same bad criteria produces up to three times the bad loans, which is why automating a process requires sound underlying business processes or the errors rapidly increase.
  • B. Bad acceptances stay near two a week, because the criteria were the problem and the criteria did not change — The criteria did not change, which is why the failure rate per application does not improve — but the number of applications reviewed tripled, so the count of bad acceptances rises with it. Holding the total steady would require the system to catch what the criteria miss.
  • C. Bad acceptances fall, because a computer applies the criteria more consistently than a tired reviewer does — Consistency is a real benefit of automation, and it is beside the point when the rules being applied consistently are the wrong rules. Applying a flawed criterion identically every time simply produces flawed results faster.
  • D. It cannot be worked out from the illustration, because tripling the number of files reviewed says nothing about how many of the extra files were bad ones — The illustration deliberately holds the criteria and the applicant mix constant so that only throughput changes, which is how it arrives at up to six bad acceptances a week — three times the volume run through the same flawed rules, drawn as cumulative errors climbing as automation increases.

3. A project team proposes a system that will clearly cut cost per transaction but has no answer to how it helps the company compete. What does the chapter say about its prospects?

  • A. It will be funded, because cost reduction is the most reliable justification an information system can offer — Cost reduction is genuine value and it is the automating rung, which the chapter treats as the least of the three ways of adding value. It is not presented as the strongest case a proposal can make in today’s business environment.
  • B. It is not likely to be funded, because a proposal is expected to deliver strategic value as well as helping people work smarter and save money — correct. The chapter states the test directly: a system that will not clearly deliver strategic value, meaning help to improve the business so that it can compete better, while also helping people work smarter and save money, is not likely to be funded.
  • C. It is not likely to be funded, because a proposal is expected to show competitive advantage instead of cost savings — The conclusion is right and the reasoning is not. The chapter’s test asks for strategic value while also helping people to work smarter and save money, so cost savings are half of what a proposal is expected to show rather than the wrong sort of argument.
  • D. It will be funded, because the strategic value of a system only becomes clear once the system is running — Strategy is set in advance through strategic planning, in which executives form a vision, convert it into measurable objectives and performance targets, and craft a strategy to reach them. Discovering the strategic value afterwards is what the funding test exists to prevent.

Section 2–1c

Where to compete: analyzing competitive forces

Every company has more ideas than money. Before anyone can sensibly say which system to build, somebody has to say what is actually pressing on the business — and this section teaches the framework the chapter uses to say it.

Organizations struggle with identifying the best uses of their resources to execute their strategy. Some companies have a competitive advantage simply by being the first to enter a market, which is what the chapter calls a first-mover advantage. Most organizations never get that opening. They must compete within established industries, against firms that were already there and customers who already have habits.

Because every industry is different, organizations need to analyze the competitive forces within their industry to better understand where to focus their resources. An industry is simply the set of firms selling the same kind of product to the same kind of customer, and the analysis asks one narrow question: of everything squeezing this industry, which pressure is doing the most damage to us right now?

The five primary competitive forces

The framework the chapter uses is Porter’s (1979) notion of the five primary competitive forces. Read them as five separate directions that pressure can arrive from, rather than as five names to memorize.

  • Traditional rivals within your industry — the rivalry among competing sellers already inside your industry, which shows up as competition in price, product distribution, and service, because all of you are chasing the same buyers.
  • Threat of new entrants into your market — the chance that firms not competing with you today will start tomorrow, which brings increased capacity in the industry, reduced prices, and decreased market share for everyone already there.
  • Customers’ bargaining power — the ability of the people who buy from you to push back on your terms, which arrives as reduced prices, a need for increased quality, and demand for more services.
  • Suppliers’ bargaining power — the ability of the firms you buy from to set the terms of the relationship, which reaches you as increased costs and reduced quality in the very things you resell.
  • Threat of substitute products or services from other industries — a different kind of product meeting the same underlying need, which brings product returns from customers, decreased market share, and losing customers for life.

The chapter draws this as one circle and four boxes: rivalry among existing firms sits at the center, and bargaining power of buyers, threat of new entrants, threat of substitute products or services, and bargaining power of suppliers each press inward on it. The picture carries the model’s claim — five forces influence the profit potential of an industry, so a firm can be competently run and still earn very little if the forces around it are severe.
