Traditional rivals within your industry — Pressure from the firms already selling what you sell

Your firm (One of several established sellers) → Established rivals (Same goods, same suppliers, same buyers) → One pool of customers (Every sale won is a sale someone else lost) → The usual weapon (Price cuts that thin every margin at once)

  • What it is — the rivalry among competing sellers in your industry, meaning the firms that already sell what you sell to the customers you already have.
  • What the chapter says it implies — competition in price, product distribution, and service, so the fight is fought on what you charge, how the product reaches the buyer, and how well the buyer is treated.
  • What the internet did to it — an increase of competitors due to wider geographic reach, and customers who can more easily compare products, so competition focuses more on price than it used to.
  • Signal and relief — you know rivalry is the strong force when every promotion is matched within days and margin falls while volume holds, and the systems that help are the ones moving the contest off price, such as reliable stock information so the advertised item is actually on the shelf.

Threat of new entrants into your market — Pressure from firms that are not in your industry yet

Outsiders (Have money, want your customers) → Barriers to entry (Capital, scale, expertise, loyalty) → Entry happens (Increased capacity in the industry) → The result (Reduced prices, decreased market share)

  • What it is — the threat of potential new entrants into your industry, which is about companies that do not compete with you today and could begin to tomorrow.
  • What the chapter says it implies — increased capacity in the industry, reduced prices, and decreased market share, because more sellers are now chasing a pool of customers that did not grow to match.
  • What the internet did to it — reduced barriers to entry, since the internet reduces the difficulty of obtaining critical resources or entering new markets, so the money and infrastructure that once kept outsiders out no longer do.
  • Signal and relief — you know entrants are the strong force when the firms taking your customers were not in this business last year, and the systems that help are the ones building what a newcomer cannot buy quickly, such as years of customer history and reordering that runs on its own.

Customers’ bargaining power — Pressure from the people who hand you money

Your customers (Comparing alternatives in seconds) → Switching cost (Lower than it once was) → What they ask for (Lower price, higher quality, more service) → Your side (Terms set partly by the buyer)

  • What it is — the bargaining power that customers have within your industry, which is their ability to insist on better terms because walking away costs them little.
  • What the chapter says it implies — reduced prices, a need for increased quality, and demand for more services, so the buyer is effectively setting part of what you charge and what you must include.
  • What the internet did to it — wider choices for customers lead to lower switching costs and higher bargaining power of customers, so the comparison a buyer once had to drive across town to make now happens in a moment.
  • Signal and relief — you know buyer power is the strong force when shoppers leave over small price differences or a few large accounts squeeze you at renewal, and the systems that help give the customer something to lose by leaving, such as a loyalty record and offers built from that customer’s own history.

Suppliers’ bargaining power — Pressure from the firms you buy from

Few suppliers (Little real choice about whom to buy from) → Terms set upstream (Prices and lead times move on their schedule) → What reaches you (Increased costs and reduced quality) → The internet twist (Equal access, but suppliers reach more buyers too)

  • What it is — the bargaining power that suppliers have within your industry, which is their ability to raise prices or dictate terms because you have few alternatives.
  • What the chapter says it implies — increased costs and reduced quality, and both of those land in the product your own customer eventually sees, so supplier pressure is never only a purchasing problem.
  • What the internet did to it — companies have equal access to suppliers and it is easier to find new ones, but suppliers also have access to more potential buyers, so this is the one row where the influence genuinely runs both ways.
  • Signal and relief — you know supplier power is the strong force when few firms can supply what you need and nobody in your company can state what the firm buys in total, and the systems that help consolidate purchasing into one record and let qualified alternatives be compared side by side.

Threat of substitute products or services from other industries — Pressure from a different answer to the same need

The underlying need (The job the customer wants done) → Your industry’s answer (The product you happen to sell) → Another industry’s answer (Meets the same need a different way) → The damage (Returns, lost share, customers lost for life)

  • What it is — the potential for substitute products or services from other industries, where the customer satisfies the same need without ever entering your industry.
  • What the chapter says it implies — product returns from customers, decreased market share, and losing customers for life, which is the harshest wording in the table and the reason this force deserves attention it rarely gets.
  • What the internet did to it — new substitutes are created by the internet and other information technologies, so an industry can acquire a competitor that did not exist in any industry a few years earlier.
  • Signal and relief — you know substitutes are the strong force when discounts stop working and the whole category shrinks rather than your share of it, and the systems that help extend your offer into the substitute’s territory instead of defending the old one.

What each force does to a firm, and what the internet did to each force

Table 2.3 sets every force beside two things: what living with it implies for a firm, and how the internet has influenced it. Read the middle column as the damage and the right column as the reason the damage grew.

Competitive forceImplication for firmInfluence of the internet
Traditional rivals within your industryCompetition in price, product distribution, and serviceIncrease of competitors due to wider geographic reach; customers can more easily compare products, so competition focuses more on price.
Threat of new entrants into your marketIncreased capacity in the industry, reduced prices, and decreased market shareReduced barriers to entry, as the internet reduces the difficulty of obtaining critical resources or entering new markets.
Customers’ bargaining powerReduced prices, need for increased quality, and demand for more servicesWider choices for customers lead to lower switching costs and higher bargaining power of customers.
Suppliers’ bargaining powerIncreased costs and reduced qualityCompanies have equal access to suppliers; easier to find new suppliers; suppliers have access to more potential buyers.
Threat of substitute products or services from other industriesProduct returns from customers, decreased market share, and losing customers for lifeNew substitutes are created by the internet and other information technologies.

One pattern runs straight down the right-hand column: almost every entry describes the internet making a force stronger, not weaker. Wider reach adds competitors, easier comparison pushes the fight toward price, barriers to entry fall, switching costs drop, suppliers reach more potential buyers, and information technologies create substitutes that did not exist before.

The same technology that hands a firm new ways to compete hands its rivals, its customers, its suppliers, and firms in other industries exactly the same gift, which is why this analysis has to be redone rather than filed.

Check yourself

Naming the force

Four options, one best answer; the company situations are generic practice examples rather than reports about real firms, and every explanation is worth reading, including the ones for options you did not pick.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. A regional retailer has lost share to two companies that have sold the same goods in the same region for decades, and every promotion it runs is matched within a week. Which competitive force is at work?

  • A. Threat of new entrants into its market, because competitors are taking customers it used to keep — New entrants are firms that were not competing in this industry before, and the distinguishing fact here is that both competitors have been selling here for decades. It would be the right answer if the companies taking share had just arrived.
  • B. Traditional rivals within its industry, because the pressure comes from established sellers competing on price and service — correct. Rivalry among competing sellers in your industry shows up as competition in price, product distribution, and service, and matched promotions between long-established sellers is precisely that pressure.
  • C. Threat of substitute products or services, because customers are choosing something other than this retailer — A substitute meets the same need from another industry, so the customer never shops your industry at all. These shoppers are still buying the same goods, simply from a different seller of the same kind.
  • D. Customers’ bargaining power, because shoppers are the ones deciding to buy elsewhere — Buyer power is about customers forcing better terms because leaving costs them little, which usually shows up as pressure on price, quality, and services across all sellers. Here the visible actor is a competitor matching offers, not a buyer negotiating.

2. According to Table 2.3, what does the threat of new entrants imply for the firms that are already in an industry?

  • A. Increased costs and reduced quality in what those firms buy and resell — Increased costs and reduced quality is the implication the table gives for suppliers’ bargaining power, because supplier terms reach you through what you purchase rather than through who else is selling.
  • B. Product returns from customers, decreased market share, and losing customers for life — Product returns, decreased market share, and losing customers for life is the table’s implication for substitute products or services, and the phrase about customers lost for life is what makes that row distinct.
  • C. Increased capacity in the industry, reduced prices, and decreased market share — correct. A new entrant adds capacity to an industry whose customer pool did not grow, so the table lists increased capacity, reduced prices, and decreased market share.
  • D. Competition in price, product distribution, and service among the established sellers — Competition in price, product distribution, and service is the implication listed for traditional rivals, which is the force describing sellers already established inside the industry rather than newcomers.

3. Why does the chapter say organizations need to analyze the competitive forces within their industry at all?

  • A. Because a first-mover advantage protects most organizations, so the analysis simply confirms the position they already hold — A first-mover advantage does exist, and it belongs to companies that are first to enter a market. The chapter’s point is the opposite of protection for most firms: most organizations must compete within established industries.
  • B. Because every industry is different, so the analysis shows where a firm should focus its limited resources — correct. Organizations struggle with identifying the best uses of their resources, and because every industry is different, analyzing its forces is how a firm decides where to concentrate what it has.
  • C. Because the analysis produces a ranked shortlist of vendors, which is what a technology investment decision needs — The model helps determine which forces matter most and which kinds of technology could address them, and that knowledge then becomes the basis for identifying investments. Naming products is a later step, and doing it first inverts the sequence.
  • D. Because the analysis forecasts how much profit this particular firm will earn next year, which is the number a technology budget has to be built from — The chapter presents the five forces as influences on the profit potential of an industry, not as a forecast of one firm’s earnings. What the model produces is a judgment about which forces matter most and which technologies could address them, which guides where money goes rather than saying how much there will be.

Telling which force is the strong one

A single lost sale can be told as a story about almost any of the five, so the real skill is not reciting the list but choosing between them from what you can actually observe. Each force leaves a different fingerprint.

  • Rivalry is the strong force when — the companies taking your customers have sold in this industry for years, discounting is the only move anyone reaches for, and each promotion is matched within days while volume stays flat and margin falls.
  • New entrants are the strong force when — the companies taking your customers were not in this business last year, and nothing you hold — capital, scale, expertise, customer loyalty — would take a newcomer long to reproduce.
  • Customers’ bargaining power is the strong force when — buyers compare your price against alternatives in seconds and leave over small differences, or a few large accounts hold most of your revenue and use that leverage at every renewal.
  • Suppliers’ bargaining power is the strong force when — few firms can supply what you need, your costs rise or your quality slips on their schedule rather than yours, and nobody in your company can state what the firm buys in total.
  • Substitutes are the strong force when — price cuts stop working because the customers you lost are not shopping in your industry at all, and the whole category shrinks rather than just your share of it.

The confusion that costs the most is rivalry mistaken for new entrants. Both look like a competitor taking share, but rivalry says the industry is crowded and you must give buyers a reason beyond price, while an entrant says your barriers to entry are low and the answer is to build something a newcomer cannot assemble in a quarter.

The second confusion is a rival mistaken for a substitute. A rival sells what you sell, so a better price or a better shelf can win the customer back; a substitute meets the same need from another industry, so the departing customer never compares the two prices and your discount reaches nobody.

Sort

Which force does this situation signal?

Each situation below is a generic, hypothetical example written for practice, with no real company named; place it under the competitive force it points to, then read why it belongs there. Every force is used twice.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Traditional rivals within your industry — Pressure from sellers already established in your industry, fought on price, distribution, and service

  • Three chains that have sold the same products in the same city for thirty years now copy each other’s advertised prices within days, and none of them gains volume. — The pressure comes from sellers already established inside the industry, and it is being fought on price, which is exactly the implication the table lists for traditional rivals.
  • A delivery firm finds that its two oldest competitors have both extended free next-day service into the same counties it serves, and margins fall for all three. — Established competitors matching one another on service and distribution is rivalry within the industry, not the arrival of anyone new.

Threat of new entrants into your market — Firms that were not competing here before, adding capacity and cutting prices and share

  • A company that has never sold in this category announces it will begin next quarter, and the permits, equipment, and web storefront it needs turn out to be inexpensive and quick to obtain. — A firm from outside the industry is entering because barriers to entry are low, which adds capacity and pushes prices down for everyone already there.
  • Two startups launch this year selling what an established manufacturer sells, renting their computing and warehousing instead of building either one. — Renting critical resources is the reduced difficulty of obtaining them that the table attributes to the internet, and it is what makes these firms entrants rather than long-standing rivals.

Customers’ bargaining power — Buyers forcing lower prices, higher quality, and more services because leaving costs them little

  • Buyers arrive at the counter having already compared the price against four alternatives on their phones, and they say so before asking for a discount. — Wider choice and easy comparison lower switching costs and raise customers’ bargaining power, which shows up first as pressure on price.
  • Four large accounts provide most of a supplier’s revenue, and each renewal brings a demand for a lower rate plus added services at no charge. — Concentrated buyers can insist on reduced prices, increased quality, and more services, which is the implication the table lists for customers’ bargaining power.

Suppliers’ bargaining power — The firms you buy from setting terms, which reaches you as higher costs and lower quality

  • Only two firms in the world make the component a product depends on, and both raised prices this year while lengthening delivery times. — Few alternatives upstream let suppliers dictate terms, and the result reaches the firm as increased costs and reduced quality in what it sells.
  • Every branch of a chain phones in its own orders, so nobody at headquarters can say what the company buys in total or what it pays. — A firm that cannot see its own purchasing has no comparison and no leverage, which leaves supplier bargaining power unopposed even when alternatives exist.

Threat of substitute products or services from other industries — The same need met from outside your industry entirely, so the category itself shrinks

  • A tool retailer’s customers have stopped buying and now rent what they need from a service that belongs to no part of the retail tool industry. — The same need is met from another industry, so the customer never enters the tool retailer’s market and a lower shelf price would reach nobody.
  • A photo-printing firm sees returns rise and share fall as customers keep their pictures on screens instead, an option no printing company sells. — New substitutes created by information technologies produce exactly the table’s implications: product returns, decreased market share, and customers lost for life.

From the force to the technology, in that order

The chapter is explicit about what the model is for: Porter’s five-forces model of competition can help you determine which forces may be most important and which specific technologies could be used to address those forces, and you then use that knowledge as the basis for identifying particular investments. The sequence is the lesson — force first, technology second, investment third.

Each force therefore has a family of systems that answers it, so naming the force narrows the shopping list before anyone opens a vendor website.

  • Against traditional rivals — systems that move the contest off price, such as accurate stock information so the advertised item is genuinely on the shelf, because when competition focuses more on price, a firm that competes only on price keeps nothing it wins.
  • Against new entrants — systems that build what a newcomer cannot simply buy, such as accumulated customer history, saved orders, and reordering that runs on its own, because the internet already lowered the barriers that permits and capital used to provide.
  • Against customers’ bargaining power — systems that give a customer something to lose by leaving, such as a loyalty record and offers built from that household’s own purchases, because wider choice has already driven switching costs down.
  • Against suppliers’ bargaining power — systems that let a firm see and consolidate its own buying and compare qualified alternatives, such as one purchasing record covering every location, because equal access to suppliers only helps a company able to act on it.
  • Against substitutes — systems that extend your offer into the substitute’s territory, such as online ordering, dependable delivery windows, and subscriptions serving the same need the new way, because the table describes a customer lost this way as a customer lost for life.
Decide

Naming the force before naming the technology

Work through four decisions for this hypothetical company, and after each one read every outcome before moving on.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

This is a hypothetical practice situation, built only to give the analysis something to work on. A regional chain of bicycle shops is losing ground, leadership wants to spend on technology, and nobody has yet said what problem the spending is meant to solve. You are the analyst in the room, and your job in each decision is to name the force before anyone names a product.

Decision 1. Two chains that have sold bicycles in this region for thirty years now match every promotion the company runs within a week. Unit sales are flat across all three, and margins are falling for all three.

  • Traditional rivals within the industry, because established sellers are competing on price and service for the same customers — the stronger call. Right. Rivalry among competing sellers shows up as competition in price, product distribution, and service, and matched promotions with flat volume is the clean signal. Naming it this way rules out any initiative that would only cut price further.
  • Threat of new entrants, because competitors are taking sales the company used to make — Losing sales to a competitor does not by itself make that competitor an entrant. These two chains have been in the industry for thirty years, and an entrant is a firm that was not competing here before. The distinction changes the response: rivalry pushes you to compete on something other than price, while an entrant tells you your barriers to entry are low.
  • Customers’ bargaining power, because customers are choosing whichever store is cheapest that week — Buyer power is real in almost every retail market, so this is a reasonable instinct. What makes it the wrong call here is that the observable behavior belongs to the competitors: they are matching each promotion. Buyer power would be the answer if the evidence were customers negotiating or leaving over small price differences with no competitor action described.

Decision 2. Separately, a national online retailer that has never sold bicycles announces regional delivery. It owns no stores, rents its warehouse space, and needed only a contract and a website to begin.

  • Traditional rivals, because it is one more company selling bicycles in this market — It will indeed become a rival, but naming it that way loses the fact worth acting on. What the situation reveals is how little it cost this company to start, and that is a statement about barriers to entry rather than about crowded competition.
  • Threat of new entrants, because a firm from outside the industry started selling here with very little standing in its way — the stronger call. Right, and the evidence is the giveaway: no stores, rented warehousing, a website. The chapter attributes exactly this to the internet, which reduces the difficulty of obtaining critical resources or entering new markets, and the consequence for incumbents is increased capacity, reduced prices, and decreased market share.
  • Suppliers’ bargaining power, because the new retailer will compete for the same manufacturers’ output — Supplier power is about the terms the firms you buy from can impose on you, such as higher prices or longer lead times. A second buyer in the market can eventually tighten supply, but nothing in this situation describes a supplier changing its terms, so the force being signaled is entry.

Decision 3. Only two manufacturers make the frames the chain sells most. Both raised prices this year and lengthened lead times, and each shop still phones in its own orders, so no one can say what the chain buys in total.

  • Customers’ bargaining power, because the price increase will have to be passed to shoppers — Passing on a cost is a consequence, not a diagnosis. Buyer power would be the finding if customers were forcing terms on you; here the terms are being set on the other side of the business, before a customer is involved at all.
  • Suppliers’ bargaining power, because few firms supply what the chain needs and the chain cannot see its own buying — the stronger call. Right on both halves. Few alternatives upstream produce the table’s implication of increased costs and reduced quality, and a chain that cannot state its own volumes has no comparison to negotiate with. The initiative follows from the finding: one purchasing record across every shop, plus qualified alternate manufacturers.
  • Traditional rivals, because competitors buy from the same two manufacturers and face the same increase — Shared exposure is a genuine observation and a useful one, since a rival with the same problem will not undercut you easily. It still does not name the pressure, which is coming from upstream rather than across the street.

Decision 4. Finally, a pattern nobody expected: households that once bought a second bicycle are buying electric scooters and using ride-hailing apps instead. Discounts on bicycles have stopped producing visits, and the customers who leave do not come back for a sale.

  • Threat of substitute products or services from other industries, because the same need is being met outside the bicycle industry entirely — the stronger call. Right, and the two symptoms confirm it: discounts stopped working, and departing customers do not return. The chapter’s implication for this force is product returns, decreased market share, and losing customers for life, and it also notes that new substitutes are created by the internet and other information technologies. The response has to extend the offer rather than defend the old one.
  • Traditional rivals, because some other company is clearly getting the money these households used to spend — Money is leaving, but not to a bicycle seller. A rival sells what you sell, which is why a better price can win the customer back. That is precisely what stopped working here, and that failure is the clue.
  • Customers’ bargaining power, because customers are refusing to buy at the current price — It looks like price resistance, and price is where the symptom appears. The tell against it is that lower prices produce no visits at all: a buyer with strong bargaining power is still buying the product, just on better terms, while these households have left the category.

Turning a finding into something a decision maker can fund

A finding is not yet a proposal. Turning one into a recommendation an executive can approve takes four parts, and they have to arrive in this order.

  1. Name the force exactly, using one of the chapter’s five names, because a recommendation that opens with a technology has skipped the diagnosis and cannot be checked against anything.
  2. Give the observable evidence that this force is the strong one, such as promotions matched within a week or a sole supplier lengthening lead times, because evidence is what keeps a meeting from being two opinions.
  3. State the initiative concretely — not “improve our digital capabilities” but “one purchasing record covering all fourteen locations, with three qualified alternate suppliers” — because only a concrete initiative can be costed and built.
  4. Commit to a measure and a date, naming the number you expect to move and when you will check it, because a system with no defined result can be defended forever and judged never.
Say it in one sentence. Because [force] is the strongest force on us, shown by [evidence], we should build [initiative], and we will judge it by [measure] on [date]. If any slot is empty, what you are holding is a preference rather than a recommendation.
Explore

Vague recommendation, fundable recommendation

Open each card and read the two versions of the same proposal side by side, one force at a time; both versions are invented practice wording rather than quotations from any real company.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Answering established rivals · Traditional rivals within your industry

  • The vague version somebody actually says: “We need to be more competitive, so we should invest in better technology for our stores.”
  • The same idea written to be funded: “Rivalry is our strongest force: both long-standing competitors match our promotions within a week and volume is flat. We will put every location on one live stock record so advertised items are actually available, and we will judge it by out-of-stock rate on promoted items at the next quarterly review.”
  • What the rewrite added: A named force, the evidence behind it, one concrete system rather than a category of spending, and a number with a date attached to it.
  • Why a decision maker cares about the difference: The first sentence would justify almost any purchase, so nobody can later say whether the money worked. The second can be argued with before it is funded and judged after.

Answering a new entrant · Threat of new entrants into your market

  • The vague version somebody actually says: “An online seller has entered our market, so we need a digital transformation strategy.”
  • The same idea written to be funded: “New entrants are our strongest force: a company with no stores began selling here this quarter, which means our barriers to entry are low. We will build purchase history and automatic reordering for regular customers, judged by the share of revenue from repeat accounts at the end of two quarters.”
  • What the rewrite added: The reason the entrant matters, which is low barriers to entry rather than one more competitor, plus a system that accumulates something a newcomer cannot rent.
  • Why a decision maker cares about the difference: Digital transformation names no force and no measure, so it cannot be compared against any other proposal competing for the same money.

Answering customer bargaining power · Customers’ bargaining power

  • The vague version somebody actually says: “Customers keep asking for discounts, so we should launch a loyalty app like everyone else has.”
  • The same idea written to be funded: “Customer bargaining power is our strongest force: switching costs are near zero and we cannot identify a repeat buyer. We will record purchases by household and make offers from that history, judged by repeat-visit rate and average basket at the six-month review.”
  • What the rewrite added: The evidence that buyer power is high, the reason the system helps, which is raising the cost of leaving, and the two numbers that will show whether it did.
  • Why a decision maker cares about the difference: Copying a competitor argues for parity and never for advantage, and it hands the technology plan to whichever rival moved first.

Answering supplier bargaining power · Suppliers’ bargaining power

  • The vague version somebody actually says: “Our costs are up. We should renegotiate with suppliers and maybe get some new software for purchasing.”
  • The same idea written to be funded: “Supplier bargaining power is our strongest force: two manufacturers supply most of what we sell, prices rose, and no one can state our total volume. We will consolidate purchasing into one record across all locations and qualify three alternates, judged by average unit cost and lead time at the next quarterly review.”
  • What the rewrite added: The specific weakness giving suppliers their leverage, the two-part initiative that removes it, and a measure covering both cost and delivery time.
  • Why a decision maker cares about the difference: You cannot renegotiate from a position you cannot describe, so the vague version asks for a better outcome without changing anything that produced the current one.

Answering a substitute · Threat of substitute products or services from other industries

  • The vague version somebody actually says: “Sales are down across the category, so we should cut prices and advertise harder until it recovers.”
  • The same idea written to be funded: “Substitutes are our strongest force: discounts have stopped producing visits and departing customers do not return, because they are meeting the same need outside our industry. We will offer subscription servicing and same-week delivery so the need can be met through us, judged by subscription sign-ups and repeat service visits after two quarters.”
  • What the rewrite added: The recognition that the lost customer is not comparing prices at all, and an initiative aimed at the need rather than at the old product.
  • Why a decision maker cares about the difference: Discounting against a substitute spends margin on people who have already left, which is why this force is the one most often answered with the wrong instrument.
Two limits worth saying out loud. The analysis tells you where to aim, and it does not do more than that:
  • It names conditions, not products — the model identifies which forces matter most and which kinds of technology could address them, so a vendor shortlist assembled before the force is named is a set of products hunting for a problem.
  • The answer expires — the internet altered all five forces at once, so any diagnosis is a photograph of an industry on one particular day, and a firm that files it away ends up defending a position that has already moved.
Check yourself

The internet, the order of analysis, and the proposal

Three questions on what the internet did to the forces and on how the analysis is meant to be used; the recommendations quoted in the last question are invented practice examples, not real proposals.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. Table 2.3 records how the internet influenced each competitive force. Which entry belongs in the row for customers’ bargaining power?

  • A. Reduced barriers to entry, as the internet reduces the difficulty of obtaining critical resources or entering new markets — Reduced barriers to entry is the entry recorded for the threat of new entrants, because it describes how easily an outsider can now assemble what it needs to start competing.
  • B. Wider choices for customers lead to lower switching costs and higher bargaining power of customers — correct. More choice lowers what it costs a customer to switch, and a customer who can leave cheaply can insist on lower prices, higher quality, and more services.
  • C. Companies have equal access to suppliers, it is easier to find new suppliers, and suppliers reach more potential buyers — Equal access to suppliers and suppliers reaching more buyers is the entry for suppliers’ bargaining power, and it is the one row where the table describes influence flowing in both directions.
  • D. New substitutes are created by the internet and other information technologies — New substitutes created by information technologies is the entry for the threat of substitute products or services from other industries, which is about needs met outside your industry rather than terms demanded inside it.

2. A project team opens a meeting by proposing a specific new system, then looks for reasons the company needs it. What does the chapter’s use of the five-forces model say about that order?

  • A. It is efficient, because starting from a concrete system keeps the discussion practical rather than theoretical — Concreteness is worth something, but a concrete answer to an unnamed question cannot be evaluated. The practical version of this meeting states the force and the evidence first, and it stays just as concrete afterwards.
  • B. It is acceptable when the proposed system is one competitors already run, because a system already working in this industry has effectively been diagnosed for you — Matching competitors argues for parity rather than advantage, and it says nothing about which force is actually pressing on this firm. A rival’s purchase is evidence about the rival’s situation, not about yours.
  • C. It reverses the sequence: the model determines which forces matter most and which technologies address them, and that knowledge then identifies the investment — correct. The model helps determine which forces may be most important and which specific technologies could be used to address those forces, and that knowledge is then the basis for identifying particular investments.
  • D. It does not matter much, because the five forces describe conditions outside the firm while a technology decision is made inside it — The forces describe pressure from outside the firm, and that is exactly why they drive internal decisions: analyzing them is how an organization decides where to focus its limited resources.

3. Which of these is a recommendation a decision maker could actually fund and later judge?

  • A. “Buyer power is our strongest force, shown by shoppers who have compared our price before they reach the counter, so we should modernize the customer experience across every channel we operate, invest in the systems that would support it, and review our progress regularly through the coming year” — This one names a force and offers evidence for it, which already puts it ahead of most proposals. Modernizing the customer experience across every channel is a category of spending rather than an initiative, and reviewing progress regularly names neither a number nor a date.
  • B. “Our three largest competitors have all installed new store systems in the past year and customers have noticed the difference, so we should adopt comparable systems this year rather than keep falling behind them on service” — This names no force at all, and its evidence is about what rivals have bought rather than about what is actually pressing on this firm. It justifies parity with competitors, and a plan built from rivals’ purchases can never do better than match them.
  • C. “Supplier power is our strongest force, shown by two manufacturers raising prices while no one here can state our total volume; we will consolidate purchasing into one record and qualify three alternate suppliers, judged by unit cost and lead time at the next quarterly review” — correct. It names the force, gives observable evidence, states a concrete two-part initiative, and commits to specific measures with a review date, so it can be argued with before funding and judged afterwards.
  • D. “Substitutes are our strongest force, shown by discounts that no longer bring departed customers back to us, so we need to become a more innovative and data-driven organization able to respond to whatever the market does next” — The force and the evidence are right, and failed discounts really are the signal for substitutes, so the diagnosis half of this proposal is sound. Innovative and data-driven then describes a wish rather than a system, so nothing here could be costed, built, or checked afterwards.

Section 2–1d

How to compete: strategy, resources, and the value chain

The five forces tell a company where the pressure in its industry comes from. They never say what to do about it. This section is the other half: once a company knows what it is up against, how does it choose what to be good at, and which systems are worth the money?

Choosing a generic strategy

To achieve superior returns, a company has to position itself within the industry it operates in so that it can counter the effects of the five forces. Figure 2.12 lays the common positions out as a grid built on two questions: is the differentiating attribute low cost or uniqueness, and is the market focus narrow or broad?

Three named strategies sit inside that grid, and each is a promise the company’s later spending has to keep.

  • Low-cost leadership strategy — the organization offers the best prices in its industry on its goods and/or services, which is how the chapter describes Walmart.
  • Differentiation strategy — the organization tries to provide better products or services than its competitors, as Porsche, Nordstrom, and IBM do, so the customer is paying for something rivals have not matched.
  • Best-cost provider strategy — a middle-of-the-road position offering products or services of reasonably good quality at competitive prices, as Dell does, placed at the center of the figure where the quadrants overlap.

Differentiation comes in two widths: a company might aim it broadly at many types of consumers, or focus on one segment, as Apple did for years with high-quality computers for home and educational markets. Crossing that choice with the two axes produces the five general types the figure names.

Type of strategyWhere it sits in Figure 2.12What the customer is promisedChapter’s example
Overall low-cost leadershipBroad market, low costThe best prices in the industry, for everyoneWalmart
Broad differentiationBroad market, uniquenessBetter products than competitors, for many types of consumersPorsche, Nordstrom, IBM (the chapter names no width)
Focused low-cost leadershipNarrow market, low costThe lowest price inside one slice of the marketThe chapter names none
Focused differentiationNarrow market, uniquenessSomething better, built for one segmentApple, for years, in home and educational computers
Best-cost providerThe center, where the quadrants overlapReasonably good quality at competitive pricesDell
Match

Generic strategies and the situations that suit them

Each situation below is a generic, hypothetical one written for practice, with no real company named. Pair it with the general type of strategy in Figure 2.12 that fits it.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Overall low-cost leadership
A company selling everyday goods to nearly every kind of buyer, whose customers choose a store mainly on price A low-cost leadership strategy means offering the best prices in the industry on goods and/or services, and the chapter names Walmart as the example. The market is broad and the differentiating attribute is cost.
Broad differentiation
A company whose buyers come from many different segments and who pay for products or services that are better than the alternatives A differentiation strategy means trying to provide better products or services than competitors, as Porsche, Nordstrom, and IBM do, and here the differentiation is aimed broadly at many different types of consumers.
Focused differentiation
A company that deliberately serves one segment of buyers and gives that segment higher quality than anyone else offers it The chapter describes exactly this width of differentiation: Apple focused for many years on high-quality computers for the home and educational markets rather than aiming at every buyer.
Focused low-cost leadership
A company competing on price, but only inside one narrow slice of the market rather than across the whole industry Figure 2.12 names this as one of the five general types, in the narrow-market and low-cost quadrant. The chapter names no company for it, so you have to recognize it by its position rather than by an example.
Best-cost provider strategy
A company offering reasonably good quality at competitive prices, sitting on purpose between the price players and the premium ones This is the middle-of-the-road strategy the chapter describes, with Dell as the example, and the figure places it at the center where all the quadrants overlap.

A chosen middle is not the same as no middle. The best-cost provider position is a real strategy with a real promise: reasonably good quality at competitive prices, held steady.

A company that has never said whether it competes on price or on uniqueness, and for whom, has no test to apply to the next proposal, so the budget goes to whoever argues best.

Resources and capabilities: the second lens

Position tells the market what to expect; it does not make the company able to deliver. Whichever generic strategy an organization pursues, it must have resources and/or capabilities superior to those of its competitors in order to gain or sustain a competitive advantage.

  • Resources — the organization’s specific assets used to achieve cost or product differentiation from competitors, such as proprietary technology, brand equity, or a loyal and established customer base.
  • Capabilities — the organization’s ability to leverage those resources in the marketplace, such as design quality or efficient operations, so a capability is something a company does rather than something it owns.
  • Distinctive competencies — what resources and capabilities produce together, such as innovation, agility, quality, or low cost, and they are what makes the product valuable to customers relative to competitors.
  • Superior value creation — what the chain is aiming at, which occurs when an organization can provide products at a lower cost or with superior, differentiated benefits to the customer.

Figure 2.13 draws that as a chain: resources and capabilities feed distinctive competencies, competencies produce a cost or differentiation advantage, and that advantage earns the name sustained competitive advantage. An asset nobody uses well never becomes a competency.

What separates a lasting advantage from a temporary one is comparative: the resources and capabilities have to be superior to those of competitors, not merely present. Anything a rival can order this afternoon fails that test.

Figure 2.14 gives eight sources of competitive advantage, one company each.

Source of advantageCompany the chapter names
QualityToyota
ServiceIBM
User baseFacebook
ProprietaryCoca-Cola
InnovationApple
BrandNike
ValueNintendo
DataUber

Several of those sources are informational rather than physical. For many organizations, the chapter says, information systems are at the heart of the different resources, capabilities, or distinctive competencies.

Strategy, resources, and capabilities

Four options, one best answer; read every explanation, including the ones for the answers you did not pick. Any company described in a question is hypothetical unless the chapter names it.

1. Which description matches the best-cost provider strategy as the chapter presents it?

  • A. Offering the best prices in the industry on goods and/or services, the way the chapter describes Walmart — That is the low-cost leadership strategy, whose whole promise is price. It occupies the low-cost end of the horizontal axis rather than the center of the figure, and the chapter names Walmart for it.
  • B. Providing products or services of reasonably good quality at competitive prices, the way the chapter describes Dell — correct. The chapter calls this a middle-of-the-road strategy, names Dell as the example, and Figure 2.12 places the best-cost provider at the center where all four quadrants overlap.
  • C. Providing better products or services than competitors and aiming them at one segment of consumers, as Apple did in home and educational computers — That is focused differentiation: the differentiating attribute is uniqueness and the market focus is narrow. Quality is aimed at one segment rather than balanced against price for everybody.
  • D. Providing better products or services than competitors and aiming them broadly at many different types of consumers rather than at one segment — That is broad differentiation. It shares the uniqueness end of the axis with focused differentiation and differs only in how wide the market is, so neither one describes a company balancing quality against price. The chapter names Porsche, Nordstrom, and IBM for differentiation without saying which width each pursues.

2. Which of these is a capability rather than a resource, as the chapter defines the two words?

  • A. Proprietary technology the company owns and no competitor can use — Proprietary technology is one of the chapter’s own examples of a resource: a specific asset the organization holds and uses to achieve cost or product differentiation.
  • B. Brand equity built up with customers over many years — Brand equity is also listed as a resource. It is something the organization possesses, and possessing it says nothing yet about how well the organization puts it to work.
  • C. Efficient operations, meaning the company runs its processes better than others do — correct. Capabilities reflect the organization’s ability to leverage its resources in the marketplace, and the chapter offers design quality and efficient operations as the examples.
  • D. A loyal and established customer base that keeps returning — A loyal and established customer base is the third resource the chapter lists. Turning that base into repeat revenue would be a capability; having the base is an asset.

3. A company holds years of purchase data and a well-known brand, but no department can agree on how to use either, and nothing the company does with them is better than what rivals do. What does the chapter’s framework say about its position?

  • A. It already has a sustained competitive advantage, because owning data and a brand is what the chapter means by resources — Resources alone do not finish the chain. The organization must have resources and/or capabilities superior to those of its competitors, and superiority is judged by what reaches the market, not by what sits in the building.
  • B. It has resources but not the capabilities to leverage them, so no distinctive competency and no advantage follows yet — correct. Capabilities are the ability to leverage resources in the marketplace; without them the resources never become distinctive competencies, and Figure 2.13 runs from competencies to a cost or differentiation advantage to a sustained advantage.
  • C. It has capabilities but no resources, since knowing about customers counts as ability rather than as an asset — This reverses the two definitions. Data and a brand are assets the organization holds, which makes them resources; the ability to use them well would be the capability that is missing here.
  • D. It has achieved superior value creation, because customers can recognize the brand more easily than they recognize rivals — Superior value creation occurs when an organization can provide products at a lower cost or with superior, differentiated benefits to the customer. Recognition without a better cost or a better benefit does not meet that definition.

Analyzing the value chain

To find where inside the company a system would actually pay, managers use value chain analysis. Think of an organization as a big input/output process: supplies are purchased and brought in, integrated into products and services it markets, sells, and distributes, with customer service after the sale.

Throughout that process, opportunities arise for employees to use information systems to add value by acquiring supplies more effectively, improving products, and selling more products. That set of activities is the value chain. Value has a plain meaning here: the analysis asks what each activity adds for the customer and what it costs to do.

Value chain analysis is the process of analyzing an organization’s activities to determine where value is added to products and/or services and what costs are incurred for doing so. It runs in three steps.

  1. Draw the chain first — flesh out each activity, function, and process where value is or should be added and performance can be improved, because nobody improves a step that was never written down.
  2. Then find the costs — determine the costs in each area and the factors that drive them or make them fluctuate, because a cost with no known driver can be complained about but not managed.
  3. Then decide what to optimize — determine which activities need optimizing to improve performance, cut costs, and gain or sustain competitive advantage, which is the first point at which naming a system is reasonable.

The chain has two halves. The primary activities run left to right as a flow, because a product passes through them on its way to a customer. The support activities are bands drawn underneath, because they serve every stage rather than one.

ActivityHalf of the chainWhat the name covers
Inbound logisticsPrimaryReceiving what was purchased and getting it inside, before any of it is sellable
OperationsPrimaryIntegrating supplies into the products and services the customer buys
Outbound logisticsPrimaryDistributing the finished product or service out to the customer
Sales and marketingPrimaryMaking customers aware and giving them a reason to choose it
ServicePrimaryLooking after the customer after the sale
Administration and firm infrastructureSupportRunning the organization as a whole, billable to no single product
Human resourcesSupportWho is hired, trained, and scheduled to do the work above
Product research and development, technology, and systems developmentSupportImproving the product and building the systems the chain runs on
ProcurementSupportThe buying decision itself, not the physical receiving of goods

The model was built for manufacturing but applies to service industries too, sometimes with different activities. The chapter walks through a hotel, and that mapping repays slow reading.

  • Inbound logistics — receiving supplies, and handling reservations, because a booking is an input that arrives and must be held until it is used.
  • Operations — checking guests in or out, cleaning rooms, and preparing breakfast, since a clean, ready, served room is the product itself.
  • Outbound logistics — work the chapter says might be performed by the hotel’s catering or event service, because that is where the finished offering reaches the guest.
  • Sales and marketing — promoting the hotel and attracting business meetings and conventions, so rooms are booked before they can be cleaned.
  • Service — the activities performed after the guest has left, such as registering or resolving guest complaints.

Other organizations may lack inbound and/or outbound logistics altogether and may classify activities differently, while the supporting activities are likely to resemble those of other organizations. The chain is a tool for analysis, not a law.

Interactive diagram

The value chain, one half at a time

Step through the primary activities, then the support activities, then the places information systems add value along the chain.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Primary activities — The flow a product travels, from arriving supplies to the customer after the sale

Supplies come in (Inbound logistics) → Inputs become the product (Operations) → The product goes out and is sold (Outbound logistics, sales and marketing) → The buyer is looked after (Service)

  • Think of the organization as a big input/output process: supplies are purchased and brought in, integrated into products and services, marketed, sold, and distributed to customers, with customer service provided after the sale.
  • The five primary activities the chapter names in Figure 2.15 are inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, sales and marketing, and service, drawn in that order and connected by arrows.
  • The model was initially created to focus on manufacturing, but it also applies to service industries, sometimes with different activities being performed — in a hotel, inbound logistics covers receiving supplies and handling reservations, while operations covers checking guests in or out, cleaning rooms, and preparing breakfast.
  • Some organizations may lack inbound and/or outbound logistics entirely, and different activities may be classified differently, so the chain is a tool for identifying and analyzing what a particular organization actually does.

Support activities — The bands drawn underneath the whole flow, because they serve every stage rather than one

Administration and firm infrastructure (Running the organization as a whole) → Human resources (Hiring, training, and scheduling people) → Product R and D, technology, systems development (Improving the product and building the systems) → Procurement (Choosing suppliers and terms)

  • Figure 2.15 draws these as layers beneath the primary flow rather than as steps inside it — administration and firm infrastructure at the top, then human resources, then product research and development, technology, and systems development, then procurement — which is the visual way of saying that their payoff appears spread across all five primary activities instead of in one of them.
  • Whereas the primary activities may differ from one organization to another, the chapter notes that the supporting activities are likely to resemble those of other organizations.
  • Procurement is the decision about whom to buy from and on what terms; inbound logistics is what happens to the goods after that decision is made. Filing one under the other sends a recommendation to the wrong department.
  • The figure shows these bands supported by a private cloud and computer-aided design systems, and names a financial decision support system, an employee self-service portal, and a supply chain management system alongside them.

Where information systems add value — The analysis that decides which system to fund, and the systems the figure places along the chain

Draw the chain (Every activity where value is or should be added) → Find the costs (And the factors that drive or move them) → Choose what to optimize (Performance, cost, advantage) → Name the system by its activity (Not by the technology it uses)

  • Because information systems can automate and optimize many activities along the value chain, using them has become one of the primary ways that organizations improve their value chains.
  • Many organizations use the internet to connect businesses with one another electronically so that they can exchange orders, invoices, and receipts online in real time, which removes waiting from the seams between activities.
  • Organizations use various social media such as blogs, X, or Instagram to connect with their customers, and Figure 2.15 shows supply chain management and customer relationship management systems, along with the website, Facebook, and X, laid across the primary flow.
  • Value chain analysis is the process of analyzing an organization’s activities to determine where value is added to products and/or services and what costs are incurred for doing so — which is why the costs come before the shopping.

The role of information systems in value chain analysis

Because information systems can automate and optimize many activities along the chain, using them has become one of the primary ways organizations improve their value chains. Figure 2.15 places ordinary systems on a sample chain.

  • Systems laid across the primary flow — supply chain management and customer relationship management systems run along the whole flow, with the website, Facebook, and X, because those touch goods coming in and customers going out.
  • Connections between businesses — many organizations use the internet to connect electronically, exchanging orders, invoices, and receipts in real time, which takes waiting out of the seams between activities.
  • Connections with customers — organizations use social media such as blogs, X, or Instagram to connect with customers, so marketing and service stop being one-way announcements.
  • Systems beneath the support bands — the figure shows a private cloud and computer-aided design systems supporting those bands, and names a financial decision support system, an employee self-service portal, and a supply chain management system alongside them.

Name a proposed system by the activity it improves. “A better app” cannot be argued about; “a system that cuts the cost driver in inbound logistics” can be costed, funded, or refused.

Sort

Which primary activity does this system improve?

Each proposed system below is hypothetical; place it in the primary activity it would strengthen, using the chapter’s own mapping of the value chain onto a hotel.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Inbound logistics — in a hotel, receiving supplies and handling reservations

  • A reservation system that records each booking as it is made and holds the right room for the right night — The chapter puts handling reservations in inbound logistics for a hotel, alongside receiving supplies, because a booking is an input that arrives and has to be held until it is used.
  • A delivery portal where linen and food suppliers confirm what will reach the loading dock tomorrow morning — Receiving supplies is the other half of inbound logistics in the chapter’s hotel example, and this system manages what arrives rather than who was chosen to send it.

Operations — in a hotel, checking guests in or out, cleaning rooms, preparing breakfast

  • A housekeeping tablet that routes cleaners room by room and marks each room ready for the next guest — Cleaning rooms is named as a day-to-day operations activity, because a clean and ready room is part of the product the guest is buying.
  • A check-in screen that issues a key card without the guest waiting in line at the front desk — Checking guests in or out is listed under operations for a hotel, since it is part of turning inputs into the service the customer receives.

Outbound logistics — in a hotel, work that might be performed by the catering or event service

  • A catering scheduler that assigns staff, food, and equipment to each function the hotel’s event service delivers — The chapter says outbound logistics activities in a hotel might be performed by the hotel’s catering or event service, so a system that plans those functions belongs here rather than under room operations.
  • A tracking system that follows each event order from the kitchen to the room where the function is being held — Outbound logistics is the half of the flow that gets the finished offering to the customer, and in the chapter’s hotel example that work sits with the catering or event service.

Sales and marketing — in a hotel, promoting it and attracting business meetings and conventions

  • A campaign tool that measures which advertisement brought more convention organizers to the booking page — Attracting business meetings and conventions is listed under sales and marketing for a hotel, and measuring what attracts them is part of the same activity.
  • A pipeline tracker showing which large organizations are choosing a host city next year so the sales team can approach them — Promoting the hotel and pursuing group business is sales and marketing, because the work is creating awareness and a reason to choose this hotel.

Service — in a hotel, the activities after the guest has left, such as resolving complaints

  • A complaint log that registers each issue a departed guest reports and tracks it until it is resolved — The chapter names registering or resolving guest complaints as customer service activities performed after the guest has left.
  • A follow-up system that flags a guest whose last stay went badly so the next stay is handled with extra care — Looking after the customer after the sale is the service activity, and this system acts on a past stay rather than on the current one.

The technology/strategy fit

If a system does things faster and saves money, who cares whether it matches the strategy? Money and time are limited. If money grew on trees an organization would build every system it could imagine; in reality it acquires only those adding the most value, meaning the ones that help it automate and learn and carry strategic value.

Managers once treated information systems as a necessary service, a necessary evil, and a distasteful expense to be minimized. Successful managers now treat them as a competitive asset to be nurtured and invested in, an enabler of opportunities and a mechanism for executing the business model.

The test has a name, business/IT alignment, and organizations try to maximize it: in most cases they do not want systems that fail to match the strategy, even when those systems offer real automating and learning benefits.

The chapter’s illustration is blunt. A firm whose strategy is overall low-cost leadership probably does not want a system that differentiates its products on high quality, because a low-cost leader values the investments that drive costs down over those that do not.

Two qualifications stop this from becoming a rule applied without thinking.

  • Strategic necessity — organizations sometimes have no choice about investments that may or may not coincide with their overall strategy, and the chapter calls such an investment a strategic necessity: something the organization must do to survive.
  • The change comes with the system — implementing a new or innovative system is not sufficient by itself, because any significant implementation needs commensurate, significant organizational change in processes, roles, culture, and mindset.

Underneath it all is a floor: an information system can be only as effective as the business model it serves, and bad business models cannot be overcome by good information systems.

Sequence

From competitive forces to a funded system

Put the eight steps of a full analysis into the order the chapter builds them, from the industry outside to the money inside.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Each step narrows the question the next one answers. Run them out of order and you end up with a technology looking for a problem.

  1. Analyze the competitive forces in the industry to see where the pressure on profit is actually coming from. — Given that every industry is different, organizations need to analyze the competitive forces within their industry to better understand where to focus their resources, so this comes before any choice about how to compete.
  2. Choose the position the company will compete from: low-cost leadership, differentiation, or the best-cost provider middle, broad or focused. — To achieve superior returns, a company positions itself within its industry to counter the effects of the five forces, and that position is what everything afterwards has to serve.
  3. Take stock of the resources and capabilities the company holds, and ask whether they are superior to those of competitors. — No matter which generic strategy is chosen, the organization must have resources and/or capabilities superior to those of its competitors in order to gain or sustain a competitive advantage.
  4. Draw the value chain, fleshing out each activity, function, and process where value is or should be added and where performance can be improved. — The chapter makes drawing the chain the first move of value chain analysis, because an activity nobody has written down cannot be measured or improved.
  5. Determine the costs within each area of the diagram, along with the factors that drive those costs or cause them to fluctuate. — Costing comes second in value chain analysis, and knowing the driver behind a cost is what separates a number you can act on from a number you can only report.
  6. Decide which activities need to be optimized to improve performance, cut costs, and ultimately gain or sustain competitive advantage. — This is the third step of value chain analysis and the first moment at which naming a system is reasonable, because now the target activity is known.
  7. Test the candidate system against the strategy, keeping the ones that match and setting aside the ones that do not, unless the investment is a strategic necessity. — Organizations try to maximize business/IT alignment and in most cases do not want systems that fail to match the strategy, though a strategic necessity is something the organization must do to survive regardless.
  8. Plan the organizational change that has to accompany the system, then take the proposal for funding with its value stated plainly. — Merely implementing a system is not sufficient; there must be commensurate, significant organizational change, and most companies are willing to spend only when they can see clear, significant value.

Position first, then the resources and capabilities that make it deliverable, then the value chain activity where a system would pay, then the alignment test a proposal must survive to be funded.

1. A hotel is deciding where an employee self-service portal for scheduling and time off belongs on its value chain. Where does it sit?

Operations, because scheduling decides who is available to clean rooms and serve breakfast — Operations covers the day-to-day activities of checking guests in or out, cleaning rooms, and preparing breakfast. Scheduling touches operations, but it touches the other primary activities just as much, which is the signature of a support activity.
  • B. Human resources, a support activity, because it serves the staffing of every stage rather than one stage — correct. Human resources is one of the support bands Figure 2.15 draws beneath the whole flow, and the figure lists an employee self-service portal among the systems it places on that chain.
  • C. Inbound logistics, because staff time is one of the inputs the hotel receives and consumes — Inbound logistics is about goods and, in a hotel, reservations arriving and being handled. Treating employees as arriving inventory stretches the definition past the one the chapter uses.
