Service, because the portal exists to serve the people who work at the hotel — Service in the value chain means looking after the paying customer after the sale, such as registering or resolving guest complaints. The word service in ordinary speech is broader than the activity the model names.

2. A firm pursuing overall low-cost leadership is offered a system that would help it differentiate its products on high quality, and the system genuinely automates work and produces useful learning. What does the chapter say the firm should conclude?

  • A. Fund it, because a system that automates work and produces learning has already justified itself — Automating and learning benefits are real but not sufficient. Organizations are constrained by time and money to acquire only the systems that add the most value, meaning those that automate and learn and also carry strategic value.
  • B. Fund it, because a company that can differentiate on quality should abandon a low-cost position — Nothing in the situation says the low-cost position was wrong. A single system offer is a weak reason to abandon a position the company has aligned its costs, suppliers, and customer promise around.
  • C. Probably decline it, because organizations do not want systems that fail to match the strategy even when they offer automating and learning benefits — correct. The chapter says an organization probably does not want a system that differentiates products on high quality when its strategy is overall low-cost leadership, because a low-cost leader values the investments that drive costs down.
  • D. Declare it a strategic necessity, because any system a competitor might also buy is something the firm has to have in order to stay level, whatever it does or does not do for the strategy — A strategic necessity is something the organization must do to survive, not a label for any purchase a competitor might also make. Applying it this loosely would let it excuse every proposal on the table.

3. Which statement about implementing a new information system matches the chapter?

  • A. A well-chosen system can carry a weak business model, which is why the system decision matters more than the model — The chapter states the reverse: an information system can be only as effective as the business model that it serves, and bad business models cannot be overcome by good information systems.
  • B. Implementing the system is the hard part, so processes, roles, and culture can be left as they are afterwards — This inverts the caution. Merely choosing and implementing new or innovative systems is not sufficient to gain or sustain competitive advantage, and the change in processes, roles, culture, and mindset is part of the work rather than an afterthought.
  • C. Any significant implementation needs commensurate organizational change, and the system can be only as effective as the business model it serves — correct. Both cautions are stated: significant implementations require commensurate, significant organizational change, and a system can be only as effective as the business model it serves.
  • D. Change the processes, roles, and culture only after the system has run long enough to show where it falls short, since reorganizing first would be premature — The chapter puts the change alongside the implementation rather than after it: in any significant implementation there must be commensurate, significant organizational change, and waiting leaves the system dropped into an organization that still works the old way.

Section 2–2a

Business models in the digital world

Before anyone can argue about which technology a company should buy, the company has to be able to say plainly how it makes its living: who it serves, what it offers them, how the offer reaches them, and where the money comes from and where it goes. That plain statement is the business model, and technology investments have to be aligned with it.

What a business model actually is

A business model is a summary of a business’s strategic direction that outlines how the objectives will be achieved. It specifies the value proposition as well as how a company will create, deliver, and capture value, and it identifies nine things: customer segments, value propositions, channels, customer relationships, revenue streams, key resources, key activities, key partners, and cost structure.

Three verbs sit inside that definition, and it is worth slowing down on them, because a company can be good at one and fail at another.

  • Create value — make something somebody genuinely wants, because a repaired bicycle, an hour of streaming, or a ride across town is worth something to the person receiving it and nothing at all if no one wants it.
  • Deliver value — get that something into the customer’s hands, because a repair nobody can reach and an app nobody can install create value that never arrives.
  • Capture value — keep a share of it as income, because a company that creates and delivers value but never captures any of it runs out of money while its customers are still delighted.

The chapter compresses the whole idea into five questions. Walk them in this order, because each answer narrows the next one.

  1. What does a company do? Name the product or service in words a stranger would understand, because everything below is meaningless until this is settled.
  2. How does a company uniquely do it? Say what makes this offer different from the one next door, because a model that could describe any competitor is not a strategy.
  3. What are the key resources and activities needed? List the assets you must have and the work you must perform, because promises you cannot staff or equip are not promises.
  4. In what way, or ways, does the company get paid for doing it? Say who hands over money and when, because the customer and the payer are not always the same person.
  5. What are the costs involved? Add up what running all of the above consumes, because a model that earns well and spends more is still a failing model.

Those answers are not an academic exercise. How a company answers these questions dictates how and where information systems investments can be utilized to execute a competitive strategy and sustain an advantage over competitors. Generally speaking, anything that has to do with the day-to-day functioning of the organization is part of its business model, and information systems can be used to support and execute many aspects of it.

Check yourself

What a business model is for

Four options, one best answer; read every explanation, including the ones for options you did not pick.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. Which statement best describes what a business model is?

  • A. A summary of a business’s strategic direction that specifies the value proposition and how the company will create, deliver and capture value — correct. That is the chapter’s definition, and the three verbs matter: creating value, delivering it, and capturing some of it are separate achievements that a company can succeed and fail at independently.
  • B. The set of information systems a company has purchased or built over the years, listed out with the vendor, the annual cost, the renewal date and the department that uses each one — That is an inventory of technology, and it answers none of the five questions. The chapter’s point runs the other way: how a company answers the business model questions is what dictates where information systems investments can usefully go.
  • C. A forecast of the revenue and profit the company expects to report over the coming financial year, broken down by product line — A revenue forecast is a number the model produces, not the model itself. Two companies could forecast identical revenue while serving different customers through different channels at wildly different costs.
  • D. A chart showing who reports to whom, so that responsibility for each part of the business can be traced to a named manager — An organization chart shows reporting lines and responsibility, which is genuine and useful information about a company’s structure. It says nothing about who the customers are, why they would choose this firm, or how the firm gets paid.

2. Someone says: “Our business model is simple — we sell coffee.” What is missing from that answer?

  • A. Nothing is missing, because naming the product answers the question of what the company does, and the other components follow from the product itself — Naming the product does answer the first question — what does the company do — and that is a real start. The rest does not follow from the product, though: two shops selling the identical cup can differ on segments, channels, relationships, and costs.
  • B. Only the price, since a product and a price together already state what is sold and how the firm gets paid for it — Price is part of the revenue streams component, so this is closer than it looks, but a price is not the same as knowing in what ways the firm gets paid. It also leaves the segments, channels, relationships, resources, activities, partners, and costs entirely unstated.
  • C. Everything after the first question: how the company uniquely does it, what key resources and activities are needed, in what ways it gets paid, and what the costs are — correct. The five questions ask what the company does, how it uniquely does it, what key resources and activities are needed, in what ways it gets paid, and what the costs are, and a one-line product description answers only the first.
  • D. Only the technology, because a business model in the digital world is mainly a description of the systems the company runs on — Technology is not itself a component of the business model; it appears through the resources, activities, and channels that the model needs. A model written as a list of systems has skipped the question of who is being served and why.

3. Why does the chapter insist that a manager answer the business model questions before deciding on information systems investments?

  • A. Because how a company answers them dictates how and where information systems investments can be used to execute a competitive strategy and sustain an advantage — correct. The model is what tells you which investment executes the strategy, which is why the chapter presents technology investment as something to be aligned with the model rather than chosen on its own merits.
  • B. Because the answers reveal which technology vendor is offering the lowest price for the systems the company needs to buy this year — Vendor pricing is a procurement question that arrives much later. The business model tells you what the system has to accomplish, and a cheap system aimed at the wrong component is not a saving.
  • C. Because the systems a company already owns are what determine which business model it is able to adopt in its industry — This reverses the chapter’s order of reasoning: how a company answers the business model questions is what dictates where systems investments go, not the other way round. Treating the installed systems as the constraint locks a firm into whichever model it happens to have inherited.
  • D. Because information systems are only relevant to the revenue streams component and can safely be ignored when writing the other eight — Revenue streams are one component of nine, and systems support many of the others directly, from the channels that reach customers to the key activities the firm performs every day.

The nine components

The chapter breaks a proper business model into nine components. Each one plays a critical role in shaping all aspects of the business, including the expenses, revenues, operating strategies, corporate structure, and sales and marketing procedures. The table gives each component, what it means, and the question it answers.

ComponentDescriptionQuestions to ask
Customer segmentsThe customers targeted with the product/service offeringWho will be our target customers? Who are the most important customers?
Value propositionThe utility that the product/service has to offer to customersWhy do customers need our product/service? What problems will our product/service solve? Why would customers choose our product/service over our competitors’ products/services?
ChannelsThe ways in which the product/service offerings reach the target customersHow will our customers be reached? Which channels are best in terms of cost and convenience for the customers?
Customer relationshipsThe relationships formed with the target customersWhat types of relationships do we build with our customers, such as one-off versus long-term? How do we maintain these relationships?
Revenue streamsThe way a firm generates incomeHow do we generate income? What are we selling? What are customers willing to pay for?
Key resourcesThe most important assets needed to make the business model workWhat key resources are needed to enable our value proposition, channels, customer relationships, and revenue streams?
Key activitiesThe most important activities needed to make the business model workWhat key activities are needed to enable our value proposition, channels, customer relationships, and revenue streams?
Key partnersThe network of partners and suppliers needed to make the business model workWho are our key partners and suppliers? What resources do they offer, and what activities do they perform?
Cost structureThe costs incurred when operating the business modelWhat are the costs incurred when operating the business model? Which resources and activities are most expensive?

It helps to read the nine in two halves. The first five face the customer and describe the promise the company is making, and each one has an example you already know. The split into halves is a reading aid rather than something the chapter numbers, but it keeps the outward promise clearly separate from the machinery that has to keep it.

  • Customer segments — the customers you are targeting, named rather than assumed, because a model that serves two different groups has to say so: Uber connects people in need of rides with drivers willing to give one, and both groups have to appear in its model.
  • Value proposition — the utility your offering has for those customers, which is your answer to why they would choose you: Walmart answers with price, pursuing low-cost leadership by offering the best prices in its industry, while Porsche, Nordstrom, and IBM answer by trying to provide better products or services than their competitors.
  • Channels — the ways the offering actually reaches those customers, chosen on cost and on convenience for the customer, which is why Amazon uses the web as an economic medium to reach a large customer base rather than opening a counter in every town.
  • Customer relationships — what kind of connection you form and how you keep it, because a one-off sale and a long-term relationship demand different work: Uber uses a rider’s past behavior to learn her preferences and provide personalized ride recommendations, which only pays off across many rides.
  • Revenue streams — the way the firm generates income and what customers will actually pay for, and the answers differ sharply: Netflix charges a monthly or annual fee for use of the service, while Google’s services are free to the user and paid for by a third party.

The remaining four face inward. They describe what the company must have, do, borrow, and spend in order to keep the promise the first five just made.

  • Key resources — the most important assets the model needs, which the chapter illustrates elsewhere with proprietary technology, brand equity, and a loyal and established customer base, because a promise resting on an asset you do not have is a wish.
  • Key activities — the most important things the company must actually do, such as the work Uber’s app performs when it automatically matches riders with drivers and anticipates surges in demand so it can change pricing accordingly, because owning an asset and never using it changes nothing.
  • Key partners — the network of partners and suppliers you depend on, together with what they supply and what they do, which is the arrangement the chapter calls affiliate marketing: Amazon’s Associates program pays businesses that bring or refer customers to it, typically through revenue sharing, so that reach is real but borrowed.
  • Cost structure — what operating the whole arrangement costs and which resources and activities are the most expensive, because this is the component that decides whether the other eight can survive contact with a bank statement.
Explore

The five component pairs beginners mix up

Open each pair and read all four panels; the third panel gives you a test you can apply in seconds.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Value proposition, not revenue stream · What they get vs. what they pay

  • What it really is: The value proposition is the utility the product or service has to offer to customers: why they need it, what problem it solves, and why they would choose it over a competitor’s offering.
  • The look-alike beside it: The revenue stream sits right next to it and answers something else entirely — the way the firm generates income, what it is selling, and what customers are willing to pay for.
  • The question that separates them: Ask “what does the customer receive?” for the value proposition, and “who hands over money, and when?” for the revenue stream. The two answers are frequently about different people.
  • What the mix-up costs: The same value can be charged for in completely different ways: Netflix charges the viewer a monthly or annual fee, while Google’s services are free to the user and paid for by a third party. If you fuse the two, you will believe that changing the price means changing the product.

Channels, not customer relationships · The route vs. the rapport

  • What it really is: Channels are the ways in which the offering reaches the target customers, and the chapter judges them on two things at once: cost to the firm and convenience for the customer.
  • The look-alike beside it: Customer relationships are the relationships formed with those customers — one-off or long-term — along with the work of maintaining them once they exist.
  • The question that separates them: A channel is a path the offering travels down; a relationship is what remains after the offering has arrived. One app can do both jobs, which is exactly why the two get collapsed into one.
  • What the mix-up costs: Uber uses a rider’s past behavior to provide personalized ride recommendations, which is relationship work happening on top of the delivery channel. A firm that counts its app as its relationship keeps spending on delivery and never understands why customers do not return.

Key resources, not key activities · What you have vs. what you do

  • What it really is: Key resources are the most important assets needed to make the model work, which the chapter illustrates with proprietary technology, brand equity, and a loyal and established customer base.
  • The look-alike beside it: Key activities are the most important things the firm must actually perform, such as the coordination of riders and drivers that Uber’s app carries out to optimize the matching of supply and demand.
  • The question that separates them: Resources are nouns you own or control; activities are verbs you perform. A delivery van is a resource, and driving the collection route every morning is an activity.
  • What the mix-up costs: Both are defined as what is needed to enable the value proposition, channels, customer relationships, and revenue streams, so leaving one out breaks the same promise. Buying the asset and never staffing the work is a quiet and expensive way to fail.

Key partners, not key resources · Owned vs. borrowed

  • What it really is: Key partners are the network of partners and suppliers needed to make the model work, described by what resources they offer and what activities they perform on your behalf.
  • The look-alike beside it: Key resources are the assets the firm itself must have. The confusion is genuine, because the same capability can often be either owned or borrowed without the customer noticing.
  • The question that separates them: Ask who would still have the capability if the relationship ended tomorrow. If the answer is not you, it belongs under partners, no matter how essential it feels.
  • What the mix-up costs: The chapter’s example of affiliate marketing is Amazon’s Associates program, which pays businesses that bring or refer customers to it, typically through revenue sharing, so that reach is real but borrowed. Filing a partner under resources hides the risk that the partner leaves and takes the capability with them.

Customer segments, not “everyone” · Naming who you are for

  • What it really is: Customer segments are the customers targeted with the offering, and the component asks two questions: who our target customers will be, and who among them are the most important.
  • The look-alike beside it: The look-alike here is not another component but a non-answer. “Anyone who needs this” feels generous and safe, and it is a refusal to choose rather than a segment.
  • The question that separates them: Try to name a person the offering is deliberately not for. If no such person exists, you have not segmented the market; you have only described it.
  • What the mix-up costs: Every other component points back at the segment, because a channel can only be called convenient for somebody in particular and a value proposition can only be compelling to somebody in particular. An unnamed customer makes the remaining eight answers unfalsifiable.

Once the nine are clear, the fastest way to test yourself is to work backwards: read the question the chapter attaches to a component, then name the component from the question alone. That direction is harder than reciting the list, and it is the direction a real conversation runs in, because people describe their difficulties as questions long before anyone knows which box the answer belongs in.

Match

Component to the question it answers

Pair each business model component with the question the chapter uses to draw it out.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Customer segments
Who will be our target customers, and who are the most important ones? This component names the customers targeted with the offering, and the second half of the question matters as much as the first, because most firms serve several groups unequally.
Value proposition
Why do customers need this, and why choose it over a competitor’s? The value proposition is the utility the offering has to customers, so the test is always comparative: a benefit a rival also provides is not yet a reason to choose you.
Channels
How will customers be reached, and which routes are best on cost and convenience? Channels are the ways the offering reaches the target customers, and the chapter weighs cost to the firm against convenience for the customer rather than either one alone.
Customer relationships
Is this one-off or long-term, and how will we maintain it? This component covers the relationships formed with target customers, and the maintenance half is where the ongoing work and the ongoing expense actually live.
Revenue streams
How do we generate income, and what are customers willing to pay for? Revenue streams describe the way a firm generates income, and the second clause is the honest one, because what a firm wants to sell and what customers will pay for often differ.
Key resources
Which assets must we have to enable the promise we just made? Key resources are the most important assets needed to make the model work, and the chapter ties them explicitly to enabling the value proposition, channels, relationships, and revenue.
Key activities
Which things must we actually perform to enable that same promise? Key activities are the most important activities needed to make the model work, and they are the verbs to the resources’ nouns, tied to the same four components.
Key partners
Who supplies us, what do they offer, and what do they perform? Key partners are the network of partners and suppliers needed to make the model work, and naming what each one contributes is what turns a contact list into a component.
Cost structure
What does operating all of this cost, and which parts are most expensive? Cost structure covers the costs incurred when operating the business model, and the chapter asks specifically which resources and activities are most expensive, because that is where a model is fixed or broken.

Why the pieces interlock

Beginners treat the nine components as nine independent boxes to fill in. They are not independent, and the chapter’s own questions show the wiring.

Look again at the questions for key resources and key activities. Both ask what is needed to enable our value proposition, channels, customer relationships, and revenue streams — so those two components are defined by the first five and cannot be settled before them. Then look at cost structure, which asks which resources and activities are most expensive. Cost is the shadow cast by the choices already made.

That wiring means a change in one place travels. Five common moves show how far.

  • Change the customer segment — and the channel usually has to change with it, because a route that is convenient for a walk-in neighbour may be unreachable for a customer thirty miles away.
  • Change the channel — and key resources and key activities change immediately, because reaching people a new way requires assets and daily work that the old way never needed.
  • Change the revenue stream — and the customer relationship changes with it, because charging once at the counter and charging every month create very different expectations about what happens after the sale.
  • Change a key partner — and you have quietly changed your resources and your risks, because a capability you borrow can be withdrawn on terms you do not control.
  • Try to change only the cost structure — and you will find you cannot, because costs are produced by the resources and activities you chose, so cutting the number without changing the choices only breaks the promise.

A business model is not nine separate answers; it is nine answers that all have to be true at the same time, which is why a single change is never really a single change.

Decide

Change one component and follow the consequences

Work through the five decisions in order, choosing the option that keeps the business model coherent.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

The situation below is hypothetical and exists only for practice; no real business is being described. You advise the owner of a small neighborhood bicycle-repair shop. Today the model is simple: local riders walk their bikes in, two mechanics repair them, customers pay per repair, and the only significant assets are a rented storefront and a wall of tools. The owner wants to change one component. Follow where that change travels.

Decision 1. The owner decides to add a new customer segment: office workers ten miles away who commute by bicycle and cannot bring one in during shop hours. Which component is forced to change next?

  • Channels, because the new segment cannot reach the storefront and the offering has to travel to them instead — the stronger call. Right. Channels are the ways in which the offering reaches the target customers, chosen on cost and on convenience for the customer. Naming a segment that cannot get to your door has not served anyone yet; the route has to change before anything else does.
  • Cost structure, because the shop should cut its expenses first so it can afford the expansion — Cost structure is the costs incurred when operating the business model, and it is the sum of the other choices rather than the first lever to pull. Cutting costs before you know what the new segment requires just makes the shop smaller and no closer to the commuters.
  • Nothing, because the value proposition is still good repairs at a fair price and that has not changed — The value proposition is the utility the offering has to customers, and “good repairs you cannot physically get to” has very little utility to a commuter. Choosing a new segment always puts pressure on the components that reach and serve it.

Decision 2. The owner picks a mobile channel: a van that collects bicycles from office parks in the morning and returns them in the evening. Which components does that choice immediately force?

  • Key resources and key activities, because the van is a new asset and the daily collection round is new work — the stronger call. Right. Key resources are the most important assets needed to make the model work and key activities are the most important things it must do, and both are defined as what is needed to enable the channels, value proposition, relationships, and revenue. A new channel almost always demands both.
  • Key partners only, because the shop can simply have a courier company carry the bicycles instead — A partner is a genuine option — key partners are the network of partners and suppliers needed to make the model work. But it does not escape the point: whether the vehicle is owned or borrowed, the model now requires a resource and an activity it did not require before. Borrowing changes which component holds them, not whether they exist.
  • Customer segments, because the shop should now drop its walk-in customers to keep things simple — Nothing about adding a channel requires abandoning the original segment, and dropping profitable walk-in customers would shrink the revenue that pays for the van. Segments change when you decide who you are for, not automatically whenever a route changes.

Decision 3. The van costs money every single day it runs, but the shop still charges only when something breaks, so income arrives at unpredictable intervals. What change to revenue streams keeps the model coherent?

  • Offer a maintenance plan the commuter pays for monthly, so income arrives on the same rhythm as the cost — the stronger call. Right. Revenue streams answer how the firm generates income and what customers are willing to pay for, and a commuter who depends on the bike daily plausibly will pay to keep it running rather than to fix it after it fails. A recurring cost met only by occasional income is one of the most common ways a well-meant model runs out of money.
  • Leave the pricing alone and assume the extra volume from the new segment will cover the van — This is a hope rather than a component. Revenue streams are supposed to state how income is generated, and volume that has not been sold to anyone yet is not a revenue stream. The van’s costs, meanwhile, arrive whether the volume does or not.
  • Add a one-time pickup fee charged at the moment of each repair — This is closer than doing nothing, and for an occasional customer it might be enough, since it does at least connect the new cost to the new service. It still ties all income to breakdowns, and the van is paid for by the day rather than by the breakdown.

Decision 4. The monthly plan means the shop has made an ongoing promise instead of completing a one-time sale. Which component now has to be rewritten?

  • Customer relationships, because a subscription is a long-term relationship that has to be maintained rather than a single transaction — the stronger call. Right. This component asks what types of relationships the firm builds — one-off versus long-term — and how it maintains them. A subscriber who hears nothing for two months and then finds a mechanic unavailable will cancel, so maintenance is now part of the offering.
  • Key partners, because the shop should sign a contract with a parts supplier to guarantee stock — A reliable parts supplier is a sensible partner and would genuinely help, since key partners are described by the resources they offer and the activities they perform. It just does not address the change in front of you, which is that the shop now owes something to the customer continuously.
  • Cost structure, because the owner should recalculate what the plan costs before doing anything else — Recalculating is worth doing, but cost structure records the costs incurred in operating the model and therefore follows from the choices made. The promise to the customer is the choice; the cost is its consequence.

Decision 5. A year on, the owner wants to know whether the whole change was worth making. Which component tells him what it actually took to run the new model?

  • Cost structure, because it records the costs of operating the model and which resources and activities are the most expensive — the stronger call. Right. Cost structure asks exactly that pair of questions, so it is where the van, the fuel, the extra hours, and the software subscription finally show up next to each other. It is also the component that tells him which single expensive activity to attack first.
  • Revenue streams, because the income from the monthly plans is the measure of whether the change worked — Revenue streams tell you how income is generated and are half of the answer, which is what makes this tempting. Income alone cannot say whether the change was worth it, because a plan that sells beautifully and costs more to deliver than it earns is a loss with good marketing.
  • Key resources, because listing the assets shows the value of what the shop now owns — Key resources name the most important assets needed to make the model work, which is useful for spotting what the model depends on. A list of assets is not a running total of what operating them consumed, and that total is what the owner is asking for.
How to write one down. Take a business you know and answer the nine questions in a single page, in the order the table gives them. Wherever an answer is “everyone,” “the usual,” or “we will figure that out,” you have found the part of the model that has not been decided yet — and almost always the part where an information system either helps or is wasted.
Check yourself

Naming components and tracing consequences

Three questions on identifying the right component and on what happens when one of them changes.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. Which component is defined as the most important assets needed to make the business model work?

  • A. Key activities — Key activities are the most important activities needed to make the model work — the things the firm performs, such as matching riders with drivers, rather than the things it holds.
  • B. Key resources — correct. Key resources are the most important assets needed to make the business model work, and the chapter’s examples of a firm’s resources include proprietary technology, brand equity, and a loyal and established customer base.
  • C. Key partners — Key partners are the network of partners and suppliers needed to make the model work, described by what resources they offer and what activities they perform. The capability is real but it belongs to somebody else.
  • D. Cost structure — Cost structure is the costs incurred when operating the business model, including which resources and activities are most expensive. It measures the assets rather than naming them.

2. A firm decides that its offering will now reach customers through a subscription app instead of a retail counter. Which component has it changed, and what must be revisited straight away?

  • A. It changed its channels, so key resources and key activities must be revisited, because both are defined as whatever enables the channels and the rest of the promise — correct. Channels are the ways the offering reaches the target customers, and because resources and activities are defined as whatever enables the channels and the rest of the promise, changing the route changes what the firm must own and do.
  • B. It changed its value proposition, and nothing else needs revisiting, because the product being sold to the customer is identical either way — The product may indeed be identical, which is what makes this tempting, but the value proposition is the utility to the customer and a change of route is a change of channel. Even if the offer were untouched, the components downstream of the channel would still move.
  • C. It changed its cost structure, and the customer segments must be renamed to match the new pattern of spending the app creates — Cost structure will certainly move, since an app has to be built and run, but it moves as a consequence rather than as the change itself. Segments are named by deciding who you serve, not by observing what you spent.
  • D. It changed its key partners, and only the partner contracts need to be rewritten, since the app will be built and hosted by someone else — Partners may well be involved in building or hosting the app, so this is a plausible reading. It still misidentifies the change, which is how the offering reaches the customer, and it wrongly implies that resources and activities can stay as they were.

3. Which statement about cost structure is accurate?

  • A. It is another name for revenue streams, viewed from the paying side of the same transaction rather than the earning side — Revenue streams describe how the firm generates income and what customers will pay for, which is money coming in. Cost structure describes money going out, and the two can be healthy or unhealthy quite independently of each other.
  • B. It is the total price the customer pays, since the costs a firm incurs are ultimately passed through to whoever buys — This confuses cost with price. Cost structure records the costs incurred when operating the model, which is money leaving the firm; what a customer hands over belongs to revenue streams, and a firm can perfectly well charge less than a thing costs it or many times more.
  • C. It lists what the company spends on technology, which is why it is the one component information systems have any effect on — Technology spending is part of the cost structure but nowhere near all of it, and information systems affect far more than costs. Systems reach the channels, the relationships, the key activities, and the revenue streams as well.
  • D. It records the costs incurred when operating the model and asks which of the resources and activities are the most expensive — correct. The component covers the costs incurred when operating the business model and asks which resources and activities are most expensive, which makes it downstream of the resource and activity choices rather than an independent decision.

Section 2–2b

Revenue models, platforms, and network effects

A business model says what a company does. This half of the story answers the blunt part: in what way does the company get paid, and who stands on the other side of that payment? Several of the answers below were impractical until digital delivery made one more customer nearly free to serve.

The revenue model: how the money arrives

A revenue model describes how the firm will earn revenue, generate profits, and produce a superior return on invested capital. Even nonprofits need one, because something has to pay for the work. Sales, transaction fees, and advertising existed offline; the internet enabled or enhanced others, such as affiliate marketing.

The table lists the typical revenue models in the digital world and who uses each.

Revenue typeDescriptionWho is doing this?
Affiliate marketingPaying businesses that bring or refer customers to another business; revenue sharing is typically used.Amazon’s Associates program
AdvertisingFree services are provided to customers and paid for by a third party.Google, Instagram, X, TikTok
SubscriptionUsers pay a monthly or yearly recurring fee for the use of the product or service.Netflix, Microsoft 365, Dropbox, Spotify, Adobe Creative Cloud
Transaction fees / brokerageA commission is paid to the business for aiding in the transaction.PayPal, eBay, Airbnb, Uber
Traditional salesA consumer buys a product or service from the website, or makes in-app purchases.Amazon, Zappos, Nordstrom, TikTok
FreemiumBasic services are offered for free, but a premium is charged for special features.Flickr, iCloud, Dropbox

Read each row by asking whose hand the money leaves. Five of the rows sort into four groups.

  • The customer pays for the thing — traditional sales, because a shopper buys the product from the website or in the app.
  • The customer pays for the time — subscription, because the fee recurs monthly or yearly for continued use, as at Netflix.
  • Somebody outside the deal pays — advertising, because a third party covers the cost, which is why Google charges users nothing.
  • The firm is paid for arranging someone else’s deal — brokerage commissions the transaction, as at PayPal, and affiliate marketing pays for the referral.

Freemium is the sixth and the odd one out, because it splits one product into a free version and a paid one.

Sort

Which revenue model is this?

Place each offer under the revenue model that describes how the money actually reaches the firm; every model in the table appears here twice, and the one item that names no company is a generic example written for practice.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Affiliate marketing — paying a business that brings or refers customers to another business, usually by sharing revenue

  • A website earns a share of the revenue every time the shoppers it sends to a large online retailer go on to buy something — the arrangement behind Amazon’s Associates program — Affiliate marketing pays businesses that bring or refer customers to another business, and revenue sharing is the typical form that payment takes.
  • A price-comparison site is paid by a merchant for each customer it refers, rather than by the customers it serves — The payment is for the referral itself, which is what separates affiliate marketing from a commission earned for aiding a transaction between two other parties.

Advertising — free services provided to customers and paid for by a third party

  • Google, Instagram, X, and TikTok let people use their services without charging them, and bill someone else instead — Under an advertising model, free services are provided to customers and paid for by a third party, and these four are the chapter’s named examples.
  • YouTube charges neither the producers who upload videos nor the consumers who watch them, and takes its money from advertisers — The chapter uses YouTube as the contrast to Airbnb: the platform monetizes a third party rather than either side of its own market.

Subscription — a recurring monthly or yearly fee for continued use of the product or service

  • Netflix customers pay a recurring monthly or yearly fee, and the service stops when they stop paying — A subscription model charges a recurring fee for the use of the product or service, which is exactly what a lapsed account demonstrates.
  • Microsoft 365, Spotify, and Adobe Creative Cloud each bill a recurring fee for continued use of the software — All three are named subscription examples, and the giveaway is that the fee buys a period of use rather than a permanent copy.

Transaction fees / brokerage — a commission paid to the business for aiding in someone else’s transaction

  • Airbnb collects a commission from both the host and the guest for aiding the booking, without owning the room — Transaction fees and brokerage mean a commission paid to the business for aiding in the transaction, and the chapter names Airbnb charging both parties.
  • PayPal and eBay are paid a commission for helping a transaction between two other parties go through — Neither firm is the buyer or the seller; each is paid for making the exchange between them possible, which is the definition of brokerage.

Traditional sales — a consumer buys the product or service from the website, or makes in-app purchases

  • A shopper buys a pair of shoes outright from the Zappos website, and Nordstrom sells the same way from its own site — Traditional sales means a consumer buys a product or service from the website, and both companies are named examples of it.
  • Amazon uses the web to reach a very large customer base, turning inventory over quickly so it can offer low prices and still make a profit on each item sold — This is the chapter’s description of using the web as an economic medium to sell goods, so the revenue still arrives as the price of a product.

Freemium — basic service free, a premium charged for special or unrestricted features

  • Dropbox and iCloud give every user an account with limited storage capacity and charge those who want more space — Freemium offers basic services free and charges a premium for unrestricted versions, and storage is one of the chapter’s listed restrictions.
  • Flickr offers a basic service at no cost and charges only for the special features on top of it — The defining feature is one product existing in a free limited version and a paid premium one, which is how the chapter defines freemium.

Why giving it away became a real strategy

In a competitive marketplace, price is set by marginal cost — the cost of producing one additional unit of output. The building blocks of a digital product are processing, storage, and bandwidth; those costs have fallen, and cloud computing turned many into variable costs.

When serving one more user costs almost nothing, an organization may give limited versions away free to build a large customer base and charge a premium for unrestricted ones, typically by subscription. That is freemium, and what the free version withholds varies.

  • Features — the free version does less, so whoever needs the missing capability pays.
  • Bandwidth — data moves more slowly, which bites hardest on the heaviest users.
  • Storage — Dropbox and iCloud limit free capacity and sell subscriptions to larger accounts.
  • Number of users — the free version covers one person or a small team, so a growing group outgrows it.
  • Class of user — the product or service is restricted to a certain class of users, such as educational users, so anyone outside that group has to pay for it.

Choosing that line is the hard part. Free offerings must be compelling enough to attract users, yet if too many features are free, few will pay for the premium version. Often a process of fine tuning and adjustment is needed, and it is hardest when the change reduces the service level of the free offering — as when the calendar app Fantastical moved previously free features into its premium offering.

Free games are the extreme case. Mobile games such as Candy Crush or Honor of Kings download free and sell in-app purchases of extra features, content, or in-game currency. In 2024 alone, Honor of Kings took in more than US$1.8 billion globally that way, and players gain too, since developers depend on that revenue and keep upgrading the game.

Check yourself

Revenue models and the economics of free

Pick the best answer, then read all four explanations — the wrong ones name what that option genuinely describes. Any situation here that names no company is a generic example written for practice.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. A cloud storage company gives every user an account with limited capacity at no charge and asks those who want more space to pay a monthly fee. Which revenue model best describes this?

  • A. Advertising, because the free accounts are being paid for by a third party — Advertising means free services are provided to customers and paid for by a third party, as at Google or TikTok. Nobody outside this relationship is paying, so the answer would need advertisers funding the free accounts.
  • B. Freemium, because a basic version is free and a premium is charged for the unrestricted version — correct. The chapter names cloud storage providers such as Dropbox and iCloud as the standard freemium case: free accounts with limited storage capacity, and a subscription for larger space.
  • C. Transaction fees and brokerage, because the company collects a fee each time a user upgrades to a larger account — Transaction fees and brokerage mean a commission paid to a business for aiding in a transaction between two other parties, as with PayPal, eBay, or Airbnb. Here the storage company is one of the two parties, so what it charges its own customer is a price rather than a commission, however it is timed.
  • D. Traditional sales, because the customer buys the larger account from the company’s website — Traditional sales is a consumer buying a product or service from the website, and money genuinely does change hands here. It misses what is distinctive, though: the free limited tier exists on purpose to build the base that the paid tier is sold into.

2. Why did falling costs make free versions of digital products practical in the first place?

  • A. Because price in a competitive marketplace is set by marginal cost, and serving one more user now costs very little — correct. The chapter’s argument runs through marginal cost — the cost of producing an additional unit of output — and the falling costs of the fundamental building blocks of digital products and services.
  • B. Because cloud computing turned what used to be variable costs into fixed ones, so every additional user is absorbed by money the firm committed long before that user arrived — This reverses the direction the chapter describes: cloud computing turned many of these costs into variable costs, not fixed ones. Variable costs are what make each additional user cheap rather than free.
  • C. Because advertising revenue rises with every free user a service adds, so free users are not really free — Some free services genuinely are funded by advertisers, which is the advertising model. But freemium firms such as Dropbox and iCloud charge their own premium users, and the chapter grounds the shift in costs rather than in ad revenue.
  • D. Because the cost of writing the software is paid once up front, so every user after the first one is pure profit — This is close enough to be tempting, and it is part of why free versions are thinkable at all, but it overstates the case. Delivering the service to one more user still consumes processing, storage, and bandwidth; the chapter says those costs have fallen and become variable, not that they vanished.

3. A company running a freemium product is deciding which features to leave in the free version. What guidance does the chapter give, and what does the Fantastical example add?

  • A. Give away as much as possible, because a larger base of free users reliably turns into a larger number of paying subscribers and the conversion rate holds steady whatever is given away — Scale does matter, and the chapter says app developers benefit from the ability to scale their user base quickly. It also states the opposite pressure: if too many features are offered for free, few people will be willing to pay for the more feature-rich premium version.
  • B. Keep the free version as thin as possible, because users decide on price alone and will upgrade once they need the product — This fails the other half of the test: the free offering must be compelling enough to attract new users in the first place. A free version nobody wants builds no base for the premium version to sell into.
  • C. The free version must be compelling enough to attract users but not so generous that few will pay, and a free feature is very hard to pull back later — correct. The chapter describes both sides of the balance, says a process of fine tuning is often needed, and notes the special difficulty of reducing the service level of the free offering, as when Fantastical moved previously free features into its premium offering.
  • D. The balance is settled at launch, because changing which features are free afterwards is a routine pricing update — The opposite is true. Fine tuning and adjustment are described as ongoing, and the Fantastical example exists precisely because a later change to the free tier is the hardest kind to make.

Pipes and platforms

Traditionally, many business models functioned like pipes: the firm produced a product and pushed it out to customers, so value flowed in one direction and the firm, not the customer, was the one producing it.

Increasing digital density enabled another shape. A platform-based business model does not provide the product or service itself; it coordinates others — businesses and users — to co-create value, building a digital ecosystem where some users produce and others consume. People uploading to Instagram or Pinterest produce what others consume, and Uber and Airbnb depend on users to offer and take the rides and rooms.

What gets exchanged on a platform is wider than most people assume.

Value created or exchangedExamples
ProductsAmazon Marketplace, eBay
ServicesAirbnb, Uber
PaymentsSquare, PayPal, Venmo, Zelle
Investments and fundingKickstarter, Lending Club
ContentWikipedia, X, YouTube, TikTok
CommunicationWhatsApp, Zoom
CollaborationDropbox
Social relationshipsFacebook, LinkedIn

Serving producers and consumers at once creates a two-sided market, whose success depends on the network effect. Who pays is a separate decision: Airbnb charges a transaction fee to both parties, while YouTube charges a third party, the advertisers.

The two shapes are not rivals on a shelf — many pipeline businesses already carry platform elements such as user reviews, so the question is how much platform a business model should contain.

Interactive diagram

Pipe, platform, and the two network effects

Pick a model to redraw it: the first two contrast the two shapes of business, and the last two show which side each network effect acts on.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

The pipe business — Value produced by the firm and pushed out one direction

Suppliers (Inputs bought by the firm) → The firm (Produces the product itself) → The product (Pushed out to the market) → Customers (Buy, consume, and that is the end)

  • Traditionally, many business models functioned like pipes, where products were produced and pushed to the customers, so the firm creates the value and the customer only receives it.
  • A jet-engine manufacturer selling engines and spare parts to airlines is the pure form: everything of value is made inside the company and sold outward.
  • Growth in a pipe means producing more or selling to more people, because there is no second group whose participation the firm could recruit instead.
  • Pipes are not obsolete. Today many pipeline-based businesses include platform elements, such as reviews created by users, so the two shapes mix inside one company.

The platform business — Value created by others whom the firm coordinates

Producers (Upload, list, drive, host) → The platform (Coordinates, matches, sets rules) → Consumers (Watch, buy, ride, stay) → Who pays (One side, both sides, or a third party)

  • A platform-based business model coordinates others — both other businesses and users — to co-create value, rather than providing the product or service itself.
  • Platform businesses create digital ecosystems where some users create value and other users consume it: people uploading to Instagram or Pinterest produce what others consume, and Uber and Airbnb depend on users to offer and consume the services.
  • Serving both groups at once creates a two-sided market, and its success depends on the network effect — a platform has value only if users participate in production or consumption.
  • Monetizing is a separate decision from building the market: Airbnb charges a transaction fee to both parties, while YouTube charges neither producers nor consumers but a third party, the advertisers.

Same-side network effects — Value changes because more users join your own side

More users on one side (Your neighbours, doing what you do) → Value can rise (Wider iOS use, wider Keynote compatibility) → Value can fall (More riders competing for the same rides) → The management tool (Surge pricing handles excessive demand)

  • Same-side network effects relate to the increase or decrease in value as additional users join on the same side of the network, so the effect comes from people in the same role as you.
  • The positive example: as more users switch to iOS, everyone benefits from wider compatibility of its Keynote presentation format, because the format is understood in more places.
  • The negative example: as more riders use Uber, competition for available rides increases, and surge pricing exists to help manage that excessive demand.
  • This is why a platform cannot simply chase user counts — platform businesses must carefully evaluate the various same-side and cross-side network effects instead of assuming every new user adds value.

Cross-side network effects — Value changes because more users join the other side

More apps arrive (Producers join the developer side) → Users gain (The app store becomes more useful) → More users arrive (Consumers join the other side) → Developers gain (More reason to build for iOS)

  • Cross-side network effects relate to the change in value for a user if users join on the other side, so the benefit arrives from the group you are matched with rather than the group you belong to.
  • The chapter’s pair points both ways: the app store becomes more useful for users as more apps are added, and app developers are more likely to develop iOS apps as more users use iOS.
  • Because each side is the reason the other side shows up, any platform-based business model must be attractive to both producers and consumers at the same time.
  • This is also the hard part of starting a platform, since a side with nobody on it gives the other side no reason to arrive — value exists only where users participate in production or consumption.

Network effects, and which side they come from

A network effect is what happens to a platform’s value when the number of people on it changes. The chapter separates two kinds, and the only difference is which side the newcomers join.

  • Same-side network effects — the increase or decrease in value as users join on the same side of the network, so people doing what you do change what the platform is worth to you.
  • Cross-side network effects — the change in value for a user if users join on the other side, so the people you are matched with change what it is worth.

Notice the phrase increase or decrease. Same-side effects run both ways, and the chapter supplies an example of each.

  • Positive: as more users switch to iOS, everyone benefits from wider compatibility of its Keynote presentation format.
  • Negative: as more riders use Uber, competition for available rides increases, which is what surge pricing manages.

Cross-side effects run between the two sides, and the chapter’s example arrives as a pair pointing opposite ways: the app store becomes more useful for users as more apps are added, and app developers are more likely to develop iOS apps as more users use iOS. Each side is why the other shows up.

So a platform has value only where users participate in production or consumption, and it must attract producers and consumers alike. That is why these firms evaluate the various same-side and cross-side effects carefully rather than chase a user count.

Reasoning from the mechanism, not a claim the chapter makes. The chapter defines the two effects but never describes a market tipping to one winner, so check this rather than memorize it. If each consumer who joins makes the platform more attractive to producers, and each producer makes it more attractive to consumers, the platform slightly ahead keeps getting easier to join, and an early lead compounds. Expect concentration, not a guarantee: a negative same-side effect, a regulator, or a stronger local rival can interrupt the loop.

Match

Platform vocabulary, and which side the effect came from

Pair each term or example with what it actually describes; three of the pairs are network effects you must place on the correct side.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Same-side network effect
The increase or decrease in value as additional users join on the same side of the network The definition allows movement in both directions, which is why a crowded side can be worth less rather than more.
Cross-side network effect
The change in value for a user when users join on the other side of the network The value arrives from the group you are matched with, which is why a platform must recruit both sides at once.
More riders join a ride-hailing service, so competition for available rides increases
A same-side effect that reduces value, managed with surge pricing The newcomers are riders and the people affected are riders, so the effect is same-side even though drivers also trade in this market.
The app store becomes more useful as more apps are added to it
A cross-side effect, since users gain from arrivals on the developer side Developers and users occupy opposite sides of the platform, so a gain that crosses between them is cross-side by definition.
More people switch to iOS, so the Keynote presentation format is compatible with more machines
A same-side effect that increases value The benefit reaches the same group that grew, which is what makes this the positive form of a same-side effect.
Two-sided market
The market a platform creates by serving producers and consumers at once, with success depending on the network effect Because both sides must be present, the platform has value only if users participate in production or consumption.
Platform-based business model
Coordinating other businesses and users to co-create value instead of providing the product or service itself Uber and Airbnb are the chapter’s cases: successful platforms that do not offer the rides or the rooms themselves.
Disintermediation
Matching providers and customers directly, without the traditional middlemen Removing the intermediary is what lets a platform connect the two sides cheaply, and the chapter flags it for later study.
Gig economy
An arrangement in which workers are not employed by the company but hired only for short-term, temporary jobs The chapter raises it as the human cost of platform disruption, because protections such as social security and job security often go missing.

The sharing economy

Many platforms match providers and customers directly, with no traditional middleman — disintermediation. As individuals began sharing physical goods and services this way, not only content, many concluded we are moving toward a sharing economy, sometimes called a collaborative economy. The chapter takes its definition from a dictionary: an economic system in which assets or services are shared between private individuals, either free or for a fee, typically by means of the internet.

The claim underneath is that ownership is not what counts; access to the asset is. Three consequences follow.

  • Assets get used harder — research cited in the chapter found that one vehicle on a car-sharing platform such as Free2Move, a subsidiary of the multinational automaker Stellantis, can replace up to 13 privately owned vehicles, and for some people Uber replaces the need to own one.
  • Goods last longer — platforms such as Craigslist or eBay encourage selling used goods, extending the usable life of many products.
  • The definition blurs — the Lyft scooters show the boundary between true sharing and refined renting becoming hard to draw.

Early sharing-economy thinking included social goals such as waste reduction and greater human interaction, which matter less now. The benefits usually cited today are practical ones: more flexible work arrangements, and the chance to earn extra income by renting out an apartment through Airbnb or driving for Uber.

These business models are not without criticism. In the gig economy, workers are not employed by the company but hired only for short-term, temporary jobs, and rights fought for since the Industrial Revolution are often neglected: no protection against discrimination, no social security, little job security, limited income opportunity. Uber and Airbnb have also sought advantage over traditional businesses by breaking, or at least bypassing, existing laws and regulations, which can often be regarded as unfair competition.

Explore

What breaks a platform

Open each card and read all four facets; every failure here comes from something the chapter says a platform business has to manage.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

One side stops showing up · The empty half of a two-sided market

  • The failure: A platform does not produce the value it sells; it coordinates others to co-create it. So a platform only has value if users participate in the production or the consumption, and a side with nobody on it leaves nothing to coordinate.
  • How it shows up on the platform: Listings go stale because no producers post, or listings sit unseen because no consumers arrive. Each side looks at the empty other side and concludes the platform is not worth joining.
  • What it costs if nobody acts: The cross-side effects run the wrong way: fewer producers make the platform less useful to consumers, and the consumers who then leave make it less useful to the producers still there.
  • What the chapter says about it: Any platform-based business model must be attractive to both producers and consumers, which makes the two sides one design problem rather than two marketing campaigns.

Crowding on one side · A negative same-side effect left unmanaged

  • The failure: Same-side network effects can decrease value as well as increase it. The chapter’s example is direct: as more riders use Uber, competition for available rides increases, so the newest arrivals make the platform worse for the people already there.
  • How it shows up on the platform: Everyone on the crowded side waits longer, is matched less often, or competes harder for the same limited attention, while the raw user count on the dashboard keeps climbing.
  • What it costs if nobody acts: Growth stops meaning what management thinks it means, because the platform is adding users to the side that is already oversupplied and quietly degrading its own experience.
  • What the chapter says about it: Surge pricing is the chapter’s named response — a mechanism that helps manage excessive demand — and the general instruction is to evaluate the various same-side and cross-side effects carefully.

No answer to who pays · Negligible marginal cost is not a revenue model

  • The failure: Platform business models are attractive partly because they often have negligible or zero marginal costs, but low costs are not income. The platform must still decide which participants, if any, are charged.
  • How it shows up on the platform: The service is popular, usage grows, and the finance conversation keeps being postponed because nothing in the growth curve reveals where the money is supposed to come from.
  • What it costs if nobody acts: The risk is that the charge arrives late and abruptly, or lands on whichever side is least able to leave — the same difficulty the chapter describes when a company reduces the service level of a free offering people have already built habits around.
  • What the chapter says about it: The chapter puts two legitimate answers side by side: Airbnb charges a transaction fee to both parties, and YouTube charges neither side but sells to advertisers instead.

The rules and the rivals catch up · Disruption is not a permanent position

  • The failure: The chapter says companies such as Uber and Airbnb try to gain a competitive advantage over traditional businesses by breaking, or at least bypassing, existing laws and regulations. An advantage held that way lasts only as long as the rules and the rivals stay still.
  • How it shows up on the platform: Lawsuits, licensing fights, and legislative protection of the incumbent industry — Uber has been sued countless times, and many locales have attempted to protect their taxi systems in court or in statute.
  • What it costs if nobody acts: A rival can copy the model and add reach the original lacks: DiDi Kuaidi merged the taxi-hailing services of Alibaba and Tencent, then widened into taxis, private cars, shared cars, shuttle vans, and buses.
  • What the chapter says about it: The chapter’s ending is blunt. Facing a hostile regulatory environment that tends to favor local businesses, Uber withdrew from China in mid-2016, selling its assets to its competitor for a minority stake.

The people doing the work are unprotected · The gig economy criticism

  • The failure: In the gig economy, workers are not employed by the platform but hired for short-term, temporary jobs, so the protections that came with employment do not follow them onto the platform.
  • How it shows up on the platform: No protection against discrimination, no social security, little job security, limited income opportunity, and few of the social interactions with coworkers that an ordinary workplace supplies.
  • What it costs if nobody acts: The disruption delivers greater choice to end customers at a cost borne by humans and society, which is the specific criticism the chapter levels at these business models.
  • What the chapter says about it: The chapter does not resolve it. It records that worker rights fought for since the Industrial Revolution are often neglected, and that bypassing existing law can reasonably be regarded as unfair competition.

When things go wrong: out-disrupting the disrupter

Uber built a successful business in many locations by using social, mobile, and Big Data to disrupt local transportation, and protected taxi monopolies struggled to react. Many locales fought back in legislatures or in court, and Uber has been sued countless times. In China a competitor tried the other approach: out-disrupting Uber.

  • The rival was itself a merger — DiDi Kuaidi combined the taxi-hailing services of Alibaba and Tencent, China’s internet giants, so it began with scale.
  • It widened the platform — renamed DiDi Chuxing, it let users pick a taxi, private car, shared car, shuttle van, or bus, and in 2025 had more than 550 million users globally in the ride-sharing market.
  • Regulation settled it — as Amazon and Google learned before, regulation in China often favors local businesses, and Uber could not beat a state-backed rival.

In mid-2016 Uber withdrew from the Chinese market, selling all its assets to its competitor for a minority stake. DiDi Chuxing kept advancing and is on the cusp of launching a self-driving taxi.

Service-based business models and XaaS

Digital density enabled one more shift: selling the use of a product rather than the product, sometimes called XaaS, or X as a service. A manufacturer that used a pipe model to build and sell goods can instead offer two kinds of service.

  • Equipment services — offering the product itself as a service, or operations and optimization services, so the customer buys an outcome rather than a machine.
  • Information services — selling data or insights generated by the customer’s usage of the product, which is revenue from something the product already produced.

Jet engines are the clearest case. Rolls-Royce and GE traditionally sold engines to aircraft owners; because the bargaining power of buyers is high, that market is competitive, and much of their revenue came from maintenance and spare parts.

Under a service-based model, GE is paid for guaranteeing continuous uptime — essentially thrust as a service. The customer buys neither engine nor spare parts and pays for hours of usage, turning fixed costs into variable ones, and the manufacturer earns only while engines run, so it gains a reason to improve the design and do preventive maintenance.

None of it works without the Internet of Things: sensors throughout the engines, connected to the internet, let GE monitor performance, predict failure, and schedule maintenance. Philips does the same on the ground, providing lighting as a service to dozens of parking garages of the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority, which needs no upfront capital while Philips earns from the energy savings.

The transition is hard, and the difficulties are internal rather than technical.

  • The manufacturing goal inverts — rather than minimizing build cost, the firm focuses on life span and ease of repair, because it lives with the product.
  • Selling changes shape — a product sale negotiates price and features, while a service needs new pricing models, new business processes, and service level agreements.
  • Capacity gets harder — managing inventories and capacity is tougher, because demand for services fluctuates as a build-and-ship schedule does not.
  • The buyer is different — the segment targeted for products is often not the one buying services, forcing changes to marketing.

Across freemium, platforms, and XaaS the same move repeats: the firm stops charging once for an object and gets paid instead for continued access, participation, or performance.
