Platforms, effects, and services

Three questions on the harder half of this section, any unnamed company being a generic example written for practice; read every explanation, because the distractors are the confusions this material usually produces.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. An app store gains several hundred new apps this month, and the people who shop in it find it noticeably more useful as a result. Which effect is that?

  • A. A same-side network effect, because the apps and the shoppers are all users of the same platform — Being on the same platform is not the same as being on the same side. Developers and shoppers occupy the two sides of the store, and the side an effect crosses is the only thing that names it.
  • B. A same-side network effect, because the new apps now compete with each other for downloads — This describes a real same-side effect, but it is the wrong one for the question asked. Competition among developers is felt by developers, whereas the question describes a change in value felt by shoppers.
  • C. A cross-side network effect, because the value changed for users on the opposite side from the ones who joined — correct. The chapter’s own example is that the app store becomes more useful for users as more apps are added, which is the definition of a cross-side effect.
  • D. Not a network effect at all, because the store simply widened its selection the way any retailer might — Widening a selection is genuinely not a network effect when a retailer buys the extra stock itself. What makes this one is that the value changed for one group because independent participants joined the other side, which is the chapter’s own app store illustration.

2. As more riders use a ride-hailing platform, competition for the available rides increases. What is happening, and what is surge pricing for?

  • A. A negative same-side effect, and surge pricing helps manage the excessive demand it creates — correct. Same-side effects can decrease value as well as increase it, and the chapter names surge pricing as the mechanism that helps manage that excessive demand.
  • B. A cross-side effect, because riders and drivers sit on opposite sides of the platform — Riders and drivers do sit on opposite sides, so this would be the right label for an effect that crossed between them. The change described here happens among riders because of other riders, which keeps it on one side.
  • C. A positive same-side effect, because a busier service is more valuable to the people using it — This assumes same-side effects can only add value, which is exactly what the definition rules out: the effect is an increase or a decrease as users join the same side.
  • D. Ordinary supply and demand rather than a network effect, because too few cars for too many riders is a capacity problem — Capacity is genuinely part of the story, but the shortage is created by users arriving on one side and is felt by the users already standing on that same side. That is what the chapter calls a same-side network effect, and surge pricing is the response it names.

3. A jet-engine manufacturer stops selling engines and spare parts and is instead paid for guaranteeing continuous uptime. What actually changes?

  • A. The customer finances the engine over time while the manufacturer keeps the spare-parts revenue it had before — Under the service model the customer does not have to purchase the engine or the spare parts at all, so this describes a financing plan for the old pipe model rather than the shift the chapter describes.
  • B. The customer pays for hours of usage, turning fixed costs into variable ones, and the manufacturer now profits from durability and preventive maintenance — correct. The customer pays for hours of usage rather than buying the engine, which transforms fixed costs into variable costs, and the manufacturer earns only while engines operate, giving it an incentive to improve design and perform preventive maintenance.
  • C. Nothing changes in the manufacturer’s priorities, since minimizing manufacturing cost still decides how profitable each engine is — The priority inverts. Rather than focusing on minimizing manufacturing costs to increase profit margins, the manufacturer must focus on life span and ease of maintenance and repair, because it now bears the cost of failure.
  • D. The arrangement needs no new technology, because maintenance intervals for engines are already well known — This model is only possible through rapid advances in Internet of Things technology: sensors throughout the engines, connected to the internet, let the manufacturer monitor performance, predict potential failure, and schedule maintenance.

Section 2–3a

Innovation and what it is worth

Ask most people what innovation means and they will describe a product — a better phone, a cleverer gadget, something you could hold up on a stage. That answer is not wrong, but it turns out to be one tenth of the picture, and this section is about the other nine tenths.

Inventing something is not the same as innovating

For organizations, innovation means creating new products, processes, or services that return value to the organization. The chapter is careful about that last phrase: in contrast to merely inventing new products, services, or processes, innovation involves realizing the value.

So a brilliant idea sitting in a notebook is an invention. It becomes an innovation at the moment it earns money, saves money, or wins a customer who would otherwise have gone elsewhere.

The stakes are not academic. Innovation is key for organizations attempting to gain or sustain a competitive advantage, whether through cost or through differentiation, and the chapter aims its warning squarely at the companies currently winning.

Being the leader is not protection. Companies that lead their markets or own strong brands often tend to find it difficult to react appropriately to new trends, and Cisco’s former chief executive John Chambers predicted that almost half of today’s leading businesses might not see the next decade. Read that as a statement about two different skills, since leading a market and reacting to a change in it are not the same job.

Two sizes of innovation

Not every innovation redraws an industry. The chapter sorts them by how new the underlying technology is and by what happens to whatever came before.

  • Incremental innovation — enhancing or upgrading an existing product, service, or process, which the chapter calls the most common form of innovation because it works with what a company already sells and already knows how to build.
  • Radical innovation — also called disruptive innovation, it uses a markedly new or different technology to reach new customer segments or to give existing customers significantly greater benefits, and it eventually marginalizes or replaces the products and services that were there before.

Telling them apart in a real case takes three questions, asked in this order.

  1. Is the technology markedly new or different? A faster version of the same machine is an upgrade; a machine that works on an entirely different principle is not, which is the first thing separating the two.
  2. Who gets the benefit? Radical innovation reaches customer segments the old product never served, or hands existing customers a significantly greater benefit rather than a slightly better one.
  3. What happens to the incumbent? If the older product or service is eventually marginalized or replaced, the change was radical; if the older product simply keeps selling in a better version, the change was incremental.

What radical innovation has already done

The chapter lists nineteen radical innovations beside the technology each one displaced or pushed to the margins, and all nineteen are reproduced below. Read them as pairs, and read the right-hand column as an industry that once looked permanent.

Radical innovationDisplaced or marginalized technology
Digital photographyChemical photography
Desktop publishingTraditional publishing
Online stock brokerageFull-service stock brokerage
Online retailingBrick-and-mortar retailing
Free, downloadable greeting cardsPrinted greeting cards
Distance educationClassroom education
Unmanned aircraftManned aircraft
Nurse practitionersMedical doctors
SemiconductorsVacuum tubes
AutomobilesHorses
AirplanesTrains
Compact discsCassettes and records
MP3 players, music downloading, streamingCompact discs and music stores
SmartphonesMP3 players, dedicated GPS navigation
Mobile telephonyWire-line telephony

Xbox, PlayStation, smartphonesDesktop computers
3D printingCNC milling
Camera dronesHelicopters for aerial filming and photography

Three things in that table are easy to read past, and each one changes how you should think about your own industry.

  • The chain does not stop — compact discs displaced cassettes and records, then music downloading and streaming displaced compact discs and music stores, and smartphones then displaced MP3 players and dedicated navigation units, so today’s radical innovation can end up as a future entry in the right-hand column.
  • Displaced is not the same as deleted — the chapter’s own heading says displaced or marginalized, and pairs such as distance education against classroom education, or nurse practitioners against medical doctors, describe a shift in share rather than an extinction.
  • Not every entry is a computer — automobiles displacing horses and airplanes displacing trains sit on the same list, because what makes an innovation radical is what it does to a market, not whether it happens to be digital.
Sort

Radical or incremental?

Each situation below is a generic, hypothetical example written for practice, with no real company named; drop it into the bucket the chapter’s definitions call for, then read why it belongs there.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Radical innovation — markedly new technology, new segments or far greater benefits, and the old product ends up marginalized or replaced

  • A camera maker stops using film and chemical developing altogether, and records the image on a sensor as data instead. — This is the chapter’s own first pair: digital photography displaced chemical photography. The technology underneath is markedly different, not a better version of the same thing, and the older technology was pushed aside rather than improved.
  • Sales of dedicated satellite navigation units collapse because one device already in the customer’s pocket does the same job alongside everything else. — The chapter pairs smartphones with MP3 players and dedicated GPS navigation as displaced technologies. A general-purpose device absorbing a single-purpose one is the marginalize-or-replace pattern in its clearest form.
  • Page layout that once required a print shop’s specialist equipment and specialist operators is done on ordinary computers on ordinary desks. — Desktop publishing against traditional publishing is one of the chapter’s pairs. The work reached people who were never going to buy typesetting equipment, which is exactly the access-new-customer-segments half of the definition.
  • Aerial filming that used to require a helicopter, a pilot, and an airfield is done with a small flying camera launched from the ground. — The chapter lists camera drones as displacing helicopters for aerial filming and photography. The cost and skill barrier falls far enough to bring in customers who could never have chartered a helicopter.
  • A manufacturer builds a part by adding material layer upon layer instead of cutting the shape out of a solid block. — 3D printing against CNC milling is one of the chapter’s pairs. Adding material and removing material are opposite principles, so this is a markedly different technology rather than a faster version of the old one.
  • A brokerage lets customers place their own trades through a website instead of telephoning a broker who advises them and charges a full commission. — Online stock brokerage against full-service stock brokerage is one of the chapter’s pairs. The service reaches investors who were never worth a full-service broker’s time, and it changes what the customer is paying for.

Incremental innovation — an existing product, service, or process is enhanced or upgraded

  • A phone maker ships this year’s model with a longer-lasting battery and a slightly brighter screen. — Enhancing or upgrading an existing product is the definition of incremental innovation, and the chapter notes this is the most common form. Nothing about the technology is markedly new, and last year’s phone is not marginalized so much as superseded by its own successor.
  • A grocery chain rewrites its checkout software so each scan completes a fraction of a second faster. — The process already exists and is being upgraded, so this is incremental. It may well be worth doing, because saved seconds at every lane add up, but no new technology and no new customer segment is involved.
  • A notebook computer maker releases a model that is thinner than last year’s and starts up more quickly. — Thinner and faster is an upgrade to an existing product, so it is incremental. Note the contrast with the chapter’s own table, where tablets appear as a radical innovation that marginalized notebook computers as a category.
  • A university records its existing lectures on video so students already enrolled in those classes can rewatch them later. — This upgrades a service that already exists for the same students, so it is incremental. The chapter’s radical entry is distance education against classroom education, which is different: it serves students who were never going to be in the room at all.

Why “we built a better product” is a fragile plan

Here is the trap the chapter is most concerned with. When people hear innovation, they often think only about innovative products or services — and products and services, even radical ones, can easily be copied.

Focusing only on them is therefore a dangerous path. Many leading companies, ranging from Apple to Dyson, all too frequently end up in lawsuits trying to protect their innovations from copycats, which is an expensive way to defend an advantage.

Successful organizations go beyond product and service innovation and add other kinds, such as new ways of earning revenue or entirely new business models. In their book Ten Types of Innovation, Keeley and colleagues set out ten distinct places a company can innovate to gain or sustain competitive advantage.

Type of innovationWhat it changesExamples the chapter gives
Profit modelFinding novel ways of generating revenues from offeringsDropbox using a freemium approach; Microsoft offering 365 on a subscription basis; GE selling “thrust as a service”
NetworkHarnessing the capabilities and strengths of othersGlaxoSmithKline or Lego using open innovation for new product or service ideas; Netflix running contests for improving its movie recommendation algorithm; luxury hotels partnering with fashion designers
StructureUsing the company’s talent and assets in innovative waysSouthwest Airlines focusing on one aircraft type; Google allowing employees to use up to 20 percent of work time for personal projects
ProcessChanging primary processes used to produce products or servicesToyota pioneering lean production; Zara moving fashion from initial design to stores in 3 weeks
Product performanceCreating novel products or improving existing products through differentiationDyson’s Airblade hand dryers; Corning’s “unbreakable” Gorilla Glass; Coke’s customizable Coke bottles
Product systemCreating bundles of complementary offeringsMicrosoft bundling individual office programs into the 365 suite; Apple offering developer tools and an app store so developers can create novel apps; Marriott letting users test drive GoPro HERO action cams
ServiceSupporting and enhancing the value of an offeringZappos’s WOW philosophy of delivering excellent customer service; Men’s Wearhouse offering customers the ability to purchase free lifetime pressing
ChannelUsing innovative ways to connect offerings with customersNiketown offering immersive experiences; Nespresso partnering with hotels and airlines
BrandPositioning the brand in innovative waysThe Virgin family of brands; German discount grocer Aldi’s Trader Joe’s markets
Customer engagementDeveloping meaningful connections with customersSwarm encouraging users to frequently “check in” to places; Apple tying customers to its ecosystem

Count the rows. Product performance — the new-and-better-product row that most people mean by the word innovation — is one entry out of ten. The other nine change how the money is made, whose capabilities are borrowed, how the firm is organized, how the work gets done, what the offering is bundled with, what happens after the sale, how the offering reaches you, what the name stands for, and what the relationship feels like.

Explore

Six of the ten types up close

None of these six changes the product itself, which is why they slip past a reader who hears the word innovation and pictures a better gadget; open each card and read all four panels.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Profit model innovation · How the money arrives

  • What it changes: Finding novel ways of generating revenues from offerings, so what changes is the shape of the payment rather than the thing being paid for.
  • The chapter’s examples: Dropbox using a freemium approach, Microsoft offering 365 on a subscription basis, and GE selling “thrust as a service”, a phrase that names the move from charging for a thing to charging for what the thing delivers.
  • Why it gets missed: It gets missed because the product on the table looks identical before and after. A subscription version of a program is the same program; only the invoice has changed, and invoices are not what people photograph.
  • What a rival would have to copy: Not the pricing page, which any competitor can rewrite in an afternoon, but the cash flow, the contracts, and the customer agreements that let a firm be paid in a different shape and at a different time than before.

Network innovation · Whose capabilities you borrow

  • What it changes: Harnessing the capabilities and strengths of others, so the firm stops treating its own payroll as the boundary of what it can do.
  • The chapter’s examples: GlaxoSmithKline and Lego using open innovation to source new product or service ideas, Netflix running contests to improve its movie recommendation algorithm, and luxury hotels partnering with fashion designers.
  • Why it gets missed: It gets missed because the credit lands on the finished product. When an outside contest produces a better recommendation algorithm, the customer experiences a better algorithm and never sees the contest.
  • What a rival would have to copy: Not the announcement of an open call or a contest, which is easy to imitate, but the partners and outside contributors who choose to show up, because a competitor copying the announcement starts with an empty room.

Structure innovation · How talent and assets are arranged

  • What it changes: Using the company’s talent and assets in innovative ways, so the same people and the same equipment are organized to produce something the usual arrangement could not.
  • The chapter’s examples: Southwest Airlines focusing on one aircraft type, and Google allowing employees to use up to 20 percent of work time for personal projects.
  • Why it gets missed: It gets missed because it is invisible from outside the building. A passenger boarding a flight cannot see that every aircraft in the fleet is the same model, even though that single decision reaches maintenance, spare parts, and crew training.
  • What a rival would have to copy: Not a feature but an arrangement: matching a single-aircraft-type fleet would mean retiring the other models a rival already owns, has trained crews on, and stocks parts for.

Channel innovation · How the offering reaches you

  • What it changes: Using innovative ways to connect offerings with customers, so the encounter happens somewhere the category has not traditionally been sold.
  • The chapter’s examples: Niketown offering immersive experiences, and Nespresso partnering with hotels and airlines, so that in both cases the customer meets the offering somewhere other than a conventional store.
  • Why it gets missed: It gets missed because the product itself is unchanged, so nothing about it looks new. The innovation is the meeting place, and customers rarely think of a meeting place as an invention.
  • What a rival would have to copy: Not the product but the route to the customer, and that route is assembled one negotiated partnership at a time, so a rival has to win each hotel and each airline rather than announce a policy.

Brand innovation · What the name stands for

  • What it changes: Positioning the brand in innovative ways, so the name itself carries an expectation that competing names do not.
  • The chapter’s examples: The Virgin family of brands, and German discount grocer Aldi’s Trader Joe’s markets, which carry a name of their own rather than the parent grocer’s.
  • Why it gets missed: It gets missed because branding is often filed under advertising rather than innovation, and because the result is a feeling in the customer’s head rather than an object you can put on a table.
  • What a rival would have to copy: Not the name but what the name has come to mean, which is the accumulated result of everything done under it, so a competitor with a budget can buy attention faster than it can buy that association.

Customer engagement innovation · What the relationship feels like

  • What it changes: Developing meaningful connections with customers, so the relationship continues between purchases instead of ending at the till.
  • The chapter’s examples: Swarm encouraging users to frequently “check in” to places, and Apple tying customers to its ecosystem.
  • Why it gets missed: It gets missed because it produces no line on a product specification. Nothing on a specification sheet explains why a customer inside an ecosystem weighs one replacement against everything else already owned.
  • What a rival would have to copy: Not the hardware, which the chapter says has already been imitated: the design and functionality of Apple’s products have been widely copied, yet other companies find it difficult to copy its product system innovations or its customer engagement innovations.

Four pairs on that list get confused constantly, and keeping them apart is most of the skill.

  • Product performance against product system — product performance innovation creates novel products or differentiates existing ones, as Dyson did with its Airblade hand dryers, while product system innovation bundles complementary offerings, as Microsoft did by combining individual office programs into one suite.
  • Channel against network — channel innovation finds new ways to connect the offering with customers, as Nespresso did by partnering with hotels and airlines, while network innovation harnesses the capabilities and strengths of others, as Lego did by using open innovation for new product ideas.
  • Brand against customer engagement — brand innovation positions the name in a new way, as the Virgin family of brands does, while customer engagement innovation builds a meaningful ongoing connection, as Apple does by tying customers into its ecosystem.
  • Profit model against process — profit model innovation changes how revenue is generated, as Microsoft did by offering 365 on a subscription basis, while process innovation changes how the thing is produced, as Toyota did by pioneering lean production.

Profit model innovation
A file-storage service gives a basic account away for nothing and charges for the extra capacity heavier users need This is Dropbox’s freemium approach. The storage service is not what changed; the way revenue is generated from it is.
Network innovation
A toy company invites people outside the firm to submit ideas for new products instead of relying only on its own designers Lego and GlaxoSmithKline are the chapter’s open innovation examples, and the point is harnessing the capabilities and strengths of others.
Structure innovation
An airline flies a single type of aircraft, so crews, spare parts, and maintenance all serve one machine Southwest Airlines is the example, and it is structural because it changes how the company’s talent and assets are arranged rather than what it sells.
Process innovation
A clothing retailer compresses the path from first design to clothes on the sales floor down to three weeks Zara is the example. The garments are ordinary garments; the primary process used to produce and deliver them is what was changed.
Product performance innovation
A glassmaker develops a cover glass tough enough to be marketed as unbreakable Corning’s Gorilla Glass is the example, and it is the classic case of creating a novel product or differentiating an existing one.
Product system innovation
Separate word processing, spreadsheet, and presentation programs are sold together as a single suite Microsoft bundling individual office programs into 365 is the example, and bundling complementary offerings is what defines this type.
Service innovation
A menswear retailer lets customers buy free pressing of their garments for life Men’s Wearhouse is the example. The suit is unchanged; what surrounds and supports the purchase is what enhances its value.
Channel innovation
A coffee-machine maker places its product with hotels and airlines so travellers meet it far from any store Nespresso is the example, and the innovation is the route to the customer rather than anything about the coffee or the machine.
Brand innovation
A German discount grocer owns a chain of markets that trade under a completely separate name Aldi’s Trader Joe’s markets are the chapter’s example of positioning a brand in an innovative way.
Customer engagement innovation
A device maker ties customers into an ecosystem, so each purchase makes sense mainly in relation to the ones already made Apple is the example, and the chapter notes rivals find this far harder to copy than the design and functionality of the products themselves.
Check yourself

Innovation, radical and incremental

Four options, one best answer; every situation here that names no company is a generic hypothetical written for practice, and every named company comes from the chapter, so read every explanation, including the ones for options you did not pick.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. A research team designs a working prototype of a new kind of battery, publishes the design, and the company then shelves it. By the chapter’s definition, what does the company have?

  • A. An innovation, because a new product was successfully created and demonstrated — Creating and demonstrating something new is real work, but the chapter draws the line elsewhere: innovation involves creating new products, processes, or services that return value to the organization. A shelved prototype has returned nothing yet.
  • B. An invention, because innovation requires that the new thing return value to the organization — correct. The chapter contrasts innovation with merely inventing new products, services, or processes, and says innovation involves realizing the value. Until the design earns money, saves money, or wins a customer, the company has an invention.
  • C. A radical innovation, because the underlying technology is markedly different from existing batteries — The technology may well be markedly different, which is half of the radical definition, but the other half is that it reaches new customer segments or delivers significantly greater benefits and eventually marginalizes what came before. A shelved design reaches nobody.
  • D. An incremental innovation, because the design improves on batteries the company already sells — This would fit if the design were an upgrade the company shipped to its existing customers, since incremental innovation means enhancing or upgrading existing products, services, or processes. Nothing here was shipped or upgraded.

2. Which of the following best matches the chapter’s definition of a radical innovation?

  • A. A software vendor releases an annual update with a redesigned menu and faster file handling — A redesigned menu and faster file handling enhance an existing product, which the chapter defines as incremental innovation and calls the most common form. Useful, and genuinely innovation, but not radical.
  • B. A manufacturer negotiates lower prices from its suppliers, passes part of the saving on to customers, and takes a share of the market from a rival that could not match the new price — Cheaper supplies can improve competitiveness through cost, and the chapter does say advantage may come through cost or differentiation, but nothing here involves a markedly new or different technology or a displaced product.
  • C. A device using a markedly different technology serves customers the old product never reached, and the old product is eventually marginalized — correct. Radical innovations use a markedly new or different technology to access new customer segments or provide significantly greater benefits to existing customers, and eventually marginalize or replace existing products or services.
  • D. A company spends more on research than any of its competitors in the same industry — Research spending is an input, not an outcome. The chapter measures innovation by the value returned to the organization, so a large budget that produces nothing customers use has not produced innovation of any size.

3. The chapter’s table pairs compact discs with cassettes and records, then pairs music downloading and streaming with compact discs and music stores. What does that sequence illustrate?

  • A. That a technology which displaced an older one can itself be displaced later, so radical innovation is a chain rather than a finish line — correct. The compact disc appears in the table first as a radical innovation and later in the displaced column, and smartphones then displace the MP3 players that displaced it, which is why leading today guarantees nothing about the next round.
  • B. That the chapter regards the compact disc as an incremental improvement on the cassette rather than a radical innovation — The table lists compact discs in the left-hand column, among the radical innovations, precisely because they used a markedly different technology and marginalized cassettes and records rather than improving them.
  • C. That displacement moves slowly enough for the leading firm in each round to move into the technology that replaces it — The table records what replaced what and says nothing about the incumbent making the jump. The chapter points the other way, noting that market leaders and strong brands often find it difficult to react appropriately to new trends.
  • D. That a radical innovation displaces a technology from its own industry, since one recorded-music format gave way to the next — The same table pairs smartphones with dedicated GPS navigation, automobiles with horses, and 3D printing with CNC milling, so the displaced technology frequently sits in a different industry from the innovation that displaced it.

Combining types is what makes an advantage stick

Because product performance innovations can often be copied easily, companies frequently combine several types at once to sustain a competitive advantage. The chapter offers two cases worth studying side by side.

  • Apple — typically known for its product innovations, and the design and functionality of those products have been widely imitated, yet other companies find it difficult to copy Apple’s product system innovations or its customer engagement innovations.
  • Dell — challenged established computer manufacturers by combining profit model innovation, collecting money before building the product, with process innovation in the built-to-order model and channel innovation in selling computers online rather than in stores, as well as other types of innovation the chapter does not name.

A rival who copies your product has copied one row of ten; a rival who wants to copy several rows at once has to rebuild the company, which is why combinations outlast clever products.

Where information systems come in

Most, if not all, of these innovations are enabled by information systems, and several of them would not be possible without one. The chapter gives three examples that make the dependency concrete.

  • Airbnb — platform-based business models such as this one would not be possible without the internet, because the platform’s entire job is to connect two groups of people who would otherwise never find each other.
  • Uber — its business model could not exist without the mobile devices carried by riders and drivers, and its dynamic pricing feature, called surge pricing, would not work without real-time analysis and prediction of traffic conditions and demand for services.
  • Manufacturers of physical goods — process innovations enabled by robotics and the Industrial Internet of Things offer improvements in efficiency, product quality, agility, and flexibility, allowing companies to mass-produce customized products.

That is why an organization often has to deploy new, state-of-the-art technologies, or redeploy existing ones in clever new ways, to gain or sustain a competitive advantage.

A firm can choose instead to keep continually upgrading its older systems rather than investing in new ones. The chapter’s warning is about what those improvements buy: often, at best, only a short-lived competitive edge.

Ten types, combinations, and the systems underneath

Three questions on where a company can innovate and on why information systems keep turning up in the answer; the manager quoted in the first one is hypothetical, while every company named is one the chapter names.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. A manager says: “Our innovation strategy is simple. We build the best product in the category and defend the patents.” What is the strongest objection the chapter supports?

  • A. Competitive advantage comes from being the low-cost producer, so a strategy built on the best product aims at the wrong target — The chapter says the opposite about the target: innovation is key for organizations attempting to gain or sustain competitive advantage, be it through cost or differentiation. Building the best product is a legitimate aim; leaning on it alone is the problem.
  • B. Product performance is one of ten types of innovation, and products, even radical ones, can easily be copied, so a product-only strategy is a dangerous path — correct. The chapter warns that innovative products or services, even radical innovations, can easily be copied and that focusing only on them is a dangerous path, which is why it presents ten types rather than one.
  • C. Improving an existing product does not count as innovation, so defending a product line is not an innovation strategy at all — Enhancing or upgrading an existing product, service, or process is incremental innovation, which the chapter calls the most common form of innovation. The weakness in this plan is its narrowness, not that improvement fails to count.
  • D. Innovation is the responsibility of the research department, so a manager outside it should not be setting an innovation strategy — Nothing in the chapter confines innovation to a research department. Profit model, structure, channel, and customer engagement innovations sit with the parts of the business that set pricing, organization, routes to market, and relationships.

2. The chapter describes Dell challenging established computer manufacturers by collecting money before building the product, building to order, and selling online rather than in stores. Which types of innovation are those three, in that order?

  • A. Brand, service, and network innovation — Brand innovation positions the name in a new way, service innovation supports and enhances the offering, and network innovation harnesses the strengths of others. None of the three describes when cash is collected, how a machine is assembled, or where it is sold.
  • B. Product performance, product system, and service innovation — These three are all about the offering itself: novel or differentiated products, bundles of complementary offerings, and support around the sale. Dell’s changes were to its finances, its assembly, and its route to market.
  • C. Profit model, process, and channel innovation — correct. Collecting money before building is a profit model innovation, the built-to-order model is a process innovation, and selling online rather than in stores is a channel innovation, and the chapter presents the combination as the reason it could challenge incumbents.
  • D. Structure, customer engagement, and brand innovation — Structure innovation rearranges talent and assets, customer engagement builds an ongoing relationship, and brand innovation repositions the name. Dell may have done these too, but they are not the three changes described here.

3. Why does the chapter say Uber’s surge pricing illustrates the link between innovation and information systems?

  • A. Because riders and drivers carry mobile devices, which is the dependency the chapter attaches to surge pricing — Mobile devices are the chapter’s condition for Uber’s business model existing at all, not for surge pricing in particular. Surge pricing is tied to something narrower: real-time analysis and prediction of traffic and demand.
  • B. Because the feature depends on real-time analysis and prediction of traffic conditions and demand, so with no system there is no feature — correct. The chapter states that Uber could not implement surge pricing without real-time analysis and prediction of traffic conditions and demand for services, just as its business model could not exist without the mobile devices riders and drivers carry.
  • C. Because surge pricing raises revenue, which is the measure the chapter uses to judge whether an innovation succeeded — Revenue matters, since innovation is defined as returning value to the organization, but the chapter raises surge pricing to show a capability that only an information system can supply, not to score its profitability.
  • D. Because a business model built on mobile devices is inherently harder for competitors to copy than one built on physical stores — The chapter argues nearly the reverse elsewhere: information systems are frequently bought from vendors and rivals can copy them, so a mobile business model carries no built-in protection.

Section 2–3b

Innovating in practice

Knowing that innovation matters is the easy part. This section is the hard part: why innovating with information systems so often fails, what a disciplined process for doing it looks like, and what an organization must change about itself first.

Nobody sees it coming

In 1999 Sir John Maddox, a physicist who edited the journal Nature for 22 years, was quoted in Scientific American saying that the most important discoveries of the next 50 years are likely to be ones we cannot now even conceive. The internet makes his point: in 1999 it was not on the radar screens of many business organizations, and firms with websites were mostly providing an electronic brochure.

The chapter’s answer is structural. Organizations that want to stay relevant must become bimodal: one part exploits existing capabilities and technologies, a focus on earning, while another discovers and develops new interactions or service offerings enabled by increasing digital density, a focus on learning.

Four reasons innovating is hard

The chapter gives four separate reasons that innovating with information systems is harder than it looks, and they are genuinely different problems rather than four ways of saying one thing.

  • Successful innovation is difficult — systems are often bought from or built by someone else, so a firm typically cannot patent its use of one, the way a soft-drink company can patent a cola formula.
  • Innovation is often fleeting — even an in-house system uses hardware, software, and networking components rivals can also buy, so smart rivals quickly duplicate or improve on any use that visibly wins.
  • Innovation is often risky — choosing among innovative investments always entails risk, because the option most experts call superior is not always the one the market settles on.
  • Innovation choices are often difficult — picking a technology is like hitting one of several equally attractive fast-moving targets, because forecasting the growth, use, and importance of an emerging technology has defeated experts and organizations again and again.

The patent point is where intuition usually fails. The data in a system may be proprietary; the system itself typically is not, particularly when purchased from a vendor. One exception matters: a system developed by a consultant or an outsourcing partner is proprietary to the organization.

Two things do resist copying. Amazon’s patented “one-click” ordering process has been successfully defended in the courts, and it is often difficult to copy the “secret sauce” key to how a system functions or succeeds.

Risk is easiest to see in consumer electronics. Most experts agreed Sony’s Betamax had better recording and playback quality than JVC’s VHS, and VHS won the marketplace anyway; later, Sony’s Blu-ray beat the HD DVD format Microsoft and Toshiba backed. For an organization the same choice is far riskier, given the size and mission-critical nature of the investment.

Forecasting is why the choices stay hard. The 1994 Technology Forecast from the consulting firm Price Waterhouse, now PwC, mentioned the word internet on five pages of a 750-page document; the next year more than 75 pages addressed it, and by the 1997 briefing it was pervasive throughout.

Explore

The four reasons innovating with information systems is hard

Open each obstacle and read all four panels; the last panel is the one that changes what you would actually do.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Successful innovation is difficult · You usually cannot own it

  • What the difficulty is: There are limits to using emerging information systems to innovate and gain or sustain a competitive advantage, because information systems are often bought from or built by someone else.
  • Why it happens: If the systems are purchased from a vendor, they are usually not proprietary technologies owned by the organization. The data in the system may be proprietary, but the information system typically is not.
  • The chapter’s example: A soft-drink company can patent the formula of a cola and a pharmaceutical company can patent a new drug, yet an organization typically cannot patent its use of an information system.
  • What it means for a decision: One exception is worth remembering: if the system is developed by a consultant or an outsourcing partner, it is proprietary to the organization. And because many business models have information systems at their very core, organizations are often forced to develop such systems regardless of what can be protected.

Innovation is often fleeting · Assume the copy is coming

  • What the difficulty is: Given the pace of change in the digital world, advantages gained by innovations often have a limited life span, so the practical question is less whether the advantage erodes than how long it holds.
  • Why it happens: Even where an organization developed an innovative system in-house, it usually did so with hardware, software, and networking components that others can also purchase, so rivals can copy innovative information systems.
  • The chapter’s example: The chapter’s classic counterexample is Amazon’s patented “one-click” ordering process, which has been successfully defended in the courts; it adds that the “secret sauce” key to the functioning or success of a system is often difficult to copy.
  • What it means for a decision: Plan for duplication rather than against it. If use of a new system causes one organization to gain a significant advantage over others, smart rivals are quick to duplicate or improve on that use, and rivals can copy innovative products, services, and processes as well, so the question worth asking early is which part of the advantage is genuinely hard to copy.

Innovation is often risky · The better technology can lose

  • What the difficulty is: Choosing among innovative investments in information systems, or among potential product, service, or process innovations, always entails risk that no amount of technical analysis removes.
  • Why it happens: The risk does not come from bad analysis; it comes from the market, not the expert consensus, settling the outcome. In the early days of the videocassette recorder, most experts agreed that Sony’s Betamax had superior recording and playback quality, yet JVC’s VHS ultimately won the battle in the marketplace, so people who made the “smart” choice at the time chose badly.
  • The chapter’s example: The rematch came with high-definition discs: Microsoft, Toshiba, and many others backed the HD DVD format while Sony led the fight for Blu-ray and incorporated it into the PlayStation 3. Sony won, with the HD DVD Promotion Group dissolving in early 2008.
  • What it means for a decision: For an organization the stakes are higher than for a shopper. Choosing among the plethora of available innovative technologies is far riskier given the size and often mission-critical nature of the investment, whereas a suboptimal video player is usually just disappointing.

Innovation choices are often difficult · Forecasts keep missing

  • What the difficulty is: Choosing new technologies in the information systems area to develop innovative products, services, or processes is like trying to hit one of several equally attractive fast-moving targets.
  • Why it happens: Given the pace of research and development in the information systems and components area, and the increasing digital density, staying current has been nearly impossible. Intel founder Gordon Moore predicted that the number of transistors squeezed onto a chip would double every 24 months, a number now often reduced to 18 months, and some computer hardware and software firms roll out new versions of their products every three months.
  • The chapter’s example: The 1994 Technology Forecast prepared by the major consulting firm Price Waterhouse, now PwC, mentioned the word internet on only five pages of a 750-page document; the next year more than 75 pages addressed it, and by the 1997 briefing it was a pervasive topic throughout.
  • What it means for a decision: Back in 1994 it would have been difficult, perhaps even foolish, to forecast that growth. The chapter’s table of predictions that were not quite correct makes the same point company by company, including Western Union’s 1876 internal memo calling the telephone inherently of no value and Steve Ballmer saying in 2007 that there was no chance the iPhone would get any significant market share, so a technology choice is better treated as a hypothesis to test cheaply than as a forecast to commit to.

What actually lasts

So what survives contact with a competitor? If you use information systems for operating efficiencies, rivals can just as easily adopt the same types of systems and achieve the same gains. Two routes hold up longer.

  • Make the product or service unique — the Israeli tech startup Waze built a routing and navigation algorithm combining map data, real-time traffic information, and crowdsourced data, and Google purchased the app in 2013.
  • Raise the customer’s switching costs — Salesforce.com stores the entire history of a firm’s interactions with each customer, so switching to a rival would cost significant time and money and take years to rebuild.

Efficiency gains are borrowable; a customer’s accumulated history is not, which is why the chapter treats uniqueness and switching costs as the durable forms of advantage.

The lean startup methodology

Traditionally companies would develop a product and then try to find a market for it, which the chapter calls inside-out thinking. Innovative companies reverse it, in outside-in thinking: they focus on the ends, meaning the customer’s job-to-be-done and the friction points preventing the customer from accomplishing their goals.

That reversal matters more now because incumbents face competition from many small, nimble startups, not just a few traditional rivals. The lean startup methodology, pioneered by Eric Ries, gives the response a shape: a company first searches for a viable product and business model, and executes that model only after finding a fit between product and market.

  • Customer discovery, in search — you establish whether the perceived problem actually exists, whether a market for a solution exists, and whether your envisioned solution addresses it, which means “getting out of the building” before building anything.
  • Customer validation, in search — you test whether customers would be willing to pay, using a minimum viable product, because a finished product is an expensive way to learn you were wrong.
  • Customer creation, in execution — you test whether it is possible to establish a repeatable business model, now that the product has stopped being the open question.
  • Company building, in execution — the final step builds the company and scales operations and the organization around an already validated model.

A minimum viable product (MVP) contains just the features needed to demonstrate how your solution meets the problem, so its purpose is to test a hypothesis cheaply.

If a hypothesis fails during the search, it is time to pivot — change direction while staying grounded in what you learned. Instagram began as Burbn, an app of features from check-ins to gaming; when users did not value them, the founders stripped it to photo sharing and commenting.

Those iterations form the build-measure-learn cycle, which enables validated learning: empirically testing hypotheses through customer feedback to improve future iterations. You build the MVP quickly, measure by collecting data such as questionnaire responses, then learn by deciding whether to pivot or persevere. Established companies from Alaska Airlines to Philips to 3M use the method too.

Sequence

The lean startup search, from first conversation to finished company

Put the six moves into the order the chapter describes, remembering that everything in the search phase happens before anything in the execution phase.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

The lean startup methodology, pioneered by Eric Ries, splits the work into a search phase and an execution phase: a company first searches for a viable product and business model, and only executes that business model once it has found a fit between the product and the market.

  1. Get out of the building and talk to potential customers, to find out whether the perceived problem actually exists and whether there would be a market for a hypothetical solution. — Customer discovery starts with the problem, not the product. The chapter is explicit that this entails talking to potential customers before starting to build something, which is why it comes first.
  2. Still within customer discovery, establish whether your envisioned solution would actually address the problem you have just confirmed is real. — A real problem and a solution that fits it are two separate hypotheses. The second step of customer discovery tests the second one, and skipping it means building for a problem you cannot solve.
  3. Build a minimum viable product containing just the features needed to demonstrate how your solution meets the problem. — The MVP is the instrument for the next test, so it comes after both discovery hypotheses hold and before anyone is asked to pay. Building it earlier means testing a solution to a problem nobody confirmed.
  4. Move into customer validation to test whether customers would be willing to pay, running build-measure-learn cycles and pivoting whenever a hypothesis does not hold. — Validation is where willingness to pay is tested rather than assumed, and it is where the build-measure-learn cycle produces validated learning. A failing hypothesis here triggers a pivot back into discovery, not a push forward.
  5. Cross from search into execution with customer creation, testing the hypothesis of whether it is possible to establish a repeatable business model. — The dividing line matters: the company only executes the business model once it has found product/market fit, so this step is meaningless before validation succeeds.
  6. Build the company, scaling operations and the organization around the model that has now been validated. — The final step entails building the company and scaling operations and the organization, which is the only point at which heavy investment is justified by evidence rather than by hope.

Open innovation

Because innovating internally is this hard, organizations increasingly realize the potential for innovation often exists outside their boundaries, and they try to harness the creativity of external stakeholders. Open innovation is the process of integrating external stakeholders into the innovation process.

Eli Lilly created InnoCentive, where companies post scientific problems, everybody can take a shot at them, and a reward is usually paid to a successful solver. P&G, Lego with Lego Ideas, and Heineken with Brewhouse have also used open innovation to solicit ideas for novel products, services, or processes.

What that arrangement changes is worth stating precisely.

  • The research network becomes ad hoc — companies rely less on a dedicated research-and-development department or on hiring specialists, because the problem is posted rather than staffed.
  • Contributors work on their own terms — people use spare time and expertise to solve problems and earn rewards, so effort arrives from outside the payroll.
  • The price is openness — the arrangement often involves making organizational data and knowledge accessible to outsiders, so benefits must be balanced against the potential drawbacks.
Check yourself

Why innovating is hard, and what lasts

Four options, one best answer; read every explanation, including the ones for the options you did not pick.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. A manager says: “Our new logistics system gives us an edge, and because we built it in-house, competitors cannot copy it.” What is the accurate correction?

  • A. The manager is right, because a system developed in-house is a proprietary technology the organization can patent — An organization typically cannot patent its use of an information system, unlike a soft-drink company patenting a cola formula or a pharmaceutical firm patenting a drug. Building it yourself changes who maintains it, not whether that use can be legally protected.
  • B. The manager is right, because information systems developed in-house are harder for rivals to copy than innovative products, services, or processes are — The chapter puts them in the same position rather than ranking them. Rivals can copy innovative information systems, and rivals can copy innovative products, services, and processes as well, which is why the caution applies across the board.
  • C. Even an in-house system is built with hardware, software, and networking components others can also purchase, so the advantage can be short-lived — correct. Even where an organization develops a system in-house it uses components others can buy, and smart rivals are quick to duplicate or improve on a use of a system that produces a significant advantage.
  • D. The manager is wrong, because any advantage the system creates belongs to the vendors that supplied its hardware, software, and networking components — Those components are purchasable by anyone, which is exactly why the advantage tends to be short-lived, but the organization is still the party that gains it. The chapter also names cases where the gain held, such as Amazon’s defended one-click patent and a hard-to-copy secret sauce.

2. Which pair of facts does the chapter use specifically to show that forecasting emerging technologies is difficult?

  • A. A 1994 consulting forecast mentioned the internet on five of 750 pages, and by the 1997 briefing the internet was a pervasive topic throughout — correct. The Price Waterhouse forecast went from five pages to more than 75 the following year to pervasive coverage three years later, which shows how fast an emerging technology can outrun expert expectation.
  • B. Betamax had better recording quality than VHS, and Sony later led Blu-ray to victory over HD DVD — Both facts are accurate and both come from the chapter, but they illustrate the risk of choosing wrong between competing formats rather than the difficulty of forecasting which technologies will matter at all.
  • C. Eli Lilly created InnoCentive, and P&G, Lego, and Heineken solicited ideas from outsiders — These are the open innovation examples. They describe one response to how hard innovation is, not evidence about anyone’s ability to predict which technologies will grow.
  • D. Instagram began life as an app called Burbn, and its founders stripped it back until nothing was left of it but photo sharing and commenting — That is the chapter’s illustration of a pivot inside the lean startup methodology, showing a company changing direction based on what it learned from users, not a claim about technology forecasting.

3. Your firm’s information systems have sharply cut operating costs. Why is that unlikely to yield a lasting competitive advantage, and what would?

  • A. Because savings in operating costs stay inside the firm, so they cannot influence how customers choose between one supplier and another — The chapter treats innovation as key to gaining or sustaining competitive advantage, be it through cost or differentiation, so a cost position is a legitimate route and customers do feel it in prices. What undermines this particular advantage is how easily rivals can imitate it, not the decision to chase efficiency.
  • B. Because efficiency gains show up in published financial results, so rivals can read them there and respond in the same quarter — Rivals do not need to read a competitor’s financial statements to catch up here. The chapter’s mechanism is simpler and harder to hide from: rivals can just as easily adopt the same types of information systems and achieve the same gains.
  • C. Because efficiency gains decay on their own over time, so the firm should relaunch the same system on a regular schedule — Nothing in the chapter says a working system decays by itself; what erodes the advantage is imitation by rivals. The chapter does warn that continually upgrading older systems rather than investing in new ones can at best give a short-lived competitive edge, so a relaunch schedule spends money without addressing the cause.
  • D. Because rivals can just as easily adopt the same types of systems and achieve the same gains; making the product unique or raising switching costs lasts longer — correct. Rivals can adopt the same efficiency systems, so the durable routes are uniqueness and high switching costs — Waze’s distinctive routing algorithm and Salesforce.com’s accumulated record of every customer interaction are the chapter’s two examples.

What an organization needs in place

Established organizations can benefit from radical approaches to innovation, but that sometimes requires fundamental changes to the organization itself: its processes, resources, and risk tolerance must be capable of adapting to and sustaining the development and implementation process.

  • Process requirements — organizational processes and incentive systems must change, because developing an MVP with agile approaches requires close collaboration of cross-functional teams, which is uncommon in established organizations.
  • Resource requirements — the firm needs enough employees with the relevant knowledge, skills, and time to quickly build MVPs, or able systems partners to outsource that development to.
  • Risk tolerance requirements — members must tolerate risk and uncertainty and be willing to test products that may not meet customers’ requirements, and to fail fast if needed.

Two details are easy to skip and expensive to miss. Accountability and incentives belong at the team level rather than the individual level, because an experiment is a shared act. And the method needs a startup-like budgeting model, where funds are approved as a project moves through the stages, or can quickly be cut if the anticipated results do not appear.

Risk tolerance reaches further than products: open innovation typically requires sharing organizational knowledge with outside partners. Where people within the organization desire low risk, gambling on cutting-edge innovations with a lean startup approach will probably not be tolerable.

Self-check

Could this organization actually innovate?

Rate each statement honestly; anything you cannot do yet has a pointer to the exact place in this section to reread.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

  • I can name the three organizational requirements for innovation and say what each one actually demands of the company. The section on what an organization needs in place: process, resource, and risk tolerance requirements.
  • I can explain why accountability and incentives have to sit at the team level rather than the individual level. The paragraph following the three requirements, where cross-functional collaboration and team-level incentives appear together.
  • I can describe the budgeting model the lean startup methodology needs, and say why a single annual approval does not fit it. The startup-like model where funds are approved as a project moves through the stages, or can quickly be cut.
  • I can state the two ways an organization can satisfy the resource requirement when it lacks the right people in-house. Enough employees with the relevant knowledge, skills, and time to build MVPs quickly, or able systems partners to outsource to.
  • I can explain why risk tolerance applies to open innovation and not only to unproven products. The risk tolerance paragraph, on sharing organizational knowledge with outside partners.
  • I can say what happens to a lean startup effort inside an organization whose members desire low risk. The closing line of the risk tolerance requirement, on gambling on cutting-edge innovations.
  • I can explain what a bimodal organization is and why the chapter recommends becoming one. The opening of this section, on the part of the organization that earns and the part that learns.
  • I can tell the difference between a requirement the organization must change and an obstacle it can only plan around. Read the three requirements against the four reasons innovating is hard, and notice which list the organization controls.

Three ways to think about radical innovations

The chapter closes by turning three familiar habits around, each uncomfortable on purpose.

  • Put technology ahead of strategy — with increasing digital density, technology is so important to strategy and success that you begin there, because retrofitting technology into an aging strategy is, many would argue, doomed.
  • Think in terms of problems before designing solutions — drop inside-out thinking for outside-in thinking, because customers understand their problems well but are not experts in solutions or in new technologies.
  • Innovation is continuous — innovative companies constantly look for the next new thing and keep getting out of the building to test new hypotheses, because the rate of technology evolution will not slow down.

Steve Jobs of Apple is quoted on the second point: you cannot just ask people what they want and then give it to them, because by the time you build it they will want something new. If your customers already know about a technology, your competitors probably do too, so it is not the one to rest your advantage on.

The third point is the troubling one. If you lead an industry you must continually learn to embrace and exploit radical innovations, potentially destroying your existing core business while building a new business around the innovation. If you fail to do this, your competition may do it for you.

Decide

Funding an innovation the disciplined way

Work through four decisions in this clearly hypothetical situation, and read every outcome before moving on, including the ones you did not choose.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

This is a hypothetical practice situation, not a report about any real company. You lead a small team at a regional appliance retailer whose leadership has set aside money for one innovation effort. The conditions below are supplied only so the reasoning has something to work on.

Decision 1. Two competing smart-home platforms are fighting to become the industry standard, and your engineers report that one of them is clearly the better technology. Leadership wants to commit the entire product line to it this quarter.

  • Commit to the technically superior platform, on the reasoning that the better technology wins in the end — This is the Betamax mistake exactly. Most experts agreed Betamax had superior recording and playback quality, and VHS ultimately won the battle in the marketplace, so the people who made the “smart” choice at the time chose badly. Technical merit is evidence about the product, not a forecast of the market.
  • Build a minimum viable product on one platform, designed so that moving to the other would be cheap — the stronger call. Right. An MVP carries just the features needed to demonstrate how your solution meets the problem, so it tests the idea without betting the product line on a format war. It also keeps the pivot affordable, and a pivot is a change of direction grounded in what you learned.
  • Delay the entire effort until one of the two formats is formally declared the industry standard — Waiting trades format risk for a worse one. Some hardware and software firms roll out new versions every three months, so a company that only moves once uncertainty clears arrives after rivals have started accumulating the customer history that makes an advantage durable.

Decision 2. Your team proposes six months of development to finish the complete feature set before showing anything to a single customer.

  • Approve the plan, because showing customers a half-finished product would damage the company’s reputation — This is inside-out thinking: develop a product, then look for a market for it. The chapter’s alternative is outside-in thinking, which starts from the customer’s job-to-be-done and the friction points in the way, and it requires getting out of the building before the building starts.
  • Skip customer conversations and run a large advertising campaign to see whether interest exists — Marketing response is a legitimate measurement inside the build-measure-learn cycle, which names the effectiveness of search engine marketing campaigns as one kind of data. But it measures reactions to a message, and you have not yet confirmed that the underlying problem exists or that your solution addresses it.
  • Send the team to talk to potential customers first, confirming that the problem is real and that your solution would address it — the stronger call. Right, and that is customer discovery in both of its steps. The chapter is blunt about the method: talk to potential customers, getting out of the building, before starting to build something. A six-month build tests nothing until the day it ships.

Decision 3. The MVP validates, but one hard technical problem inside it sits outside your team’s expertise, and nobody currently on staff can solve it.

  • Post the problem publicly and pay a reward to whoever solves it, accepting that some organizational knowledge becomes visible — the stronger call. Right. This is open innovation, the process of integrating external stakeholders into the innovation process, as Eli Lilly did with InnoCentive, where companies post problems, everybody can take a shot, and a reward is usually paid to a successful solver. You also named the cost correctly: such initiatives often involve making organizational data and knowledge accessible to outsiders.
  • Hire and train a specialist team of your own over the next year — Resources genuinely are one of the three organizational requirements, and having employees with the relevant knowledge, skills, and time to quickly build MVPs is what that requirement asks for. The trouble is the clock: a year of recruiting is not quick, and the chapter offers routes designed for exactly this gap.
  • Drop the feature, on the grounds that the organization cannot build what it cannot staff — The resource requirement offers an alternative before it offers a surrender: the organization must have resources and able systems partners available to outsource the development of such systems if necessary. Dropping the feature answers a staffing problem by abandoning a customer problem you already validated.

Decision 4. Finance will fund the work only through a single annual approval, and the company rewards individual employees for hitting their own personal targets.

  • Accept the terms, because securing the funding matters more than the shape the funding takes — The shape is the part that decides whether the method can run at all. The iterative nature of the lean startup methodology necessitates a more startup-like budgeting model, where funds are approved as the project moves through the stages, or can quickly be cut if the project does not bring the anticipated results.
  • Keep the annual budget and reassure leadership that none of the experiments will fail — A promise like that quietly converts a search phase into an execution phase. Validated learning means empirically testing assumptions or hypotheses through customer feedback, and a hypothesis nobody is permitted to disprove is not being tested, only announced.
  • Ask for staged funding and team-level accountability, and say plainly that some experiments are expected to fail — the stronger call. Right on all three counts. The chapter asks for funds approved as the project moves through the stages, for accountability and incentives at the team level rather than the individual level, and for members with an appropriate tolerance for risk and uncertainty and the willingness to fail fast.

Startups and crowdfunding

Startups are typically technology-based new ventures with high potential for scalability and growth, often cofounded by entrepreneurs, developers, or designers with a promising idea. They were long built around services or platforms enabled by information systems, but 3D printing has enabled hardware startups built around physical objects, from Coin’s electronic credit card to the Square Reader.

Prototyping quickly is not the whole job. Reaching manufactured stock also requires knowledge of the business environment, connections with the business community, and often substantial financial resources, and startups seek that support in four places.

  • Startup incubators — they provide various types of education and other resources, which is what an unproven idea usually needs first.
  • Startup accelerators — they typically provide education, investment, and intense mentorship for cohorts of startups, so money and guidance arrive together.
  • Angel investors — they can be a valuable source of funding, but often provide only limited education or mentorship, so the venture supplies its own direction.
  • Crowdfunding — through platforms such as Kickstarter or Indiegogo, it secures business financing from individuals in the marketplace, the “crowd,” typically for a consumer-based product.

Crowdfunding has one rule that makes it unlike ordinary investment. Backers pledge a certain amount in return for certain benefits, generally one count of the item backed. If, and only if, the campaign reaches its funding goal are backers charged and the product produced; otherwise the campaign fails and nobody is charged. Kickstarter has helped fund more than 280,000 projects totaling more than US$8 billion in pledges.

Equity crowdfunding, sometimes called crowdinvesting, secures financing the same way but changes what comes back: backers receive equity in return for their investment rather than a product.

Innovation, as this chapter treats it, is not a flash of cleverness; it is a search process with a budget model, a team structure, and a tolerance for being wrong in public.

Check yourself

Lean startup, open innovation, and funding the venture

Three questions on the method itself and on where the money and the ideas come from.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. What is a minimum viable product for?

  • A. Releasing a cheap cut-down edition of a finished product to customers who cannot afford the full version — An MVP is not a budget edition aimed at a lower-priced segment. It belongs to the search phase, and its audience is the potential customers whose problem and willingness to pay you are still trying to confirm.
  • B. Containing just the features needed to demonstrate how your solution meets the problem, so a hypothesis can be tested — correct. The MVP exists so that customer validation can test whether customers would be willing to pay, which is why it carries only the features that demonstrate the solution.
  • C. Proving to investors that the engineering team can deliver a complete product on schedule — Delivery capability is a genuine concern, and the resource requirement does ask whether an organization has people who can build MVPs quickly. But the MVP itself is an instrument for learning about customers, not a demonstration of engineering throughput.
  • D. Locking in the product design before customer feedback arrives, so the team avoids expensive changes later — This inverts the method. The build-measure-learn cycle exists precisely so that feedback changes the product, and discovering that a hypothesis does not hold is the signal to pivot rather than something to design around.

2. A company posts an unsolved technical problem on a public platform and pays a reward to whoever solves it. What has it gained, and what has it accepted?

  • A. It has gained a permanent research department at no cost, and accepted that it must pay a reward to everyone who submits an attempt — The network created this way is ad hoc rather than a permanent department, and the reward is usually paid to a successful solver rather than to everyone who takes a shot at the problem. The cost the chapter names explicitly is a different one entirely.
  • B. It has gained legal ownership of every idea submitted, and accepted a longer development timeline — Ownership of every submission is not what the chapter describes; it describes rewards paid to successful solvers. A longer timeline is not the point either, since open innovation is a response to how slow and hard internal innovation can be.
  • C. It has gained a way to avoid hiring specialists, and accepted that it can no longer run a research department of its own — The first half is close, because companies can rely less on a dedicated research-and-development department or on hiring specialists. The second half does not follow, since relying less on an internal department is not the same as giving it up.
  • D. It has gained an ad hoc research-and-development network, and accepted that organizational data and knowledge become accessible to outsiders — correct. An ad hoc research-and-development network is created, and integrating external stakeholders often involves making organizational data and knowledge accessible to them, so the benefits must be balanced against that exposure.

3. A hardware startup runs a Kickstarter campaign for a new gadget and falls short of its funding goal. What happens, and what would equity crowdfunding have changed?

  • A. The campaign fails and no backers are charged any money; under equity crowdfunding, backers would receive equity rather than the product — correct. Backers are charged if and only if the campaign reaches its funding goal, and equity crowdfunding, sometimes called crowdinvesting, is the version where backers receive equity in return for their investment.
  • B. Backers are charged what they pledged and then receive a partial refund; equity crowdfunding would have removed the funding goal entirely — Backers are charged only when the goal is met, so there is nothing to refund. Equity crowdfunding changes what backers receive for their money rather than whether a campaign carries a target at all.
  • C. The campaign proceeds at a reduced scale, and equity crowdfunding would have added mentorship alongside the money — A campaign that misses its goal fails rather than shrinking to fit. Mentorship belongs to incubators and accelerators, with accelerators typically providing education, investment, and intense mentorship for cohorts of startups.
  • D. Backers automatically become part owners of the venture, and equity crowdfunding would have converted their pledges into ordinary pre-orders — This reverses the two models. Ordinary crowdfunding backers pledge in return for benefits, generally one count of the item being backed, while equity crowdfunding is the version in which backers receive equity instead.

Application supplement · 2–4

AI in the strategy workflow

Imagine two regional chains subscribing to the same artificial intelligence service in the same week. One asks it what the company should do and believes the answer. The other uses it to assemble the evidence, then argues in a room full of people about what that evidence means. Same subscription, different place in the workflow. This supplemental section is about choosing that place deliberately.

How this supplement relates to the chapter. Chapter 2 is about how information systems create value and how they win advantage, and it names the conditions that make an advantage last or fade — the technology/strategy fit, the ten types of innovation, and the plain warning that innovation is often fleeting because rivals can copy it. Artificial intelligence appears in the chapter only in passing, monitoring equipment alongside IoT sensors and imagining a shopping assistant that has not arrived yet. What this section adds is where AI fits inside that same analysis — the analysis does not change just because the technology is new. That is why this appears as a labeled supplement rather than as a fourth chapter learning objective.

The question this section answers
