Chapter 2 gives an information system three ways to add value. Automating is doing things faster, organizational learning is doing things better, and supporting strategy is doing things smarter. The chapter draws them as three bars of business value added, with automating the shortest and strategizing the tallest.

Artificial intelligence is not a fourth bar. It is a new means to those same three ends, so a proposal to buy it answers exactly the questions any other system answers.

  • Faster — the tool shortens work people already do, such as condensing a year of customer complaints into a readable list, and that is an automating benefit measured in time and cost like any other.
  • Better — the tool helps the organization use past behavior and data to improve a business process, such as noticing that those complaints cluster in one region, which is what the chapter calls organizational learning.
  • Smarter — the tool serves the plan the company chose for gaining or sustaining advantage over rivals, because a system that strengthens no chosen activity is not supporting a strategy at all.

The chapter is blunt about which of the three has to be present. A proposed system that will not clearly deliver strategic value, while also helping people work smarter and save money along the way, is not likely to be funded. Nothing about the letters A and I exempts a purchase from that test.

Where AI enters the strategy workflow

Strategy work has a shape. Someone gathers evidence about what is squeezing the business, someone turns that evidence into a claim about which force or which activity matters, and someone executes the initiative that follows. AI can enter all three of those places, and it enters each one differently.

  1. Gathering the evidence — it reads and condenses a great deal of material quickly, such as a stack of supplier contracts or a year of messages, which shortens the slowest part of a diagnosis without making any of that material true.
  2. Analysing the evidence — it can lay out how the same pattern reads as rivalry, as a new entrant, and as a substitute, which is useful precisely because one lost sale can honestly be told as a story about any of the five forces.
  3. Executing the initiative — it can carry the repetitive work inside whatever system the company decides to build, such as sorting arriving messages by topic, and this is where most of the measurable hours are actually saved.

There is a fourth step it does not enter. Choosing which force to answer, and what the company will therefore not do, is an executive-level decision, and the chapter calls those decisions unstructured because few or no procedures for them can be specified in advance.

Interactive diagram

Where AI enters, and where it does not

Pick a place in the strategy workflow to redraw it: what the step produces, what AI genuinely helps with there, what it cannot supply, and the control that keeps the step honest.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Gathering the evidence — Before the claim — assembling the material a diagnosis will rest on

The raw material (Complaints, contracts, prices, notes) → What AI does well (Reads a great deal, condenses fast) → What it cannot supply (Whether any of it is true) → The control (Someone who can check, checks)

  • What the step produces — the observable facts a claim will stand on, such as sales falling only at the locations a new competitor reached. Evidence is what stops a strategy meeting from being two opinions.
  • What AI genuinely helps with — volume. Condensing a year of messages or a shelf of contracts is the slowest part of a diagnosis and the part where a tool saves hours that can be counted.
  • What it cannot supply — truth. A summary reads exactly the same whether every line came from the source or one line did not, so nothing in the output signals which sentences to distrust.
  • The control — a person who already knows the material verifies the checkable parts, meaning figures, dates, names and terms, before any of it enters a recommendation that someone will fund.

Analysing the evidence — The claim — turning a pattern into a named force or a named activity

The pattern (Sales fell only where the club opened) → Competing readings (Rivalry, new entrant, or substitute) → What AI does well (Argues all three readings quickly) → What it cannot decide (Which reading the firm will act on)

  • What the step produces — one named force from the five, or one named activity in the value chain, plus the reason that name beats the alternatives. Name the wrong one and the company buys the wrong system.
  • What AI genuinely helps with — making the alternatives visible. Asked to argue the case for rivalry, for a new entrant, and for a substitute, it produces three readings faster than a team can, which is a real service when a lost sale fits all three.
  • What it cannot decide — which reading the organization commits to. That commitment sets what the firm will not do, and the chapter classes decisions of that kind as unstructured, meaning no procedure for them can be written in advance.
  • The control — the analyst states the chosen reading, the evidence for it, and the strongest argument against it, so the room is deciding between named alternatives rather than nodding at the only one presented.

Executing the initiative — After the decision — the repetitive work inside the system the firm builds

The initiative (One record of every supplier quote) → Work inside it (Sorting, matching, drafting, tagging) → Where the hours are (Volume, not judgment) → The limit (It runs the plan; it is not the plan)

  • What the step produces — the working system itself, and the change in how people do the job around it. The chapter is firm that a significant implementation requires commensurate, significant organizational change rather than dropping software into an unchanged process.
  • What AI genuinely helps with — the high-volume, low-stakes steps inside that system, such as tagging arriving messages by topic or matching a quote to the right contract, where being wrong is cheap and easily corrected.
  • Where the value shows up — this is the automating rung, doing the same work faster and more cheaply. That is a genuine benefit, and on its own it is the shortest of the chapter’s three bars of business value added.
  • The limit — execution cannot rescue a badly chosen initiative. Automating a flawed process magnifies its errors, which is exactly the chapter’s point about a loan department reviewing three times as many applications and approving three times as many bad ones.

Owning the recommendation — The step AI does not enter — deciding, and answering for the decision

The decision (Which force the firm will answer) → Its character (Unstructured, complex, long-term) → Who signs (A named person, before funding) → What they owe (An explanation at the review date)

  • What the step produces — a named person who says this is what we should do and why, and who is still there when the measure is read. A recommendation with no owner is a document, not a decision.
  • Why it stays human — executive-level decisions are unstructured, complex and nonroutine, with broad and long-term ramifications for the whole organization, and the chapter says few or no procedures for them can be specified in advance.
  • What is being owned — not the words but the consequences. Funding one initiative means not funding another, and firms are constrained by time and money to build only the systems that add the most value.
  • The failure to avoid — treating an output as the decision. If nobody in the room can explain why this force and not another, the organization cannot defend the spending and cannot learn from it when the numbers arrive.

Augment, automate, or leave it alone

The previous module offered a three-way decision for any piece of work. Strategy work is itself a set of tasks, so the same three words apply to it, and the vocabulary is kept identical on purpose so that the two modules agree rather than compete.

  • Augment — the system drafts, ranks or summarizes and a person decides, which suits work where a starting point saves real time but the judgment still matters, such as a first pass over three years of sales figures.
  • Automate — the system acts on its own inside limits written before launch, which suits high-volume, low-stakes, reversible work, such as pulling competitors’ published prices into one weekly list.
  • Leave it alone — the task stays entirely with people because the stakes or the sensitivity are too high, such as choosing the generic strategy the firm will pursue, or anything resting on material that must not leave the company.

Most strategy work belongs in the first bucket, because an analysis is only worth as much as the argument a named person can make for it out loud, in a room, to people who disagree.

Sort

Augment, automate, or keep it human?

Each item is a piece of strategy work at a hypothetical regional chain of bicycle shops. Place it in the mode it belongs to, judging by what one wrong answer would cost.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Augment — the system drafts, ranks or summarizes and a person decides before anything is acted on

  • Condensing a year of customer complaint messages into a short list of recurring themes an analyst then interprets — Reading the pile is the slow part and interpreting it is the judgment, so the system supplies the themes and the analyst decides what they mean.
  • Setting out how the same sales decline reads as rivalry, as a new entrant, and as a substitute, so an analyst can weigh all three — Producing the competing readings is genuinely useful, and choosing among them is the diagnosis itself, which is the shape of augmentation.
  • Summarizing nine supplier contracts into one table of prices, terms and expiry dates that a buyer checks against the originals — A missed clause changes what the chain is bound to, so the summary saves the reading time while a person still verifies the terms that matter.
  • Drafting the first version of the one-sentence recommendation, which the analyst rewrites before it reaches the board — A blank page is the expensive part of writing and the claim is the risky part, so the draft comes from the system and the wording stays with the analyst.

Automate — the system acts on its own inside limits written in advance — high volume, low stakes, reversible

  • Collecting competitors’ published prices into one weekly list that nobody assembles by hand — It is high volume, low stakes and reversible, since a price copied wrongly is corrected the moment anyone compares it with the published page.
  • Tagging arriving customer messages by topic so a weekly count of each theme is ready on Monday morning — A message filed under the wrong topic is refiled in seconds, and no decision rests on any single message, so acting without a reviewer is worth it here.
  • Reformatting last quarter’s figures into the chart layout the board pack has always used — The numbers are already agreed and the task has one obvious right answer, so this is clerical work whose only possible error is visible at a glance.

Keep human-only — the stakes or the sensitivity are too high, so the task stays entirely with people

  • Choosing whether the chain will compete as a low-cost leader or on differentiation — This is the unstructured executive decision every later system is judged against, and the chapter says no procedure for such a choice can be specified in advance.
  • Deciding which of two underperforming stores closes when the analysis says one of them must — The consequences fall on named employees and a named community, it cannot be reversed, and the person accountable has to be able to explain it.
  • Preparing the confidential file naming the smaller chain this company is considering acquiring — The document itself is the secret, so sending it to an outside service is the harm rather than a risk of one, whatever the quality of the output.
Check yourself

Where it fits, and in which mode

Three questions on how AI relates to the chapter’s three ways of adding value, and on which step of strategy work it can take.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. A manager argues that artificial intelligence is a fourth way for an information system to add value, alongside automating, learning and supporting strategy. What is the most accurate response?

  • A. It is a fourth way, because no earlier technology could produce written analysis without a person doing the writing — Novelty of the technique is not what the chapter’s three categories measure; they describe the kind of value produced. A genuinely new fourth kind of value would have to be something other than faster, better or smarter.
  • B. It is a new means to the same three ends, so a proposal to buy it is judged by the same three questions — correct. The three ways describe what an information system does for the firm, so a new technology enters through them rather than beside them, and the proposal still has to show which of the three it delivers.
  • C. It belongs under automating only, because generating text faster than a person is by definition an efficiency gain — Automating is often where it lands first, and confining it there would miss the rest. The same tool can also reveal patterns in past behavior, which is organizational learning, and can serve the chosen strategy directly.
  • D. It replaces the three, because a system that can analyse and recommend no longer needs a category to sit in — This overstates what any system does. The categories describe value delivered to the organization, not the sophistication of the software, and a system that analyses still has to be shown to help the firm compete.

2. In the strategy workflow, which step is the one AI does not take?

  • A. Condensing a large volume of source material into a readable summary of what it contains — Condensing volume is the clearest thing it does help with, and it is the slowest part of gathering evidence, which is exactly why the verification control belongs immediately after it.
  • B. Laying out how a single sales decline could be read as rivalry, as a new entrant, or as a substitute — Producing the competing readings is genuinely useful work, since one lost sale can be told honestly as a story about several forces, and seeing all of them is what makes a choice between them possible.
  • C. Committing the organization to one reading and to what it will therefore not do — correct. Committing to one reading is an executive-level decision, and the chapter calls such decisions unstructured because few or no procedures for them can be specified in advance.
  • D. Carrying repetitive work inside the system the organization has decided to build — Repetitive work inside a chosen system is the automating rung, which the chapter presents as real value, and it is where most of the countable hours are saved once the decision has already been made.

3. An analyst wants a tool to produce the first draft of the recommendation that will go to the board, which the analyst will then rewrite. Which mode is that, and is it defensible?

  • A. Automate, and defensible, because drafting is repetitive work and the board will read the document anyway — Automate means acting without a reviewer, and here a person rewrites the document before anyone sees it, so the description does not match the arrangement being proposed.
  • B. Augment, and defensible, because the draft saves time while the claim and the wording stay with the analyst — correct. A blank page is the expensive part of writing and the claim is the risky part, so the system supplies the first and the analyst keeps the second, which is what augmentation means.
  • C. Augment, and indefensible, because any strategy document is too sensitive for a system to touch at all — Sensitivity is a real reason to keep some work human, and it applies to material that must not leave the company, such as a confidential acquisition file, rather than to every document about strategy.
  • D. Keep human-only, and defensible, because a recommendation is an unstructured decision and no procedure exists for it — Deciding what to recommend is indeed unstructured and stays with the analyst. Writing a first draft of a decision the analyst has already made is a different task, and refusing help with it costs hours for no reduction in risk.

Why buying AI is not the same as gaining advantage

This is the heart of the section, and the chapter answers it directly. Innovation is often fleeting: even a system built in house is assembled from hardware, software and networking components that others can also purchase, so rivals can copy it and the advantage is short-lived.

A service any competitor can subscribe to the same afternoon is the clearest possible case of that warning. It is a commodity, and a commodity is where an advantage cannot live.

What a rival cannot buy is everything around the subscription. The chapter locates advantage in resources such as proprietary technology, brand equity and a loyal, established customer base, and in capabilities, meaning the organization’s ability to leverage those resources in the marketplace. Three of those stay yours.

  • Your data — the record of what your customers actually did would take a competitor years to accumulate, which is why the chapter lists data among the sources of competitive advantage and gives Uber as its example.
  • Your processes — the chapter insists that any significant implementation demands commensurate, significant organizational change, so the firm that redesigns the work around a tool gets a result the firm that merely installs it never sees.
  • Your people — capabilities such as design quality or efficient operations exist in the people who exercise them, and resources plus capabilities are what produce the distinctive competencies a strategy is built on.

Then there is the fit. The chapter’s technology/strategy fit says organizations do not want systems that fail to match their strategy, even when those systems offer real automating and learning benefits. Its own illustration is a firm pursuing overall low-cost leadership, which probably does not want a system that differentiates its products on high quality.

A purchase that does not serve the strategy the company chose is spending, not strategy — and the chapter’s name for the narrow exception is strategic necessity, something an organization must do to survive whether or not it matches the plan.

The run below is a hypothetical practice situation, invented so the reasoning has something to bite on; no real company is described.

Decide

Advising on an AI investment

Work the four decisions in this hypothetical company; after each one, read every outcome before continuing, including the ones you did not choose.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

This is a hypothetical practice situation, not a report about any real company. A regional chain of bicycle shops has set money aside after two competitors publicly announced artificial intelligence projects. The chain has already chosen its strategy: overall low-cost leadership in its region, competing on price and on how cheaply it can run the repair counter. It also holds eight years of repair records that nobody has ever analysed. You are the analyst in the room.

Decision 1. First decision: what is the money actually for? Leadership wants to move this week, and three sentences are on the table.

  • Buy the most capable general assistant available and give every employee an account, then see what people find to do with it — This is the tempting answer and it buys a commodity. The subscription is available to every rival at the same price on the same day, no activity has been named, so nothing can be measured and nothing has been made harder to copy. It is spending in the shape of a strategy.
  • Name one activity the chain competes on, then ask what a tool would change inside it — the stronger call. Right, and in that order. The chain competes on running the repair counter cheaply, so the question becomes what happens to the cost of a repair, which is narrow enough to measure and specific enough to reject proposals that would not touch it.
  • Buy whatever the two competitors announced, so the chain is not left behind on a technology the market clearly expects — This justifies parity and never advantage, and it hands the technology roadmap to rivals. It also assumes the competitors diagnosed their own business correctly, which is an assumption nobody in this room can check.

Decision 2. Second decision: a vendor offers a system that recommends premium components and custom fittings to each customer, promising a more differentiated, higher-quality buying experience. Another proposal would cut the time a mechanic spends diagnosing a common fault.

  • Take the premium recommendation system, because a better customer experience helps any retailer — It probably would help some retailer, and it does not fit this one. The chapter’s own illustration is exactly this mismatch: an organization pursuing overall low-cost leadership does not want a system that differentiates its products on high quality, however real the benefits are.
  • Take the diagnosis proposal, because lowering the cost of the activity the chain competes on is what its chosen strategy values — the stronger call. Correct, and the reason is the technology/strategy fit. Under a low-cost leadership strategy, investments that drive costs down are valued over those that do not, so this proposal is judged against the plan the company already made rather than against how modern it sounds.
  • Fund both, since each one is defensible on its own and the chain can decide later which mattered — Funding both is how a company ends up with neither. Organizations are constrained by time and money to build only what adds the most value, and running two initiatives at once means neither gets the organizational change the chapter says a significant implementation requires.

Decision 3. Third decision: the board asks where the advantage would come from, given that the same tools are for sale to everyone in the region.

  • From the model itself, because the chain will subscribe to the most capable one on the market — This is the commodity trap stated out loud. Innovation is often fleeting precisely because a system is assembled from components others can also purchase, and a subscription a rival can start tomorrow is the least defensible asset the chain could name.
  • From the eight years of repair records, plus rebuilding the counter process around what they show — the stronger call. Right on both halves. The records are a resource no rival holds and would take years to accumulate, which is why the chapter lists data among the sources of competitive advantage, and the process change is what turns the resource into a capability rather than a spreadsheet.
  • From being the first chain in the region to announce it, which the other two have not yet done — Being first to announce is not a first-mover advantage in any market, and an announcement is the easiest thing in this entire plan for a competitor to copy. Nothing about it makes the chain harder to imitate next quarter.

Decision 4. Fourth decision: the board will fund the initiative and wants to know how the chain will judge it.

  • Report how many employees use the tool each week, which shows the investment is being taken up — This measures activity rather than results. Usage rises simply because the tool exists and staff were asked to try it, and the number would keep rising even if no repair got cheaper and no customer noticed anything at all.
  • Name the average cost of a common repair as the measure, fix the review date now, and name the manager answerable for the result — the stronger call. That is the full shape: a number tied to the activity the chain competes on, a date set before anyone has seen results, and a named person who has to explain the outcome. Keep, change and stop are all still genuinely available at that review.
  • Use the vendor’s dashboard, which reports the hours the tool saved across the business — The vendor is scoring its own product, and hours saved somewhere in the business is not the same as cost removed from the activity the strategy names. A measure the buyer cannot reconstruct is a claim rather than evidence.

AI as more than a product feature

Chapter 2 lists ten types of innovation, and two of them are worth setting side by side here. A product performance innovation creates a novel product or improves an existing one through differentiation. A process innovation changes the primary processes used to produce products or services.

In an established company, AI usually lands as the second kind. The tool rarely becomes the thing the customer buys; it changes how that thing is made, sold or supported. The chapter’s examples of process innovation are Toyota pioneering lean production and Zara moving fashion from initial design to stores in three weeks.

That difference decides who has to be involved.

  • A product change is owned by the people who design and sell the product, and customers deliver the verdict on it.
  • A process change lands on the people doing the work, so their managers, their steps and their measures all have to change with it.

The chapter also explains why one type is rarely enough. Product performance innovations can often be easily copied, so companies frequently combine several types at once. Dell is the worked example, combining a profit model innovation in collecting money before building the product, a process innovation in the built-to-order model, and a channel innovation in selling computers online rather than in stores.

What goes wrong in strategy work specifically

These are not general complaints about the technology. Each failure damages a strategic analysis in particular, and each has a control that belongs inside the workflow rather than in a policy document nobody opens.

  • Evidence nobody verified — a confident summary of a market or a contract can contain a claim that is simply not in the source, so a person who can check has to check the figures, dates and terms before any of it reaches a recommendation.
  • Bias in the customer data underneath — an analysis of customer behavior can only describe the customers the company recorded, so a conclusion built on that record silently ignores whoever the company has never served.
  • Confidential strategy material leaving — a strategy document names what a firm intends to do next, and an outside service is still outside, which is the same balance the chapter asks companies to strike when open innovation makes organizational data and knowledge accessible to external stakeholders.
  • Accountability — a person still owns the recommendation, because a board asked to fund an initiative is entitled to ask who believes this and why, and no committee can act on the answer that the system suggested it.

The discipline this module keeps returning to

Whether or not a machine helped produce it, a recommendation is judged the same way it was judged before any of this existed. Name the force or the activity, give the evidence, state the initiative, then commit to a measure and a date.

Say it in one sentence. Because [force or activity] is [strong or weak], shown by [evidence], we should build [initiative], which we will judge by [measure] at [date]. AI can help you fill every slot in that sentence. It cannot be the person who says it, and it cannot be the person answerable when the date arrives.
Check yourself

Commodity, fit, and the type of innovation

Three questions on why a purchase is not an advantage, on matching a system to the chosen strategy, and on where AI usually lands among the ten types of innovation.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. A board is told that subscribing to the most capable AI service available will give the company a lasting advantage. On this chapter’s reasoning, what is wrong with the claim?

  • A. Nothing is wrong, because a system built to gain or sustain advantage keeps producing it for as long as it runs — Sustaining an advantage is continuing work rather than a property a system acquires at purchase, and the chapter says the opposite of this option: advantages gained by innovations often have a limited life span.
  • B. The claim fails because information systems are a commodity, so technology spending belongs on cost reduction only — This states a stronger position than the chapter takes. The chapter does not say technology spending must be limited to cost reduction; it says spending has to match the strategy and show clear, significant value.
  • C. The advantage can be fleeting, because rivals can subscribe to the same service and copy the same use of it — correct. The chapter warns that innovation is often fleeting because systems are built from components others can also purchase, so smart rivals are quick to duplicate or improve on any use that visibly wins.
  • D. The claim fails because the service was not developed in house, and only in-house systems create any advantage — In-house building is not the dividing line the chapter draws. It notes that even an in-house system is assembled from purchasable components, and separately that a system built by a consultant or outsourcing partner is proprietary to the organization.

2. A chain pursuing overall low-cost leadership is offered an AI system that would let it recommend premium, customized products to each customer. It genuinely automates work and reveals useful patterns. Should it buy?

  • A. Yes, because the system delivers both automating and learning benefits, which are two of the chapter’s three kinds of value — Automating and learning benefits are real and the chapter still says they are not enough on their own, since organizations do not want systems that fail to match the strategy even when those benefits are present.
  • B. Probably not, because a system that differentiates on quality does not match a low-cost leadership strategy — correct. This is the chapter’s own illustration of the technology/strategy fit: a firm pursuing low-cost leadership probably does not want a system differentiating its products on high quality.
  • C. Yes, because pursuing differentiation as well as low cost gives the chain two sources of advantage instead of one — The chapter does describe a middle position, the best-cost provider strategy offering reasonably good quality at competitive prices, but that is a strategy a company chooses deliberately rather than a bonus acquired by buying a mismatched system.
  • D. Probably not, because the chain should fix its cost position before it spends on anything customer-facing — Sequencing sounds prudent but is not the objection. The problem is not that this comes too early; it is that a system built to differentiate on quality pulls against a low-cost position no matter when it is bought, so waiting would not make it fit.

3. A manufacturer uses an AI system to change how it schedules and runs its production line. The product itself is unchanged. Using the chapter’s ten types of innovation, what kind of innovation is this?

  • A. A product performance innovation, because the output of the line will be more consistent for customers — Product performance innovation means creating novel products or improving existing ones through differentiation, as with an unbreakable glass or a distinctive hand dryer, and here the product has deliberately not changed.
  • B. A profit model innovation, because lower production cost changes how the company generates its revenue — Profit model innovation means finding novel ways of generating revenues, such as offering software on a subscription or selling thrust as a service, and a cheaper line does not change what the company charges for.
  • C. A process innovation, because it changes the primary processes used to produce products or services — correct. The chapter defines process innovation as changing the primary processes used to produce products or services, and gives Toyota’s lean production and Zara’s three-week design-to-store cycle as its examples.
  • D. A channel innovation, because it changes how the finished product reaches the people who buy it — Channel innovation means using innovative ways to connect offerings with customers, such as selling computers online instead of through stores, and nothing in this scenario changes how the product reaches a buyer.

Application supplement · 2–5

The analyst’s toolkit: getting the evidence yourself

Every framework in this module ends in a claim — buyer power is our strongest force, inbound logistics is where the margin is leaking, this category is where our value is disappearing. A claim without evidence is a preference. This supplement is about producing the evidence yourself, with two tools that sit on almost every analyst’s desk: a spreadsheet and a database query.

How this supplement relates to the chapter. Chapter 2 teaches the analysis — the competitive forces, the value chain, the business model. It also sets its own end-of-chapter exercises in a spreadsheet and a database, because the analysis has to be fed. This section takes the chapter’s exercises and makes them runnable: you type a real formula or a real query on this page and watch it work on real rows. It is a labeled supplement because the tools serve the chapter’s analysis rather than being a fourth learning objective of their own.

Why an analyst touches the data directly

It is tempting to think of data work as somebody else’s job — that an analyst asks and a technical team answers. In practice the gap between the question and the answer is where most of the time goes, and the person who can close it themselves is the person whose recommendation arrives while the decision is still open.

Two skills close most of that gap, and both appear in this chapter’s own exercises:

  • Cleaning and reshaping text — real data arrives inconsistent, with stray spaces, mixed capitalisation and invisible characters, and none of it can be grouped or matched until it is made uniform, which is why the chapter opens its spreadsheet exercise on exactly that problem.
  • Asking a database a precise question — a query turns a stored record into an answer about the business, and the discipline of writing one forces you to say exactly which rows and which columns your claim actually rests on.

The chapter puts the business case plainly: clean contact data matters because it makes communication, customer segmentation and personalized marketing possible, and those are the things a competitive advantage is built out of.

Part one: cleaning text in a spreadsheet

A spreadsheet function takes a value and returns a new one; it never changes the original. That is why cleaning is done in new columns rather than by editing the raw data in place — the original stays available when someone asks where a number came from.

The chapter names the functions this kind of work needs. These are the ones the exercises below use:

  • TRIM — removes extra spaces from a string, leaving only single spaces between words, which matters because a trailing space makes two otherwise identical addresses look like two different customers.
  • CLEAN — removes non-printable characters that may sit in raw data without being visible in the sheet, so a value that looks correct but refuses to match another one usually needs this.
  • LOWER — standardises capitalisation, and its companions UPPER and PROPER do the same job in the other directions, because a system that treats two capitalisations as two values will double-count a customer.
  • FIND — returns the position of one piece of text inside another, counting from one, and it is case sensitive; SEARCH does the same job without caring about case.
  • LEFT, RIGHT and LEN — take characters from the start of a string, from its end, and count how many there are, which together let you split a value at a marker you have located.

Start with the cleaning step. The raw column below is deliberately untidy, in the way exported contact data usually is. Fill each column with one formula and watch it run down every row — the formula is written once for row 2 and applied to the rest, which is exactly how it behaves in a real sheet.

Spreadsheet

Make the addresses uniform

Type one formula for row 2 in each column, then run it; it is applied to every row the way a filled-down formula behaves in a real sheet.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Columns: Raw email · Trimmed · Cleaned and lowercased

1. Column B: remove the stray spaces from the raw address, leaving the text otherwise untouched.

=TRIM(A2)

TRIM strips the leading and trailing spaces that came in with the export. The capitalisation is left alone, which is the next problem.

2. Column C: produce the fully standardised address, with no stray spaces and nothing capitalised.

=LOWER(TRIM(A2))

Nesting runs the inner function first and hands its result to the outer one, so the spaces go and the case is standardised in a single formula. Now two records for the same person will match.

Splitting a value at a marker

Once the addresses are uniform, they can be taken apart. The username is everything before the @ and the domain is everything after it, but neither has a fixed length, so you cannot simply take the first eight characters. You have to find the marker first and measure from it.

That is the whole idea behind the two formulas the chapter gives, and it is worth reading them slowly, because the same pattern splits a product code, a postcode or a file name:

  1. Locate the marker. FIND returns the position of the @ counting from one, so in priya.raman@northside.edu it returns 12, because the twelfth character is the @ itself.
  2. Take everything before it. The username is one character shorter than the marker’s position, which is why the formula subtracts one: LEFT of eleven characters gives priya.raman and stops just before the @.
  3. Take everything after it. The domain’s length is the whole string minus the marker’s position, so LEN minus FIND gives the number of characters to take from the right — no counting by hand, and it works on an address of any length.

Work the three columns below. The addresses have already been cleaned, so you can concentrate on the splitting.

Spreadsheet

Split each address at the marker

The addresses are already cleaned. Find the @ first, then measure from it.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Columns: Clean email · Username · Domain · Domain length

1. Column B: extract the username — everything before the @.

=LEFT(A2, FIND("@", A2) - 1)

FIND locates the @ and LEFT takes everything up to one character before it. Because the position is calculated per row, addresses of different lengths all work.

2. Column C: extract the domain — everything after the @.

=RIGHT(A2, LEN(A2) - FIND("@", A2))

LEN gives the total number of characters and FIND gives the marker's position; the difference is exactly how many characters sit to the right of the @.

3. Column D: how many characters long is each domain? Build on what you just wrote.

=LEN(RIGHT(A2, LEN(A2) - FIND("@", A2)))

Functions compose: any formula that returns text can be handed straight to LEN. This is how short, readable steps are combined without needing extra helper columns.

The habit worth keepingNotice that nothing in those formulas mentions a specific address. They describe a rule — find the marker, measure from it — which is why one formula handles six rows or sixty thousand. Writing rules rather than answers is the difference between a spreadsheet that scales and one that has to be redone every month.

Part two: asking a database a business question

A spreadsheet is the right tool while the data is small and you are still shaping it. Once records are shared, updated by several people and expected to stay consistent, they belong in a database, and you get at them with a query.

A query has a fixed shape, and reading it in the right order makes it far less mysterious than it looks:

  • SELECT names the columns you want back, and an expression such as PurchasePrice - CurrentValue can be one of them, given a name with AS.
  • FROM names the table the rows come from, and is the part that actually decides what you are counting.
  • WHERE keeps only the rows that satisfy a condition, so it runs before anything is totalled and quietly determines every number that follows.
  • GROUP BY collapses the surviving rows into one row per distinct value, which is what lets COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX report per category rather than per record.
  • HAVING filters those grouped rows, and it exists because WHERE has already finished its work by the time the totals exist.
  • ORDER BY sorts the result, and LIMIT keeps only the first few rows, which together answer questions phrased as “the worst three” or “the largest.”

The table below is an asset register of the kind the chapter’s database exercise describes: an item, what it is, its condition, what it cost and what it is worth now. Everything on this page is a hypothetical practice situation, invented so the queries have something to bite on. Open the tables, then answer each question with a query — any query that returns the right answer is accepted, not just the one that was expected.

Database

Question the asset register

Write a SELECT for each question and run it. Any query returning the right answer is accepted, so there is more than one correct way through.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

assets — ItemID, ItemName, Category, Condition, AcquisitionDate, PurchasePrice, CurrentValue, Dept (10 rows)

depts — Dept, Manager (3 rows)

1. List the name and current value of every software asset.

SELECT ItemName, CurrentValue FROM assets WHERE Category = 'software'

SELECT chooses the columns and WHERE chooses the rows. Both decisions are yours, and confusing them is the most common early mistake.

2. Which three assets have lost the most value since purchase? Show the item and the amount lost.

SELECT ItemName, PurchasePrice - CurrentValue AS ValueLost FROM assets ORDER BY ValueLost DESC LIMIT 3

An expression is a perfectly good column. Naming it with AS lets ORDER BY refer to it, and LIMIT turns a sorted list into an answer to 'the worst three'.

3. For each category, how many assets are there and what are they worth in total? Show the most valuable category first.

SELECT Category, COUNT(*) AS Items, SUM(CurrentValue) AS Value FROM assets GROUP BY Category ORDER BY Value DESC

Grouping is what turns a register into a summary. Notice the software category holds far more value in fewer items than the hardware category does.

4. Which departments hold assets in poor or fair condition, and how many each? Show the worst first.

SELECT Dept, COUNT(*) AS Ageing FROM assets WHERE Condition IN ('poor','fair') GROUP BY Dept ORDER BY Ageing DESC

WHERE runs before the grouping, so only the ageing assets are counted. This is the query behind a finding about where equipment is being run too long.

5. Name every asset in poor condition together with the manager responsible for it.

SELECT a.ItemName, d.Manager FROM assets a JOIN depts d ON a.Dept = d.Dept WHERE a.Condition = 'poor'

A join puts related rows from two tables side by side on a matching column. Prefixing columns with the table alias keeps it unambiguous when both tables use the same column name.

6. Which departments have spent more than 5,000 in total on purchases? Show the biggest spender first.

SELECT Dept, SUM(PurchasePrice) AS Spent FROM assets GROUP BY Dept HAVING SUM(PurchasePrice) > 5000 ORDER BY Spent DESC

WHERE filters rows and HAVING filters groups. Trying to put a SUM condition in WHERE fails because the total has not been calculated at that point.

From a result set back to the analysis

A query result is not yet a finding, and a finding is not yet a recommendation. The last query above returns a number per department; on its own it is a fact nobody has to act on. It becomes useful only when it is attached to the analysis this module has been building.

The chain runs in one direction, and skipping a link is what makes a proposal easy to refuse:

  1. The result is what the query returned — for instance that one department holds most of the assets recorded in poor or fair condition.
  2. The finding is what that means in the business — equipment in that part of the operation is being run past the point where it works reliably.
  3. The framework says where it bites — if that equipment sits in inbound logistics or operations, the value chain tells you the cost is landing on an activity the customer eventually pays for.
  4. The recommendation names the initiative, the measure and the date, which is the same discipline the earlier sections asked for and the only form a decision-maker can actually approve or reject.
Check yourself

Tools, evidence, and claims

Each question is about the reasoning behind the tool rather than the syntax; read every explanation.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. An analyst filters a sales table to this year’s orders, groups by region, and totals the revenue. A colleague asks why one region looks so weak. What is the first thing worth checking?

  • A. Whether the totals were sorted in the right direction before being read — Sorting changes the order rows are presented in, not their values. A region that looks weak will look equally weak wherever it appears in the list.
  • B. Which rows the filter kept, because a condition applied before grouping silently decides every total that follows — correct. Right. The filter runs before the grouping, so anything it excluded is missing from every total. A region with orders recorded slightly outside the filtered range would look weak for a reason that has nothing to do with its sales.
  • C. Whether a different aggregate such as AVG would make the region look stronger — Choosing the aggregate that flatters a result is the opposite of analysis. AVG and SUM answer genuinely different questions, and switching between them to get a nicer number is how an analysis stops being evidence.
  • D. Whether the region column should have been selected after the grouping instead of before it — The order in which columns are named does not change which rows were counted. Grouping needs the column to be available, and it is, so this would not alter the result at all.

2. Two customer records read R.Osei@Wexler-Foods.com and r.osei@wexler-foods.com . A segmentation report counts them as two customers. What has actually gone wrong?

  • A. The database is missing a rule that would prevent two records for one person — A constraint would help future records, but it cannot explain this one: the system is behaving correctly by treating two different strings as different. The data was already inconsistent when it arrived.
  • B. The values differ in capitalisation and trailing space, so they are two different strings until they are standardised — correct. Right. A trailing space and a capital letter make the strings genuinely different, which is exactly why the chapter puts TRIM and LOWER at the start of its exercise. Standardising first is what makes the match possible.
  • C. The report should be counting domains rather than full addresses — Counting domains would answer a different question entirely, about which organizations the customers belong to. It would also merge everyone at the same company into one, which is worse.
  • D. The addresses need to be split into username and domain before they can be compared — Splitting is useful for other purposes, but it does not fix this. Splitting these two values would produce two usernames that still differ in case and spacing.

3. A query shows that one department holds most of the assets recorded in poor condition. Which statement turns that result into something a decision-maker can act on?

  • A. The register shows that department holds the most assets in poor condition — This is the query result restated. It is true and it is where the work starts, but it names no consequence, no initiative and no measure, so there is nothing to approve.
  • B. Equipment reliability is a concern right across the organization and deserves the attention of senior management before the next budget round begins — This is a sentiment rather than a finding. It names no place, no evidence and no test, which means it can never be shown to have worked or failed.
  • C. Ageing equipment is slowing the operations activity, so replace the four worst units this quarter and judge it by unplanned downtime hours — correct. Right. It names the value chain activity affected, rests on the observable result, states a specific initiative, and commits to a measure and a date — the four parts that make a recommendation fundable rather than merely reasonable.
  • D. That department should be given a larger equipment budget than the others next year — This jumps from evidence straight to a budget decision without saying what the money would buy or how anyone would know it worked. It also assumes spending is the answer before the cause has been established.

Application supplement · 2–6

Strategy as code, and questions a database can answer

The analysis in this module produces claims: this force binds us, that activity is where the margin goes, this revenue model suits what we sell. Each of those claims is a calculation somebody is doing in their head, usually inconsistently. This supplement writes four of them down as functions, and then goes back to the database for the harder questions a single table could not answer.

How this supplement relates to the chapter. Nothing here adds to the chapter’s material. The five forces, the value chain, the revenue models and the discipline of committing to a measure are all from the sections above; what this section adds is an executable form of each, so that a claim can be checked rather than asserted. The queries extend the previous supplement from one table to three.

Why write the analysis down

A framework applied in conversation drifts. The same analyst, given the same evidence a week apart, will weigh it differently, and two analysts will never agree on what they were even comparing. Writing the step as a function fixes three things at once:

  • The inputs become explicit — a function signature forces you to say precisely what evidence the conclusion rests on, which is the same discipline the recommendation format asks for.
  • The tie stops being invisible — when two forces score equally the honest answer is that the evidence does not yet separate them, and a function has to return something for that case rather than quietly picking one.
  • The result is reproducible — anyone can rerun it on the same inputs and get the same answer, which is what makes it evidence rather than an opinion with numbers attached.

Each exercise below gives you a stub, a contract and tests. Your code runs on this page with nothing installed and no network; a loop that never ends is stopped after two seconds. Ctrl-Enter runs the tests, Tab indents, and there is always more than one implementation that passes.

Write the code

Four analysis steps as functions

Write each function so every test passes; a failing test prints what your code returned beside what was expected.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. An analysis has to end in a single answer. Implement bindingForce(signals): return the name of the strongest force, or 'tie' when two or more share the top score.

Signature: bindingForce(signals) -> string

function bindingForce(signals) {
  var keys = Object.keys(signals);
  if (keys.length === 0) return 'tie';
  var top = Math.max.apply(null, keys.map(function (k) { return signals[k]; }));
  var winners = keys.filter(function (k) { return signals[k] === top; });
  return winners.length === 1 ? winners[0] : 'tie';
}

The tie case is the one that matters. An analysis that always returns a single force will manufacture one from noise, and a recommendation built on a one-point difference is not evidence. Reporting the tie sends you back for better data instead of forward with false confidence.

2. The value chain says margin is what survives after every activity takes its cost. Implement margin(revenue, activities), returning the amount left and the costliest activity.

Signature: margin(revenue, activities) -> { margin, costliest }

function margin(revenue, activities) {
  var total = activities.reduce(function (s, a) { return s + a.cost; }, 0);
  var worst = null;
  activities.forEach(function (a) {
    if (worst === null || a.cost > worst.cost) worst = a;
  });
  return { margin: revenue - total, costliest: worst ? worst.name : null };
}

Naming the costliest activity is what turns arithmetic into an argument. 'Margin is 400' invites no decision; 'operations consumes 40 percent of revenue' points at exactly where a system would have to pay for itself.

3. The same product earns differently under different revenue models. Implement revenue(model, usage) for the three the chapter names.

Signature: revenue(model, usage) -> number

function revenue(model, usage) {
  if (model === 'subscription') return usage.users * usage.monthlyFee * usage.months;
  if (model === 'freemium') return usage.users * usage.payingShare * usage.monthlyFee * usage.months;
  if (model === 'transaction') return usage.transactions * usage.perTxnFee;
  return 0;
}

Notice what each branch does not read. Transaction revenue never looks at the user count, and subscription never looks at transactions. A business model is as much about which numbers you stop caring about as which ones you chase.

4. A recommendation needs a measure and a date. Implement paybackMonths(cac, monthlyMargin, monthlyChurn): how many whole months until a customer repays what it cost to win them, or -1 if they never do.

Signature: paybackMonths(cac, monthlyMargin, monthlyChurn) -> number

function paybackMonths(cac, monthlyMargin, monthlyChurn) {
  if (monthlyMargin <= 0) return -1;
  var months = Math.ceil(cac / monthlyMargin);
  var lifetime = monthlyChurn > 0 ? 1 / monthlyChurn : Infinity;
  return months <= lifetime ? months : -1;
}

This is the shape of every honest IT business case: a cost, a rate of return, and a horizon that decides whether the return ever arrives. The -1 cases are the useful ones, because they are the proposals that look profitable until you ask how long the customer stays.

Look back at what each function refuses to do. bindingForce will not name a winner it cannot justify, and paybackMonths will not report a payback that arrives after the customer has gone. Both refusals are the analysis being honest in a way prose lets you avoid.

Questions that need more than one table

The previous supplement queried a single asset register. Real questions rarely sit in one table, because the facts are deliberately kept apart: who the customer is, what they subscribe to, and what that plan costs are three different kinds of fact that change on three different schedules.

Joining is how they are brought back together for one question, and two ideas cover most of what you will need:

  • A join matches rows on a shared value — every subscription carries a customer identifier, so matching it against the customer table puts the name beside the subscription without ever storing the name twice.
  • HAVING filters groups rather than rows — WHERE has finished its work before any total exists, so a condition about a count or a sum has to wait until after the grouping, which is the distinction that catches most people out.

The three tables below describe a hypothetical subscription business; every company in them is invented. Answer each question with a query, and remember that any query returning the right answer is accepted.

Database

Three tables, harder questions

Each question needs a join, and some need grouping too. Any query that returns the right answer is accepted.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

customers — CustomerID, Name, Region, JoinedOn (6 rows)

subscriptions — SubID, CustomerID, Plan, Status, Months (7 rows)

plans — Plan, MonthlyFee (3 rows)

1. Which customers have an active subscription? Show the customer name and the plan, sorted by name.

SELECT c.Name, s.Plan FROM subscriptions s JOIN customers c ON s.CustomerID = c.CustomerID WHERE s.Status = 'active' ORDER BY c.Name

A join puts related rows side by side on a matching column. Note that the name is stored once, in one place, and borrowed by every query that needs it.

2. What is each active subscription worth per month? Show the name, the plan and its monthly fee, dearest first.

SELECT c.Name, s.Plan, p.MonthlyFee FROM subscriptions s JOIN customers c ON s.CustomerID = c.CustomerID JOIN plans p ON s.Plan = p.Plan WHERE s.Status = 'active' ORDER BY p.MonthlyFee DESC

Joins chain. The price is deliberately not stored on the subscription, so changing a plan's fee is one edit rather than one edit per subscriber.

3. How much revenue has each plan booked to date, counting every subscription and every month it ran? Biggest first.

SELECT s.Plan, SUM(s.Months * p.MonthlyFee) AS Booked FROM subscriptions s JOIN plans p ON s.Plan = p.Plan GROUP BY s.Plan ORDER BY Booked DESC

An expression can be aggregated, not just a stored column. The premium plan dominates on revenue despite having the fewest subscriptions, which is exactly the kind of fact a per-row listing hides.

4. Which regions have more than one subscription on record, and how many each?

SELECT c.Region, COUNT(*) AS Subs FROM subscriptions s JOIN customers c ON s.CustomerID = c.CustomerID GROUP BY c.Region HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 ORDER BY Subs DESC

WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters the groups afterwards. Putting a COUNT condition in WHERE fails because there is nothing counted yet at that point.

5. How much booked revenue has been lost to churn in each region? Worst first.

SELECT c.Region, SUM(s.Months * p.MonthlyFee) AS Lost FROM subscriptions s JOIN customers c ON s.CustomerID = c.CustomerID JOIN plans p ON s.Plan = p.Plan WHERE s.Status = 'churned' GROUP BY c.Region ORDER BY Lost DESC

The losses are heavily concentrated in one region. A single number for the whole business would have averaged that away and pointed at nothing.

6. On average, how many months did churned customers stay, by plan? Longest first.

SELECT Plan, AVG(Months) AS AvgMonths FROM subscriptions WHERE Status = 'churned' GROUP BY Plan ORDER BY AvgMonths DESC

Not every question needs a join, and reaching for one out of habit costs clarity. Read the question, then look at which table already holds the columns it mentions.

From a result to a recommendation

The last two queries are worth sitting with, because together they say something neither says alone. One reports the revenue lost to churn by region; the other reports how long customers stayed before leaving, by plan.

  1. The results are two tables, and neither is a finding. One region lost far more than the others, and one plan retained customers for far longer than another.
  2. The finding is what they mean together: the losses are concentrated, and they are concentrated in a plan whose customers were expected to stay longest.
  3. The framework says where it bites — if the customers leaving are the ones a competitor is courting, this is rivalry or buyer power rather than a service problem, and the two call for different responses.
  4. The recommendation names the initiative and the number that should move, which is the only form that can be approved, rejected, or later shown to have worked.
The habit this section is really teachingEvery claim in a strategy document is either a calculation somebody can reproduce or an assertion somebody has to trust. Writing the calculation down — as a function, as a query, or as both — is what lets the argument be checked instead of merely believed. It is also, not incidentally, the difference between analysis that survives a challenge and analysis that does not.
Check yourself

What the code and the queries settled

These ask about the reasoning, not the syntax; read every explanation.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. Your bindingForce returns 'tie' when two forces score equally. A manager asks you to make it always name one force so the report reads decisively. What is the strongest objection?

  • A. Ties are rare enough in practice that the change would almost never matter, and a rule that fires once in a hundred analyses is not worth the extra branch in the code — Rarity is not the issue and is not knowable in advance. Even a single manufactured winner sends real money at the wrong problem.
  • B. The function would need considerably more code to break ties fairly — Code length is not the objection, and a tie-breaking rule would be short. The problem is that any such rule invents a distinction the evidence did not supply.
  • C. A tie means the evidence does not separate the two forces, so naming one manufactures a certainty the analysis does not have and points spending at a guess — correct. Right. The tie is information: it says go and get better evidence before committing. Converting it into a confident answer hides the one fact the decision-maker most needs.
  • D. Naming one force would break the tests, and the tests are the specification — The tests would indeed change, but tests follow the specification rather than justify it. This answer describes a consequence and skips the reason.

2. paybackMonths(100, 25, 0.5) returns -1: four months to repay, but a two-month expected lifetime. A colleague proposes returning 4 anyway, since that is the arithmetic. What is lost?

  • A. Nothing meaningful, because the payback period and the average customer lifetime are separate measures taken from different parts of the business and were never intended to be read together — They are separate measures whose whole point is to be compared. Reporting one without the other is what makes a losing proposition look profitable.
  • B. The single fact that decides the case — that the customer leaves before the cost is recovered, so the acquisition loses money every time it succeeds — correct. Right. A payback that arrives after the customer has gone never arrives at all. Returning 4 describes a repayment that does not happen, which is precisely the error the horizon was added to catch.
  • C. Precision, since four months is a rounded figure and the true value has a fractional part — Rounding up is deliberate, since a partial month still costs a whole one, and it is not what the objection turns on.
  • D. Consistency with the other functions, which all return a number rather than a sentinel value — Return-type consistency is a style question. Here the sentinel is carrying the finding, and a uniform number would carry none.

3. A query totals revenue per plan by joining subscriptions to plans and summing Months * MonthlyFee. Why is the fee stored on the plan rather than copied onto each subscription?

  • A. Because a join is the faster way to reach a value than reading it from the row itself — This has the trade-off backwards: reaching a value through a join generally costs more at query time than reading it from the row. Normalising is done for correctness, and the join is the price paid for it.
  • B. Because SQL does not permit an arithmetic expression inside SUM — SQL is perfectly happy aggregating an expression, which is exactly what this query does. Nothing here is a limitation of the language.
  • C. Because the fee is a fact about the plan, so storing it once means a price change is one edit rather than one per subscriber, with no chance of some rows disagreeing — correct. Right. One fact, one place. Copying the fee onto every subscription creates as many opportunities to disagree as there are rows, and the disagreement surfaces later as totals nobody can reconcile.
  • D. Because storing the fee on every subscription row would make the table too large to query quickly once the service has several hundred thousand subscribers on its books — A few more bytes per row would not trouble any database. The cost of duplication is inconsistency, not size.

4. Churned revenue is concentrated in one region, and the plan with the longest average tenure is also the one losing the most money. Which statement is a finding rather than a result or a recommendation?

  • A. Two queries returned totals grouped by region and by plan — That describes what was run rather than what was learned, and no decision follows from it. It is the result, the step before a finding.
  • B. The customers we expected to keep longest are the ones leaving, and their departures account for most of the revenue lost — correct. Right. It states what the numbers mean together, in business terms, without yet proposing an action — which is exactly what a finding is and what a recommendation must be built on.
  • C. We should introduce a retention programme aimed at premium customers next quarter, and fund it out of the acquisition budget the analysis has shown to be producing so little — This is a recommendation, and a thin one: it names an initiative but no measure and no date, so nobody could later say whether it worked.
  • D. Churn is a problem the business needs to take more seriously — This is a sentiment. It names no evidence, no place and no test, so it can be agreed with indefinitely without anything changing.

Application supplement · 2–7

Putting the whole analysis together

Everything before this section teaches one move at a time: name the force, place a system in the value chain, tell a fundable recommendation from a vague one. A finished piece of analysis is not one move. It is four of them joined so that each one carries the next, and the joins are where the credibility lives. This supplement rehearses the whole shape on one hypothetical firm, end to end, including the part almost nobody practises — the short piece of writing at the end.

How this supplement relates to the chapter. Chapter 2 supplies the frameworks and this module has already taught them: the five competitive forces in one section, the value chain in the next. What the chapter never does is say what a finished analysis looks like once the frameworks are written down together — how many areas to name, how many initiatives to recommend, and how long the closing argument should run. That shape comes from the way analyses of this kind are commissioned and read, so it appears here as a labeled supplement rather than as a fourth chapter learning objective.

The four parts, and the arithmetic between them

A brief of this kind arrives as four requests. They look independent and they are not: each one is built out of the answer to the one before it, which is why an analysis that is strong in three places can still fall apart at a join.

  1. Name the pressure. Apply the five competitive forces to the firm, give every force a sentence, and then argue that one of them is doing the damage — naming the observation that makes it the strongest rather than simply asserting that it is.
  2. Find the areas. Walk the value chain and name at least two internal activities where a system could create an operational or customer-focused advantage, each with the evidence that put it on the list.
  3. Recommend the initiative. Choose exactly one thing to build, sitting inside one of the areas you just named, described concretely enough to cost, and attached to the measure and the date that will decide whether it worked.
  4. Write the comparison. Set the firm beside a real company you can actually read about, say where the two are alike and where they differ, and finish with the practice that carries across — in 150 to 200 words, which is shorter than it sounds.

Two of those numbers pull against each other on purpose. At least two areas, and exactly one initiative: a floor on the searching and a ceiling on the proposing. Readers who mark work of this kind are looking for both, and the commonest failures are a scan that stopped at one idea and a recommendation that turned into a shopping list.

  • Two areas is a floor because one area is not a scan — a single area could be the first thing that occurred to you, and nobody reading it can tell whether you examined the rest of the chain or stopped at the first leak you noticed.
  • One initiative is a ceiling because recommending is choosing — three proposals hand the decision back to the reader, hide which one the analysis actually believes in, and make the work impossible to be wrong about, since something in a list of three will always look like it worked.
  • The initiative has to come out of the areas you named — if the recommendation appears from nowhere, the value chain section was decoration, and the reader is entitled to ask what the diagram was for.
  • The area you do not build still earns its place — it is the alternative your recommendation was preferred over, which is what turns a preference into a choice somebody can argue with.

Read the four parts below one at a time. Each card shows what the part has to contain, a version that does the job, a version that does not, and the reason a reader needs it at all.

Explore

The four parts of a finished analysis

Open each card and read the strong and weak versions side by side; both are invented practice wording rather than quotations from any real company.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

The competitive forces analysis · Which pressure, and how you know

  • What this part must contain: All five forces named and given a sentence each, then one of them argued as the strongest, resting on an observation rather than on an assertion that it is.
  • A version that does the job: “Entry is our strongest force: two national booking platforms began taking reservations in this region last year, and nothing keeps a contractor from renting elsewhere next week. Supplier power is low, substitutes are limited, rivalry among the established yards is steady, and buyer switching cost is close to zero.”
  • A version that does not: The weak version describes all five forces in general terms and calls none of them strongest, so the reader arrives at the value chain with no idea which pressure the technology is meant to answer.
  • Why the reader needs it: Everything downstream depends on this choice. If no force is named as the strongest, the recommendation at the end cannot be judged, because nothing has been stated that it is supposed to relieve.

The value chain scan · At least two areas, not one

  • What this part must contain: A walk through the primary and support activities, with at least two named as places where a system could create an operational or customer-focused advantage, each carrying the evidence that put it on the list.
  • A version that does the job: “Two areas stand out. In sales and marketing, every rental begins as a phone call, so requests arriving outside counter hours are lost without being counted. In operations, machines wait in the yard for a service check nobody has scheduled, so equipment the firm already owns earns nothing.”
  • A version that does not: The weak version names one area, usually the first one that occurred to the writer, and never says what was considered and set aside, so a reader cannot tell a scan from a hunch.
  • Why the reader needs it: The second area is what makes it a scan. It proves the whole chain was examined, and it becomes the alternative the recommendation was preferred over.

The single recommended initiative · One, not a list

  • What this part must contain: One system, described concretely enough to cost, sitting inside one of the areas you just named, plus the measure and the date that will settle whether it worked.
  • A version that does the job: “We recommend one initiative: a reservation system that publishes true fleet availability and lets a contractor hold a machine without speaking to anyone, judged by the share of rentals booked outside counter hours at the end of the next quarter.”
  • A version that does not: The weak version recommends three things at once, or recommends a category such as better digital capability, which names nothing anyone could build, cost, or later argue about.
  • Why the reader needs it: A reader being asked for money needs one thing to say yes or no to. Three recommendations is a wish list, and a category is a mood.

The written comparison · 150 to 200 words, every one of them spent

  • What this part must contain: Continuous prose setting the firm beside a real company you can read about: where the two are alike, where they differ, what each does that the other does not, and which practice carries across.
  • A version that does the job: “The national platform we compared ourselves with competes on availability rather than on price, which is our pressure in a larger body. The practice that transfers is publishing what is genuinely free today instead of promising to check the yard and call back.”
  • A version that does not: The weak version spends its words on the history of the firm and on admiration for the larger company, then finishes without naming one thing anyone would do differently on Monday.
  • Why the reader needs it: This is where the analysis stops being a set of diagrams and becomes an argument. The band is short deliberately: it leaves room for the lesson and no room for background.

Running it once, on a firm with no stake in your answer

The fastest way to learn the shape is to run it on something invented, where nothing is riding on the conclusion and you can afford to make the wrong call and read why it was wrong.

The practice situation below is hypothetical. It has been built only to give the four moves something to work on, and every fact in it exists because the exercise needed one.

Decide

The four moves, in the order a finished analysis makes them

Work through five decisions for this hypothetical firm, and read every outcome, including the ones you did not choose, before moving on.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

This is a hypothetical practice situation, invented only to give the analysis something to work on. A regional equipment rental business rents scaffolding, generators and floor sanders to building contractors. Revenue has slipped for two years running, leadership wants to spend on technology, and nobody has yet said what the spending is meant to fix. You are the analyst, and the five decisions below come in the order a finished piece of work makes them.

Decision 1. Three observations from the first week. Two national booking platforms began taking reservations in this region last year, and both publish live availability. The counter opens at seven and closes at five, while contractors plan their week between six and half past six in the morning. And no contractor has ever been asked to sign anything that would keep them from renting elsewhere next week.

  • Rivalry among existing competitors, because two rivals with the same equipment are chasing the same contractors — The platforms are not two more yards competing on price and service; they arrived in this region last year with a different way of selling. Calling this rivalry would push the firm toward matching rates, which is the response rivalry calls for and not the one this evidence asks for.
  • The threat of new entrants, because firms that were not competing here have arrived on the strength of low barriers, and the firm holds nothing that keeps a customer — the stronger call. Right. Entry into this region happened last year, and the third observation says why it was easy: nothing holds a contractor from one week to the next. Naming the force this way rules out a price response and points at building something a newcomer cannot rent, which is what the value chain scan then looks for.
  • Supplier bargaining power, because the manufacturers who sell the machines set the terms of the fleet — Nothing in the three observations concerns buying machines. Supplier power shows up as terms hardening, lead times stretching, or a single maker of equipment the firm cannot substitute, and none of that was seen.
  • The threat of substitutes, because a contractor could buy a machine outright instead of renting one — Buying instead of renting is a genuine substitute and deserves a sentence, but the evidence points at where reservations are being taken, not at contractors leaving the rental market. A substitute argument would need purchases to be rising.

Decision 2. Now walk the value chain. The evidence file holds four observations: requests arriving outside counter hours are never recorded; machines wait in the yard for a service check nobody has scheduled; delivery routing is done by one dispatcher who is rarely wrong; and the fleet is bought from three makers on annual terms the firm is happy with. Which pair goes into the analysis?

  • Sales and marketing, and operations — the lost after-hours requests and the machines standing idle — the stronger call. Right. Each rests on an observation, each is an internal activity the firm controls, and each is somewhere a system could create an operational or customer-focused advantage. Naming both is what makes this a scan, and the one you do not build becomes the alternative your recommendation beat.
  • Sales and marketing on its own, because the after-hours problem is plainly the biggest one — It may well be the biggest, and it is where the recommendation will land. But one area does not show that the rest of the chain was examined, and a reader cannot tell whether you compared anything or stopped at your first idea.
  • Outbound logistics and procurement — the dispatcher and the three suppliers — Neither observation reports a problem. A dispatcher who is rarely wrong, and terms the firm is happy with, are the parts of the chain that are working. An activity belongs on the list because something is leaking there, not because it exists.
  • All four activities, so that nothing is left out of the scan — Listing everything is close to listing nothing: it hands the reader four candidates with no ranking and no sign of judgement. Two is the floor because two proves a scan; the ceiling is however many you can actually support with evidence.

Decision 3. Two areas are on the table and the force has been named. Leadership asks the question they were always going to ask: what should we build?

  • A reservation system that publishes true fleet availability and lets a contractor hold a machine without speaking to anyone, judged by the share of rentals booked outside counter hours at the end of the next quarter — the stronger call. Right.
