It is one thing, it sits inside one of the two areas named, it answers the force the analysis called strongest, and it carries a measure and a date, so it can be argued with before it is funded and judged after.
  • A reservation system, a maintenance scheduler and a routing tool, so that both areas and the dispatcher are covered — Three initiatives is a wish list. It asks the reader to approve rather than to choose, conceals which one the analysis believes in, and guarantees that whatever happens, some part of it can be called a success.
  • An investment in modern digital infrastructure across the yard — Nobody can cost this, build it, or later say whether it worked. It names a direction rather than a system, which is exactly the difference between a preference and a recommendation.
  • A maintenance scheduler, because idle machines are the clearer waste of equipment the firm already owns — This is a defensible initiative in the second area, and it would win if the strongest force were something inside the yard. It loses because it does not touch the force that was named: a contractor who cannot book at six in the morning is still lost, however well the machines are serviced.

Decision 4. The summary has to set this firm beside a real company. Four candidates are proposed in the room, and each has a supporter.

  • A national equipment rental company that publishes how its online booking works and reports the same pressure, even though it is many times larger — the stronger call. Right. Same line of business, the same pressure, and enough published about the practice you care about to describe it accurately. The difference in size is not a problem, because what transfers is a practice rather than a budget.
  • The largest technology company anyone in the room can name, because everybody has heard of it — Name recognition is not evidence. If nothing is published about the specific practice you need, the summary ends up admiring a company instead of learning anything from it.
  • The rental yard on the other side of town, because it is the closest competitor — A close competitor is a firm you compete with, not one you can study. Nothing about how it schedules work or takes bookings is visible from outside, so there is nothing to read and nothing to compare.
  • A company from a completely unrelated industry that the writer already finds interesting — A distant industry can occasionally teach something, but it makes the transfer argument much harder to carry, and the usual result is a summary that explains the other company at length and never comes back to this one.

Decision 5. The last sentence of the summary is the one a reader remembers. Four drafts are on the table, and the analysis will be judged on which one closes it.

  • The other company is far larger and better funded than this firm, which explains the difference in their results — This states a difference and stops. It is probably true and it teaches nothing, because a gap in size is not something anybody reading this can act on.
  • The practice that transfers is publishing what is genuinely available now rather than promising to check and call back, and it can be done at this size with the fleet records the firm already keeps — the stronger call. Right. It names a practice rather than a company, says why the practice survives the difference in scale, and points at something the firm could begin doing, which is what a lesson that transfers actually means.
  • This firm should aim to match the other company’s technology within two years — This borrows an ambition rather than a lesson. It commits the firm to a target set by somebody else’s balance sheet and says nothing about which practice is worth copying.
  • Both companies show how important technology has become in this industry — This would fit any two companies in any industry, which is the test it fails. A sentence that could close any comparison has not compared anything.

Which sentence belongs in which part

Once the thinking is done, the analysis has to be laid out, and this is where a good piece of work most often loses its shape. A finding about an internal activity drifts into the forces section; the measure gets separated from the initiative it was supposed to judge; a paragraph of company history opens the summary and eats a quarter of the word budget.

Sorting sentences into the part they belong in is a mechanical skill, and it is worth practising mechanically. Some of the sentences below belong nowhere at all, which is the hardest call and the one that buys the most room.

Sort

Which part does this sentence belong in?

Every sentence below comes from a draft about the hypothetical rental firm; place each one in the part of the analysis where it does its work, and be willing to cut.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

The forces section — the pressure the firm is under, and which force is doing the damage

  • Two national booking platforms began taking reservations in this region last year, and nothing keeps a contractor from renting elsewhere next week — This is the evidence that entry was easy and that the firm holds no customer, which is what makes the threat of new entrants the strongest force. It belongs where the pressure is argued.
  • Supplier power is low: three makers supply the fleet on annual terms the firm is happy with — A weak force still gets a sentence. Saying so briefly is what shows the reader that all five were considered rather than only the one you wanted to write about.

The value chain section — internal activities where a system could create an advantage

  • Requests that arrive outside counter hours are never recorded, so sales and marketing loses work nobody can count — This names an internal activity and the leak inside it, which is exactly what a value chain area is. It is not a force, because it is something the firm controls.
  • Machines wait in the yard for a service check nobody has scheduled, so equipment the firm already owns earns nothing — Operations is the activity and idle equipment is the evidence. Keeping it here rather than folding it into the recommendation preserves it as the alternative the chosen initiative was preferred over.

The recommendation — the single initiative, with its measure and its date

  • Build a reservation system that publishes true fleet availability and lets a contractor hold a machine without a phone call — This is the single thing being proposed. It names a system rather than a direction, and it sits inside one of the two areas the scan produced.
  • Judge it by the share of rentals booked outside counter hours at the end of the next quarter — A measure and a date belong with the initiative they will judge. On its own a number is a statistic; attached to the proposal it is what makes the recommendation fundable.

The written comparison — the real company, the likenesses and differences, and the lesson

  • The company we compared ourselves with competes on availability rather than on price, which is the same pressure in a much larger business — This is the comparison itself, setting the two firms side by side on one axis and saying what they share. It has no place in the forces section, because it is about the other company.
  • The practice that transfers is publishing what is genuinely free today instead of promising to check and call back — This is the lesson, and it is the sentence the whole comparison exists to produce. A comparison that never reaches one has described two companies and taught nothing.

Cut it — true perhaps, but it earns no words in a piece this short

  • The firm has served contractors in this region for many years and is proud of how it looks after regular customers — It is probably true and it is certainly warm, but it is background. In a summary capped at two hundred words, every sentence of history is a sentence the lesson does not get.
  • Technology is changing every industry, and companies that fail to adapt will be left behind — This sentence would fit any analysis of any firm, which is how you can tell it carries no information about this one. Opening or closing with it spends words and buys nothing.

The summary, and a word band you can actually check

A range of 150 to 200 words is roughly six to eight sentences. That is the whole budget, and five things have to fit inside it: the pressure, the first area, the second area, the initiative, and the lesson that carries across from the company you compared with.

Divide it out and each of those gets somewhere between thirty and forty words — about one sentence each, with a little left over. Nothing else fits. Company history does not fit, admiration for the larger company does not fit, and a general observation about how technology is changing every industry costs fifteen words and returns none.

A word band is not a formatting rule. It is a forced choice about what the analysis is for, and the first thing it cuts is background.

The draft below is the write-up of the practice run you have just finished, laid out in the six parts it was built from. Read the first five straight through and you have the summary as it would be handed over; the sixth is the paragraph the writer was tempted to add at the end.

Part of the summaryDraft wording (hypothetical)
1. The pressureThe force squeezing this rental business hardest is the threat of new entrants: national booking platforms arrived in our region last year, and nothing we hold keeps a contractor from renting elsewhere next week.
2. First value chain areaIn sales and marketing, every rental still begins as a phone call, so a customer who cannot reach anyone simply calls the next firm on the list and we never learn that the request happened.
3. Second value chain areaIn operations, machines wait in the yard for a service check nobody has scheduled, so equipment that could be earning revenue stands still for days and the fleet looks smaller than it really is.
4. The one initiativeWe recommend one initiative: a reservation system that publishes true fleet availability and lets a customer hold a machine without speaking to anyone, judged by the share of rentals booked outside counter hours at the end of the next quarter.
5. The comparison and the lessonThe national platform we compared ourselves with competes on availability rather than on price, and the practice that transfers is publishing what is genuinely free today instead of promising to check the yard and call back.
6. Background the writer addedThis business has served contractors in the region for many years and staff often mention the reputation it has built for looking after regular customers, which the owners believe explains why it came through earlier downturns in construction.

Spreadsheets have no word-count function, so a count has to be built out of what they do have. Measure the text as it stands, measure it again with every space removed, and the difference is the number of gaps between words; add one and you have the words. Build three columns on that draft below — the count for each part, the running total, and the verdict against the band.

Spreadsheet

Count the summary against the band

The draft below is hypothetical, written in six parts. Type one formula for row 2 in each column and run it; it is applied down every row the way a filled-down formula behaves in a real sheet.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

Columns: Part of the summary · Draft wording (hypothetical) · Words · Running total · Length check

1. Column C: count the words in each part. A spreadsheet has no word function, so measure the text twice — once as it stands, once with every space removed.

=LEN(TRIM(B2))-LEN(SUBSTITUTE(TRIM(B2)," ",""))+1

The count is built out of what a spreadsheet does have. TRIM comes first because two spaces between sentences would otherwise be counted as two gaps and quietly inflate every row.

2. Column D: show the running total, so you can see which word the draft is on at the end of each part.

=SUM($C$2:C2)

Pinning one end and releasing the other is how a running total is written. The first row totals one cell and the last totals all six, so the column shows exactly where the draft crosses each edge of the band.

3. Column E: turn the running total into a verdict against the band of 150 to 200 words. Column D is the reader’s own working rather than a given, so rebuild the total inside this formula instead of pointing at it.

=IF(SUM($C$2:C2)<150,"Keep drafting",IF(SUM($C$2:C2)>200,"Cut it back","In the band"))

Nesting IF is how a spreadsheet says between. Read the finished column downwards and the draft tells its own story: short for four parts, inside the band once the comparison is written, and outside it again the moment background is added.

What the finished column tells youRead the verdict column downwards. The draft is under the band for its first four parts, crosses into it at 179 words only when the comparison is written, and leaves it again at 217 the moment a paragraph of company history is added at the end. That is the usual life of a summary of this length: it is not short because you have said too little about the business, it is long because you have said too much about it.

Choosing the company you set beside it

The comparison is the part students most often treat as decoration, picking a company they admire and describing it. It is not decoration. The other company is a measuring instrument: it exists in the analysis to show what a firm under the same pressure did about it, so that a practice can be lifted across.

Four things make a company usable for that job, and only one of them is about the company being impressive:

  • Enough of it is published — you need to be able to describe the specific practice accurately, which means articles, filings or the company’s own material about how the thing actually works, not just a logo everyone recognises.
  • It faces the same pressure — the point of comparison is what somebody did about a force you are also under, so a company whose hardest force is completely different will not teach you much about yours.
  • It is close enough in what it does — a practice carries across most reliably when the value chain looks similar, because then the activity you are improving is genuinely the same activity.
  • Its size does not matter, and its reachability does — a firm many times larger is fine, because what transfers is a practice rather than a budget; a direct local competitor is usually useless, because nothing about how it works is visible from outside.

Having chosen one, compare on fixed axes rather than impressions. Three axes are enough, and they are the three this module has already taught:

  1. Which force each firm faces hardest — this is what establishes that the two situations are comparable at all, and it is the sentence that earns the rest of the paragraph.
  2. Which value chain activity each strengthens with technology — and whether it is the same activity, because a practice moved between different activities usually stops making sense.
  3. What each measures to know it worked — the measure is the most portable thing in the whole comparison, since it survives every difference in size and market.

Two words in a brief of this kind are worth reading carefully. Complement asks what each firm does that the other does not, which is a two-way question rather than a ranking. Lessons that transfer asks for a practice that still makes sense once the budget, the scale and the brand are stripped away.

Check yourself

The rules of the shape, and why they are there

Each question is about why the deliverable is built this way rather than about the frameworks themselves; read every explanation.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. A brief asks for at least two internal areas where technology could help. Why does the floor sit at two rather than at one?

  • A. Because two areas give the reader a choice, and a reader offered a choice is likelier to approve something — Approval is not what the scan is for, and offering two things to build is precisely what the single-initiative rule forbids. The second area is evidence of searching, not a second proposal.
  • B. Because naming two areas is what shows the whole chain was examined, and it gives the recommendation something it was preferred over — correct. Right. One area could be the first idea the writer had. Two, each with its own evidence, demonstrates a scan, and the one you do not build becomes the alternative your recommendation beat.
  • C. Because a value chain has nine activities, so fewer than two would leave most of the chain undescribed — Describing the chain and naming opportunity areas are different jobs. You can walk all nine activities and still conclude that two of them are leaking, which is a perfectly good result.
  • D. Because two initiatives can then be funded together and share the cost of the same underlying system — This confuses an area with an initiative. Areas are places in the chain where a system could help; the recommendation that follows is deliberately limited to a single one.

2. The same brief asks for one recommended initiative. An analyst has two strong candidates and wants to propose both. What is the argument against it?

  • A. A single initiative is cheaper than several, and cost is what decision makers care about most — Cost matters, but the rule is not about the size of the bill. One expensive initiative is still a single recommendation, and three cheap ones are still a wish list.
  • B. The reader is being asked to make one decision, and a recommendation that names three things hides which one the analysis actually believes in — correct. Right. Recommending is choosing. Several proposals hand the choice back to the reader and make the work impossible to be wrong about, since something in the list will look like it worked.
  • C. Building more than one system at a time is beyond what most organizations can manage in a year — Plenty of organizations run several projects at once. The limit here is a limit on the argument being made, not on the firm’s capacity to build things.
  • D. The second area exists in order to be recommended later, in a follow-up study commissioned once the first initiative has been delivered and its results have been reviewed — The second area is not a queued proposal. It is the evidence that a scan happened and the alternative against which the chosen initiative was measured.

3. A comparison summary has to end with the lessons that transfer from the other company. Which of these is a lesson in that sense?

  • A. A target the smaller firm should aim to reach within a fixed period — Borrowing somebody else’s ambition is not a lesson. A target set by a far larger balance sheet tells this firm nothing about what to do differently on Monday.
  • B. A statement of how much larger and better resourced the other company is — That is a difference rather than a lesson. A gap in scale is the first thing anyone notices about two companies and the last thing anyone can act on.
  • C. A practice that survives the difference in size, described concretely enough that the smaller firm could start doing it — correct. Right. The test is whether the practice still makes sense once the budget, the scale and the brand are stripped away. Publishing real availability is a practice; owning a national fleet is not.
  • D. A general observation about how important technology has become across the industry — A sentence that would fit any two companies in any industry has compared nothing. It is the most common way a comparison ends without producing anything usable.

4. Why would a brief cap the written summary at a band as narrow as 150 to 200 words?

  • A. It keeps the writing short enough that a busy reader will finish it, which is the reason any limit is set — Brevity is part of it, but a limit this tight does more than save a reader time: it forces a choice about which of the things you could say are actually worth saying.
  • B. It forces the words onto the comparison and the lesson, because there is no room left for company history once those are written — correct. Right. Five things have to fit: the pressure, two areas, the initiative, and the transfer. At roughly thirty-five words each that is the entire budget, which is why background is the first thing to cut.
  • C. It makes every summary the same length so that they can be compared with each other fairly — Uniform length is a side effect rather than a purpose. Two summaries of identical length can differ completely in how much of the band was spent on anything that matters.
  • D. It signals that the written part matters less than the framework analysis, which carries no limit at all — The band is short because the writing is dense, not because it is minor. The closing argument is the part that says what all the diagrams were for.

Knowing the rule is not the same as catching it in someone else’s draft. The rules above stay abstract until you have used them to judge a report you did not write, about a company you have not seen before — which is closer to the situation the graded version puts you in than one more pass over the same rental company is. None of the six companies below is real; each is invented for exactly this question.

Apply it

Six companies you have not seen before

Each question drops you into a different, invented company midway through this exact deliverable. Judge what is already there before you read the explanation.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

1. A regional group of veterinary clinics has grown mostly by referral. A national telehealth-vet chain has just entered the same three-county area, offering video consultations that are faster and cheaper for routine cases, and existing clients have started asking whether they can “do the checkup online first.” Which competitive force is doing the most damage right now?

  • A. Rivalry among the existing clinics in the area — Nothing here describes another physical clinic undercutting on price or service — the pressure is coming from outside the set of firms that look like this one.
  • B. The threat of substitute services from outside the industry — correct. Right. A video consultation is not a clinic; it is a different way of meeting the same need, which is exactly what a substitute is. It arrives from outside the industry’s usual rivals.
  • C. The bargaining power of veterinary drug suppliers — No supplier tension of any kind is described. Nothing here is about the cost or availability of medicine.
  • D. The threat of new entrants opening additional physical clinics — The entrant is not opening more of the same kind of clinic — it is replacing the visit itself, which is a substitute, not a new rival in the same class.

2. An HVAC installation company’s owner lists two “weak links” in a report: (1) technicians lose up to an hour a day driving between jobs because routes are still scheduled by hand, and (2) the company’s biggest competitor operates a much larger fleet of trucks. Which of these is actually a value-chain opportunity area for this firm?

  • A. Both, since either fact could justify spending money on a new system — Motivation is not the test. A value-chain area has to be an activity this firm performs, not a fact about someone else’s.
  • B. Only the fleet-size one, since matching a rival’s scale is the more urgent problem — This is the trap the question is testing. A rival having more trucks is a competitive fact, not a leak inside this company’s own activities — there is nothing here to build a system around.
  • C. Only the driving-time one; the fleet size is a fact about a competitor, not this firm’s own chain — correct. Right. Hand-scheduled routing sitting inside operations or outbound logistics is something this firm does and a system could change. The competitor’s fleet size describes the competitor, not this firm’s chain.
  • D. Neither, since a genuine value-chain area has to show up as a line item in the budget first — Value-chain activities span the whole firm, from inbound logistics through service; whether something is already budgeted is not what makes it a real activity.

3. A regional print shop’s owner writes: “We should modernize our order process.” A consultant rewrites it as: “Add a self-serve online quoting and file-upload page by the start of next quarter, so a customer can price and submit a job without calling in; success is measured by the share of new orders placed without a phone call.” What does the rewrite supply that the owner’s version is missing?

  • A. It names something specific enough to build, with a date and a measure attached — correct. Right. “Modernize our order process” could mean almost anything and could never be marked finished. The rewrite names the artifact, the date, and the number that will say whether it worked.
  • B. It is shorter, which on its own tends to make a recommendation easier to fund — Length is not the test the earlier questions established; a longer sentence that names the thing, the date and the measure still beats a short vague one.
  • C. It avoids naming any particular piece of software or vendor — The rewrite is just as much about technology as the original — the difference is precision, not the absence of a system, and it still does not name a vendor.
  • D. It removes any mention of what the change might cost to build — Nothing here says the initiative is free. What changed is specificity, not cost, and the rewrite still gives no budget either.

4. A comparison summary for a small independent bookstore says: “The larger national chain we compared ourselves to processes online orders through a fully automated warehouse, and we should build the same thing.” Does that lesson transfer?

  • A. Yes — copying the more successful, better-resourced company’s exact system is the safest recommendation to make — This is the trap the assignment’s own comparison step exists to catch: borrowing a solution that only makes sense at a much larger scale is not a lesson, it is a wish.
  • B. No — the comparison company is too different in size to be a fair one to compare against in the first place — Size difference is exactly why a comparison is useful, not a reason to avoid it — the earlier material is explicit that the two companies do not need to be the same size, only worth reading about.
  • C. Yes — both are booksellers, so any practice at the larger one should transfer straight to the smaller one — Being in the same industry does not make every practice scale-appropriate; a lesson still has to survive being resized before it transfers.
  • D. No — the warehouse itself is scale-dependent; the lesson is the smaller practice underneath it — correct. Right. The practice worth keeping is the underlying idea — a customer not having to call to check on an order — separated from the scale-specific system that happens to deliver it at a national chain.

5. A regional moving company’s dispatcher says business has been steady, but drivers report that more customers are booking through a national moving-marketplace app that compares quotes from several local movers at once and takes a fee for every booking it sends. Which one-sentence diagnosis both names the pressure correctly and points at a fundable next step?

  • A. Customers are price-shopping more because the economy is uncertain right now, so the firm should simply lower its prices across the board — This names a symptom, not the pressure, and the response is a race to the bottom rather than a system anyone could build.
  • B. A new intermediary is capturing the relationship and a fee before the job reaches us, so we should build our own instant-quote booking page — correct. Right. The pressure is a new channel sitting between the firm and its customers; the response names a concrete, buildable page and a way it would be used, not just a wish that customers came back.
  • C. Drivers are complaining about long days, so we should hire more drivers to spread the workload evenly across the week — This addresses a complaint that was never the point of the scenario and proposes no system at all — more drivers does nothing about a channel problem.
  • D. The marketplace app is unfair competition and should be reported to a regulator or a trade association — Whether it is fair is not the question a competitive-forces analysis asks, and a complaint filed with a regulator is not an IT initiative.

6. A landscaping company’s draft report names two “opportunity areas”: (1) “improve customer service” and (2) “improve how the office handles customers on the phone.” Do these count as two distinct value-chain areas?

  • A. Yes, because they are worded differently — Different wording for the same activity is still one activity. The floor of two exists to prove a scan happened, and a scan that finds one thing twice has not happened.
  • B. No, because customer service is not part of the value chain at all — Service is one of the primary value-chain activities. The flaw here is duplication, not miscategorization — customer service belongs in the chain, just not twice.
  • C. Yes, because customer service is the most important function in any company — Importance does not create a second area; a critical activity is still one activity, however it is phrased.
  • D. No, because they describe the same activity twice, so the scan really only found one leak — correct. Right. Both sentences point at the same service activity from slightly different angles. A second, genuinely different area would have to come from somewhere else in the chain — inbound scheduling, the crews themselves, billing.

Before you hand it over

The last thing worth building is the habit of checking the shape before anyone else does. The list below is the shape itself, turned into questions you can answer honestly in about two minutes.

Self-check

The shape, before anyone else reads it

Rate each statement honestly; anything you cannot do yet has a pointer to the exact place in this section to reread.

Lesson and answer summary — the interactive version of this activity loads when scripting is available.

  • I can name all five forces on one firm and then argue that one of them is the strongest, using an observation rather than an assertion. The forces card above, then the first decision in the practice run.
  • I can walk a value chain and come back with at least two areas, each carrying the evidence that put it on the list. The value chain card, then the second decision, where naming a single area is the trap.
  • I can say why the area I did not build is still worth naming in the analysis. The fourth bullet in the arithmetic list at the top of this section.
  • I can write one recommendation that names the system, the measure and the date, and I can tell it apart from a category of spending. The single-initiative card, and the third decision in the practice run.
  • I can choose a real company to compare with on stated grounds rather than on how well known it is. The four criteria under choosing the company you set beside it, and the fourth decision.
  • I can finish the comparison with a practice that survives the difference in size, and say why it survives. The fifth decision in the practice run, and the third question in the check-yourself set.
  • I can count the words in a draft and say which part to cut first when it runs over the band. The worksheet above: the running total column shows exactly where the draft crosses each edge.

The frameworks are the easy half. What separates a finished analysis from a set of diagrams is that every part points at the next one: the force chooses the areas, the areas choose the initiative, the initiative is what the comparison is testing, and the last sentence names the one thing somebody could start doing.

Reference

Chapter vocabulary

Every term the chapter defines, in one place, written so it makes sense on its own. Search by word, or filter by the objective the term belongs to. Use this while you read rather than after — a good deal of the difficulty in this chapter is two terms that sound alike meaning genuinely different things, such as efficiency and effectiveness, or a resource and a capability.

2.2affiliate marketing
A revenue model in which a business pays other businesses that bring or refer customers to it; revenue sharing is typically used. It is one of the revenue models the internet has enabled or enhanced, alongside the sales, transaction fee, and advertising models already common offline.For example: A creator posts a link to a pair of headphones and earns a cut of the price when a follower buys through that link, the way Amazon’s Associates program works.
2.3augmented reality
Using information systems to enhance what a person perceives of the real world by supplying relevant information about their surroundings. Special glasses or another device layer computer-generated content on top of the actual view rather than replacing it.For example: Google Glass, eyeglasses with a tiny built-in screen, could show the wearer weather, transit schedules, and reviews of the restaurant they were looking at.
2.1automating
A way of thinking about technology that asks how to get an existing task done faster, more cheaply, and perhaps more accurately and consistently — in other words, how to raise efficiency. It speeds up the work that is already being done rather than questioning whether the work is being done well.For example: A bank that once had staff key in paper loan applications lets customers fill the same form out online, so the checking and data entry happen the instant it is submitted.
2.1best-cost provider strategy
A middle-of-the-road position in which a company offers products or services of reasonably good quality at competitive prices, rather than being the absolute cheapest or the most distinctive. The chapter gives Dell as an example.For example: Buying the laptop that is not the cheapest on the shelf and not the most expensive, because it is decent quality for what it costs.
2.1business/IT alignment
Making sure the information systems an organization builds or buys actually match the strategy it is pursuing. Companies try to maximize this, and generally do not want a system that fights the strategy even if that system would save time or money.For example: A store competing purely on low prices funds a system that squeezes cost out of its warehouse rather than one that adds a luxury personal-shopper service.
2.2business model
A summary of a company’s strategic direction that lays out how its objectives will be reached: what it does, how it uniquely does it, what resources and activities that takes, how it gets paid, and what it all costs. It names the value proposition along with the customer segments, channels, customer relationships, revenue streams, key resources, key activities, key partners, and cost structure.For example: Writing out, on one page, who would buy your food-truck tacos, how they would hear about you, what you charge, and what the truck and ingredients cost you.
2.1business process
The activities an organization performs to reach its business goals. These include core activities that take inputs and turn them into outputs, plus supporting activities that make those core activities possible.For example: Everything a coffee shop does between a customer ordering and walking out with a drink — taking the order, pulling the shot, handing it over — along with the ordering of beans that keeps it possible.
2.1capabilities
An organization’s ability to actually put its assets to work in the marketplace. Owning something valuable is not enough; capabilities are what let a firm turn it into cost savings or a better product.For example: Two restaurants buy the same ingredients from the same supplier, but only one has cooks who can turn them into a dish people line up for.
2.2collaborative economy
Another name the chapter uses for the sharing economy: an economic system in which assets or services are shared between private individuals, either free or for a fee, typically by means of the internet. What matters is access to the asset rather than owning it.For example: Borrowing a neighbor’s drill through an app instead of buying a drill you would use twice a year.
2.2cross-side network effects
The change in value a user gets when more people join the other side of a platform. Platforms have two sides — those who produce and those who consume — and growth on one side pulls the other side along.For example: An app store gets more useful to you as more apps are added, and developers get more interested in building for it as more people use it.
2.3crowdfunding
Securing business financing from individuals in the marketplace — the crowd — to fund an initiative, typically some consumer-based product. The supporters, called backers, pledge an amount in return for certain benefits, and on a platform such as Kickstarter or Indiegogo they are charged only if the campaign reaches its funding goal.For example: Pledging money toward a board game on Kickstarter and paying nothing at all, because too few backers were interested and the campaign never reached its goal.
2.3customer creation
The first step of the execution phase in the lean startup approach, where a company tests whether it can establish a business model that repeats reliably rather than working just once. Building and scaling the company itself follows after this.For example: After a few strangers pay for your tutoring service, checking whether you can keep finding paying students week after week instead of only the first three friends of friends.
2.3customer discovery
The first search step in the lean startup approach: finding out whether the problem you think exists actually does, whether there would be a market for a solution, and then whether the solution you have in mind would really address it. It means talking to potential customers before you build anything.For example: Asking twenty students whether finding a study partner is genuinely a hassle for them, before writing a single line of an app to fix it.
2.3customer validation
The second search step in the lean startup approach, where a company puts its minimum viable product in front of people to test whether they would actually pay for the solution. Saying a problem is annoying and handing over money are two different things.For example: Putting a price on the study-partner app and seeing how many of the students who said they liked the idea will actually subscribe.
2.1differentiation strategy
Competing by providing better products or services than rivals rather than cheaper ones. A company can aim that broadly at many kinds of buyers or focus it on one segment, as Apple did for years with high-quality computers for home and educational buyers.For example: Paying more for a pair of shoes because that brand fits and lasts better, not because it was the lowest price on the rack.
2.1digital twin
A digital representation of a physical object, used to model how that object behaves and interacts with its environment. Feeding it live sensor data lets people troubleshoot or plan maintenance on equipment that is hard or impossible to reach.For example: NASA kept physical replicas of space modules such as Apollo 13 on the ground to work out how to operate or repair the real one; a digital twin does the same job in software.
2.3disruptive innovation
Another name the chapter uses for a radical innovation: something built on a markedly new or different technology that reaches new customers or gives existing ones far greater benefits, and eventually pushes aside the product it competes with.For example: Streaming music pushed compact discs and music stores to the margins.
2.1distinctive competency
What an organization’s resources and capabilities add up to in the marketplace — things like innovation, agility, quality, or low cost. These are what make its product genuinely valuable to customers compared with what rivals offer.For example: Toyota being known for quality and Nintendo for value are the kinds of competencies the chapter lists as sources of competitive advantage.
2.1effectiveness
The extent to which goals or tasks are accomplished well. It is about doing the right things properly, which is not the same as doing them quickly.For example: A tutor who actually gets you to understand the material, even if the session runs long.
2.1efficiency
The extent to which goals are accomplished faster, at lower cost, or with relatively little time and effort. Systems at the operational level are usually aimed at this.For example: A self-checkout lane that gets you out of the store in two minutes instead of ten.
2.1executive level
The strategic level of an organization, where the president and chief executive officer, chief information officer, vice presidents, and possibly the board handle long-term questions such as which products to make and which countries to compete in. Their decisions are unstructured and carry broad, long-term consequences.For example: The people who decide whether a company should stop making a product line entirely, a call that changes employment and profit for years.
2.1first-mover advantage
The edge a company can get from being the first to enter a market. Most organizations do not have this luxury and must instead compete inside industries that are already established.For example: The first food-delivery app in a college town gets known as the one everybody uses before a second one shows up.
2.2freemium
A blend of free and premium: giving away a limited version of a digital product or service at no charge to build a large user base, then charging for the unrestricted version, usually on a subscription. It works because the cost of serving one more user of a digital product has fallen so low.For example: Dropbox and iCloud hand out free accounts with a small amount of storage and charge you once you want more space.
2.1functional area information system
A system built to support the particular business processes of one discrete part of an organization, such as marketing, accounting and finance, human resources, or production and operations. Each area has its own activities and therefore needs its own kind of system.For example: The payroll system that pays employees is separate from the system marketing uses to plan advertising.
2.2gig economy
An arrangement in which workers are not employed by the company at all but are hired for short-term, temporary jobs. The chapter notes it often leaves workers without protection against discrimination, without social security, with little job security, and with limited contact with coworkers.For example: Driving for a ride-hailing app on weekends with no set schedule, no benefits, and no manager or coworkers you ever meet.
2.2in-app purchase
Buying extra features, content, or in-game currency from inside an app you downloaded for free. It lets a product build a huge user base quickly while still producing a continuous stream of revenue.For example: Downloading a free-to-play game such as Candy Crush and then spending real money inside it on extra content or in-game currency.
2.3innovation
Creating new products, processes, or services that return value to the organization. The chapter is careful to separate it from mere invention: innovation means actually realizing the value, not just having the new idea.For example: Plenty of people sketch a better shopping cart; innovation is the company that builds it, sells it, and makes money on it.
2.1key performance indicator (KPI)
The handful of metrics judged most critical for assessing progress toward a particular goal. They are usually shown on digital dashboards so managers can see at a glance where things stand.For example: A store manager’s dashboard showing sales per hour, items per transaction, and how much inventory is left.
2.3lean startup methodology
An approach pioneered by Eric Ries in which a company first searches for a viable product and business model and only executes that model once it has found a fit between the product and the market. The older habit was to build a product first and then hunt for customers.For example: Testing whether people want your idea by talking to them and shipping a rough version, instead of spending a year building the polished thing nobody asked for.
2.1low-cost leadership strategy
Competing by offering the best prices in the industry on your goods or services. The chapter gives Walmart as the example.For example: A store that wins your business simply because the same box of cereal costs less there than anywhere else.
2.1managerial level
Also called the tactical level, where functional managers in areas like marketing, finance, manufacturing, and human resources monitor and control operational activities and pass information up to higher levels. Their decisions are moderately complex, usually stay inside one business function, and look days to months ahead.For example: A marketing manager deciding how to split the advertising budget across the coming three months.
2.3minimum viable product (MVP)
A product built with just the features needed to demonstrate how your solution meets the problem, and nothing more. It exists to test a hypothesis quickly, not to impress anyone.For example: A single working screen that lets someone match with a study partner, with no profile pictures, messaging, or settings yet.
2.3open innovation
Bringing outsiders into the innovation process because good ideas often exist beyond the organization’s own walls. It usually means opening some organizational data and knowledge to those outsiders, which is a tradeoff a company has to weigh.For example: Eli Lilly created a site called InnoCentive where companies post scientific problems, anyone can attempt a solution, and a reward goes to whoever solves it.
2.1operational level
The bottom and widest level of an organization, where routine day-to-day business processes and customer interactions happen. Foremen and supervisors here make highly structured, recurring decisions, and planning covers only a few hours or days.For example: The supervisor on a store floor confirming that the system’s automatic reorder of running shoes should go through.
2.1organizational learning
An organization’s ability to use its past behavior and its own data to improve its business processes. It builds on automating, because the data a system creates while automating work can reveal how that work should change.For example: A bank studying which approved loans later went bad, then tightening the rules it uses to approve the next batch.
2.1organizational strategy
A firm’s plan for accomplishing its mission and goals and for gaining or sustaining a competitive advantage over rivals. Information systems are judged by whether they help carry that plan out.For example: A company deciding it will win on speed of delivery, and then funding every project that makes deliveries faster.
2.2platform-based business model
A model in which the company does not supply the product or service itself but coordinates others — other businesses and its own users — so they create value for each other. That makes it a two-sided market whose success depends on the network effect.For example: Airbnb owns none of the rooms and Uber owns none of the cars; both depend on users to offer the service and other users to consume it.
2.3radical innovation
An innovation built on a markedly new or different technology that opens up new customer segments or gives existing customers significantly greater benefits, and eventually marginalizes or replaces what came before. The chapter contrasts it with incremental innovation, which just enhances or upgrades what already exists.For example: Digital photography displaced chemical photography, and smartphones displaced MP3 players and dedicated GPS units.
2.1resources
The specific assets an organization uses to achieve lower cost or a product different from its competitors’. Proprietary technology, brand equity, and a loyal, established customer base are the examples the chapter gives.For example: The chapter names a proprietary asset at Coca-Cola, a user base at Facebook, and a brand at Nike among its sources of competitive advantage — assets a rival cannot simply go out and buy.
2.2revenue model
A description of how a firm will earn revenue, generate profits, and produce a superior return on the money invested in it. Even nonprofit organizations need one.For example: Netflix charging a recurring monthly fee, while Google gives its service away and charges advertisers instead.
2.2same-side network effects
The rise or fall in value that happens when more users join your own side of a network. More users on your side can help you, but they can also crowd you out.For example: As more people switch to iOS, everyone on it benefits from wider compatibility for the Keynote presentation format; but as more riders open Uber at once, competition for available rides pushes prices up.
2.1semistructured decision
A decision where some of the procedure can be laid out in advance but not enough to produce a specific recommendation, so judgment and expertise are still required. This is the typical shape of managerial-level decision making.For example: A production manager looking at sales forecasts, inventory levels, and capacity, then deciding which product to build first.
2.2sharing economy
An economic system in which assets or services are shared between private individuals, either free or for a fee, typically by means of the internet. Platforms make it work, and the point is being able to access an asset rather than owning it.For example: Using a car-sharing service instead of buying a car, since a shared vehicle sits idle far less of the day than a private one.
2.3startup
A new venture, usually technology based, with high potential to scale up and grow quickly. They are often cofounded by entrepreneurs, developers, designers, or others with a promising idea, and may turn to incubators, accelerators, angel investors, or crowdfunding for support.For example: Two people with an idea and a prototype working out of a shared office, hoping to reach millions of users rather than one town.
2.1strategic necessity
An investment an organization has no real choice about — something it must do simply to survive, whether or not it lines up neatly with the overall strategy. Not every system a company funds is chosen freely.For example: A store that has to accept contactless payment because customers now expect it, even though it wins the store no advantage over rivals who all accept it too.
2.1strategic planning
The work senior managers do to form a vision of where the organization needs to head, turn that vision into measurable objectives and performance targets, and craft a strategy for reaching them. It happens at the executive level.For example: Leadership setting a three-year target for entering two new countries and deciding what has to be built to get there.
2.1structured decision
A decision where the procedure to follow in a given situation can be specified ahead of time. Because they are so straightforward, they can be programmed right into operational systems and made with little or no human involvement.For example: An inventory system that watches stock levels and automatically orders more shoes whenever the count drops below a set number.
2.1transaction
Anything that happens as part of a firm’s daily business that it must keep a record of. These pile up at the operational level and become the raw material higher levels analyze later.For example: Every single sale rung up at a register, along with the timestamp and the items in the basket.
2.1unstructured decision
A decision for which few or no procedures can be specified in advance, because the problem is complex and nonroutine. Executives face these, and must weigh the effects on the whole organization.For example: Top managers deciding whether to launch an entirely new product or kill an existing one, knowing either choice reshapes employment and profit for years.
2.3validated learning
Testing your assumptions empirically through real customer feedback so the next version is better informed. It is what the build-measure-learn cycle produces: you build the smallest thing that tests a hypothesis, measure how people respond, then decide whether to change direction or keep going.For example: Instagram began as an app called Burbn crammed with features from check-ins to gaming; once the founders learned users did not value all that, they stripped it down to sharing photos and commenting.
2.1value chain
The whole set of activities inside an organization that add value as supplies come in, get turned into products and services, and are marketed, sold, distributed, and supported after the sale. Employees can use information systems at any point along it to add more value.For example: For a hotel, the chain runs from receiving supplies and taking reservations, through checking guests in and cleaning rooms, to resolving a complaint after the guest has gone home.
2.1value chain analysis
The process of examining an organization’s activities to determine where value is added to its products or services and what it costs to add that value. You map out each activity, work out the costs and what drives them, and then decide which activities to optimize to cut costs and gain an advantage.For example: A pizza shop laying out every step from buying flour to delivering the box, pricing each step, and finding that delivery routing is what is quietly eating the profit.
2.1value creation
What happens when an organization can offer its products at a lower cost or with better, more differentiated benefits than customers can get elsewhere. Distinctive competencies are what make it possible, and it is how a company gains a competitive advantage.For example: A phone that costs the same as its rivals but has a camera nobody else can match gives you more for your money.
2.2value proposition
The usefulness a product or service offers to its customers — the reason they need it, the problem it solves, and why they would pick it over a competitor’s. It is one of the core components of a business model.For example: A meal-delivery service’s promise that you get a hot dinner without cooking, shopping, or leaving your apartment.
2.3virtual reality (VR) headset
A head-mounted device that creates an immersive three-dimensional experience, replacing what you see with a computer-generated environment. Companies redeploy this kind of technology in new ways to gain an advantage.For example: Architects and interior designers let clients walk through a planned building with a headset such as the Apple Vision Pro or Meta Quest before construction has even started.
2.2XaaS
Short for X as a service: a business model built on providing something as an ongoing service instead of selling it as a product. The customer pays for use rather than buying the equipment, which turns their fixed costs into variable ones and gives the provider a reason to make the equipment last.For example: Rather than selling an airline an engine and spare parts, GE is paid for guaranteeing continuous uptime — essentially selling thrust as a service.
Put it together

Final challenge

Thirty-nine situations rather than thirty-nine definitions. Each describes something happening in an organization and asks what is actually going on, which is the form this material takes once you are the person being asked. Answer all of them, then score: the result breaks out by objective, so a weak area points at the section to reread instead of disappearing into a single number.

Final challenge

Final challenge

Answer key — the interactive, self-scoring version loads when scripting is available.

1. 2.1 At a hypothetical parts distributor, three decisions are made on the same morning. A shift supervisor confirms a reorder the inventory system proposed when a bin fell below its set level. A marketing manager allocates next quarter’s advertising budget across four product lines. The executive committee debates discontinuing a product line altogether. Which decision does the chapter call structured, and what follows from that?

  • A. The supervisor’s, because the procedure for this situation can be specified in advance, so it can be programmed straight into an operational system — correct. Structured decisions are those in which the procedures to follow for a given situation can be specified in advance, and because they are relatively straightforward they can be programmed directly into operational information systems and made with little or no human intervention. The chapter’s own example is an inventory system that issues an order when levels drop below a set point and the manager simply confirms it.
  • B. The manager’s, because a quarterly budget allocation follows an established annual procedure even though the amounts change every time — That is a semistructured decision at the managerial level, where some procedures can be specified in advance but not to the extent that a specific recommendation can be made. The chapter uses a marketing manager allocating a quarter’s advertising budget as its illustration of exactly this level.
  • C. The executive committee’s, because discontinuing a line follows the formal governance rules the company has already written down — That is an unstructured decision at the executive level, where few or no procedures for the situation can be specified in advance, and the chapter’s example is top managers deciding to develop a new product or discontinue an existing one. Governance rules settle who decides, not what the decision should be.
  • D. None of the three, because any decision that commits money needs human judgment and so cannot be fully specified beforehand — Money is committed at all three levels, so spending cannot be what separates them. The chapter’s dividing line is whether the procedure can be written down beforehand, and an automatic reorder shows that some decisions involving money can be.

2. 2.1 The chief executive of a hypothetical hospital group asks for a system that will show her how the group is trending, where it stands against comparable groups, and what the next two years look like under different assumptions. A vendor proposes a screen showing yesterday’s ward-by-ward patient throughput hour by hour. What is the accurate objection?

  • A. There is no objection to make, because operational detail is the raw material every level works from, so a system that reports it serves an executive as well as a supervisor — Operational data does feed the higher levels, and the chapter says so: systems at the operational level help automate repetitive activities but also gather valuable data for higher decision-making levels. Passing that detail upward unaggregated is not the same as summarizing it, and the chief executive asked for trends, projections, and comparisons.
  • B. The proposal belongs at the managerial level, since monitoring and controlling operational activity is what midlevel managers do, so the executive should receive the same screen weekly rather than daily — Monitoring and controlling operational activities is indeed the managerial level’s work, and this screen would be a reasonable managerial tool. Changing how often an executive receives operational detail does not turn it into the aggregate summaries and projections the chapter says executive decisions require.
  • C. The proposal fails because executive systems work from unstructured external data such as economic conditions and changing customer tastes, so anything built from the group’s own records cannot serve that level — Executives do need unstructured data such as global economic factors, demographic changes, and shifting customer tastes, which is why this option sounds right. The chapter also has executive systems providing key performance indicators that balance performance across the organization and benchmark it against competitors, and those come from the organization’s own records.
  • D. The proposal serves the operational level, where systems automate routine activity to improve efficiency, while the executive level needs aggregate summaries, projections of the future, and benchmarks against competitors — correct. Information systems at the operational level automate routine and repetitive activities to improve efficiency, while at the executive level they provide aggregate summaries of past data, projections of the future, and indicators that benchmark the organization against its competitors. The vendor has answered a supervisor’s question with an executive’s budget.

3. 2.1 A hypothetical lender’s approval criteria let weak applications through: reviewers handled about four applications a day and accepted roughly two poor ones a week. The lender then automated the same criteria, reviewers now handle about twelve a day, and poor approvals have climbed. Nothing in the software is malfunctioning. Which reading matches the chapter?

  • A. The system was implemented badly, because a correctly built approval system would have identified the weak applications as it processed them — A system that screened applications on better criteria would indeed catch them, and that is the point: the criteria are the thing that is wrong. Blaming the build implies the specification was right, when the chapter’s example is a specification that approves a borrower carrying heavy debt merely because no payment was recently late.
  • B. Volume is the whole story: more applications processed produces proportionally more mistakes, and the rate of bad approvals per application is unchanged — More decisions do produce more errors, and this reading stops one step early. Figure 2.9 shows cumulative errors rising at an accelerating rate as automation increases, and treating the increase as arithmetic leaves the faulty acceptance criteria untouched and unnoticed.
  • C. Automating a flawed process magnifies the existing business problem and can mask it, which is why the chapter pairs automating with learning from the data the system creates — correct. The chapter’s worked example moves from four applications a day with about two bad approvals a week to twelve a day with up to six, and says the technology would serve only to magnify the existing business problems. Without learning it is more difficult to uncover the bad business process underlying the system, which is why an automating use can mask the problem rather than reveal it.
  • D. The criteria were sound and the reviewers stopped attending to them once the work sped up, so the remedy is retraining people rather than changing the process — Attention does fall when work speeds up, and retraining is a common first response. Nothing here suggests reviewers are departing from the criteria; they are applying criteria that were producing bad approvals before the system arrived.

4. 2.1 Three proposals sit on the table at a hypothetical building-supply firm. A: scan delivery tickets at the dock so nobody retypes them into the system. B: analyze two years of delivery exceptions by route, season, and crew, and change how routes are planned as a result. C: build reordering from each customer’s own consumption history, which no competitor offers. Which proposal is the clearest example of an information system used for organizational learning?

  • A. A, because capturing the ticket at the dock removes handling time and errors, and the chapter treats faster and more accurate work as the first form of value a system adds — A is an automating use: it helps complete a task faster, more cheaply, and with greater accuracy. That is genuine value and it is the base of the chapter’s ladder, which is why this would be the right answer to a question about improving efficiency at the operational level.
  • B. B, because organizational learning is using past behavior and data to improve business processes, and this proposal changes how the work is done on the strength of what the data showed — correct. Organizational learning is the ability of an organization to use past behavior and data to improve its business processes, and the chapter’s illustration is a loan system whose accumulated records let a manager see patterns and change how the work is planned. Analyzing two years of exceptions and rewriting the routing rules is the same move.
  • C. C, because the system that produces a competitive advantage is the one the organization has learned the most from building and running — C is a strategizing use, the top of the chapter’s ladder, because it looks for competitive advantage rather than for understanding of the process. It would be the answer to a question about which proposal serves the organization’s strategy.
  • D. None of them, because learning happens only when a system adjusts its own rules without a person intervening — Learning in this chapter is something the organization does, not something the software does unattended. The manager who reads the trend and changes the criteria is where the learning happens, and the chapter’s loan example works exactly that way.

5. 2.1 A hypothetical commercial printing firm is in trouble. Its two long-standing competitors match every price cut within days, and margins at all three are thin. Its own market study shows something else as well: total pages printed by all three firms together has fallen by about a third over three years, as clients moved documents into shared online workspaces. Which force is the strongest here?

  • A. Traditional rivals, because the competitors matching every price cut are the visible cause of the lost margin, so the answer is to compete on service rather than on price — Rivalry is genuinely present and it explains why nobody in the industry earns much on the pages still being printed. It cannot explain why a third of the pages disappeared, because a rival taking work would move share between the three firms rather than shrink the total.
  • B. Threat of new entrants, because the workspace providers have entered a market the printing firms used to hold and found the barriers low enough to walk through — A new entrant is a firm that starts selling what you sell. A shared online workspace prints nothing and sells no pages, and that difference is exactly what separates an entrant from another industry’s answer to the same need.
  • C. Customers’ bargaining power, because clients are refusing to pay printing prices and are holding up the online alternative as leverage in every negotiation — Buyer power is customers forcing better terms while still buying from your industry, which shows up as pressure on price, quality, and service. These clients are not negotiating over a page rate; they have stopped needing the pages.
  • D. Threat of substitute products or services, because the same need is being met from outside the industry and the whole category is shrinking rather than one firm’s share of it — correct. A substitute meets the same underlying need by a different route, so the customer never enters your industry, and the chapter’s implications for this force are product returns, decreased market share, and losing customers for life. The tell is the category-level decline, which nothing happening inside the industry could produce.

6. 2.1 A hypothetical chain of fourteen bakeries buys its flour blend from one of only two mills that make it. Both raised prices this year and lengthened lead times, and the chain has switched to a coarser blend that customers have noticed and mentioned. Each shop still phones its own order in, so nobody at head office can state what the chain buys in total. Which force is at work, and what does the chapter say it implies?

  • A. Suppliers’ bargaining power, whose implications the chapter gives as increased costs and reduced quality, both of which have already reached the customer here — correct. Suppliers’ bargaining power is the ability of the firms you buy from to set terms because you have few alternatives, and Table 2.3 gives its implications as increased costs and reduced quality. Both landed in the product the customer eats, and a chain that cannot state its own total volume has nothing to negotiate with even when an alternative exists.
  • B. Traditional rivals, because competing bakeries buying from the same two mills face the same increase, and none of them can undercut the others while it lasts — Shared exposure is a real and useful observation, since a rival facing the same cost will not undercut you easily. It still does not name where the pressure originates, which is upstream of the bakeries rather than between them.
  • C. Customers’ bargaining power, because the customers who noticed the coarser product are the ones who will now press for a lower price or leave — Buyer power is customers forcing your price down or your quality up because leaving costs them little. Customers here are reacting to a change that was made to them; the terms were set two steps earlier, by the mills.
  • D. Threat of new entrants, because two mills serving a whole region shows the barriers to entry in that market are low enough to attract others — The threat of new entrants concerns firms beginning to compete in your industry, which for this chain would mean a new bakery. Two mills supplying a whole region is evidence of high barriers in milling rather than low ones.

7. 2.1 A hypothetical furniture manufacturer builds a system that lets its designers assemble and stress a chair frame virtually before any tooling is cut, so weak joints are found in the model rather than on the production line. Where does this initiative sit on the value chain?

  • A. Operations, because the chair is what the customer buys and this system exists so that it is built correctly — Operations integrates supplies into the products and services the customer buys, and a better frame certainly reaches operations eventually. Naming the activity a system actually changes is what keeps the analysis usable, and no one is cutting or assembling anything at the point this system is used.
  • B. Inbound logistics, because the timber, the fittings and the finishes the model specifies between them determine exactly what has to be received into the workshop before any production can begin — Inbound logistics is receiving what has been purchased and getting it inside before any of it is sellable. A design decision changes what will later be ordered and received, which puts it upstream of this activity rather than inside it.
  • C. Product research and development, technology, and systems development, a support activity, because it improves the product and the systems the whole chain runs on — correct. The support band covering product research and development, technology, and systems development is where the product and the processes themselves are improved, and Figure 2.15 places computer-aided design systems among the systems feeding that supporting layer. The payoff is spread across the whole chain, which is the signature of a support activity.
  • D. Procurement, because deciding which joint and which fitting to use is a buying decision taken before anything is manufactured — Procurement is the decision about whom to buy from and on what terms, and it is a support activity in its own right. Specifying a joint is a design choice; choosing the supplier who will provide the fitting is the procurement decision that follows it.

8. 2.1 A hypothetical regional insurer competes on the speed and care of its claims handling. Its industry then adopts a shared electronic claims exchange: connecting confers no distinction because every carrier will be on it, but brokers will have no way to submit claims to a carrier that is not. The investment committee is split. What does the chapter’s framework support?

  • A. Decline it, because organizations try to maximize business/IT alignment and a system that offers no differentiation fails that test — Alignment is the general rule and the chapter states it plainly: in most cases organizations do not want systems that fail to match the strategy. This is the recognized exception to that rule, and applying the rule without the exception would disconnect the insurer from the brokers who bring it work.
  • B. Fund it as a strategic necessity, which the chapter describes as an investment an organization must make to survive and which may or may not coincide with its overall strategy — correct. The chapter says organizations sometimes have no choice about investments that may or may not coincide with their overall strategy, and calls such an investment a strategic necessity, something the organization must do to survive. Survival, not differentiation, is the test being applied.
  • C. Fund it and present it to the board as a competitive advantage, since being connected to the exchange is something the insurer will be able to offer its brokers — Every carrier will be connected, so this buys parity rather than advantage, and the chapter reserves competitive advantage for what rivals have not matched. Calling a necessity an advantage also hides the real reason for spending, which makes the next proposal harder to judge.
  • D. Defer it until the exchange has proved itself, because a system every rival will also hold cannot repay what it costs to build — Waiting is a reasonable posture toward an optional system whose value is unproven, and it would be the right instinct if the only question were payback. Here brokers cannot submit claims to a carrier that is not connected, so deferring is a decision to lose the work in the meantime.

9. 2.2 A hypothetical home-repair booking company employs nobody who holds a wrench. Repairs are carried out by independent tradespeople it recruits, rates, and pays per job, and its own scheduling and dispatch software is the thing rivals have not been able to reproduce. Using the chapter’s business model components, how should those two be classified?

  • A. The tradespeople are key resources and the software is a key activity, because the people are what customers actually pay for and dispatching is what the company spends its day doing — This reverses both definitions. Key resources are the most important assets needed to make the business model work, which fits the software rather than the tradespeople, and key activities are the most important things the company does rather than a piece of software it owns.
  • B. Both are channels, because between them they are how the service reaches the customer who booked it — Channels are the ways the product or service offering reaches the target customers, such as an app or a counter. The people and the software are how the service is produced and coordinated, which the model files under partners and resources instead.
  • C. The tradespeople are a customer segment, because the company recruits them, rates them, and has to keep them satisfied to stay in business — Producers on a two-sided market do have to be attracted and kept, which is why this reading is tempting. Customer segments names the customers targeted with the offering, and the component for the outside people and firms the model depends on is key partners.
  • D. The tradespeople are key partners and the software is a key resource, because partners are the network needed to make the model work and resources are its most important assets — correct. Key partners are the network of partners and suppliers needed to make the business model work, which is what independent tradespeople are here, and key resources are the most important assets needed to make it work, which is what proprietary scheduling and dispatch software is.

10. 2.2 A hypothetical language-learning app has three sources of income. Anyone can use it free with advertisements. Learners who want the advertisements removed and extra practice sets pay a monthly fee. When a learner books a session with an independent tutor through the app, the app keeps a commission. How should its revenue model be described?

  • A. It runs three at once — advertising, a freemium subscription and a transaction fee — because the revenue streams component can hold more than one — correct. A revenue model describes how the firm will earn revenue, and the business model component is revenue streams, plural: the chapter’s own examples show firms combining approaches, with Dropbox freemium and subscription, Amazon selling and running an affiliate program. Naming only one here would leave two thirds of the income unexplained.
  • B. Freemium, because the whole design is a limited free version sitting alongside a paid version with the restrictions removed, and the other two streams are incidental to that central arrangement — Freemium is accurately described in this option, and it does cover the free tier and the paid tier: limited versions given away to build a base, with a premium charged for the unrestricted version. It says nothing about the advertisements or the commission on bookings.
  • C. Advertising, because the free tier is what brings in the users that everything else depends on — Advertising is free services provided to customers and paid for by a third party, which is exactly what the free tier does. It is one of the three streams rather than the whole answer, and it would be the right answer if the paid tier and the tutor commission did not exist.
  • D. Transaction fees, because the commission is the only income tied to something the app actually arranges for the learner — Transaction fees or brokerage is a commission paid to the business for aiding in a transaction, which the tutor booking fits precisely. Being the income most visibly attached to a service does not make it the only income the model earns.

11. 2.2 A hypothetical kitchenware manufacturer has always made its own pans and sold them through its website. It now adds two things: reviews written by owners, and a marketplace where independent restorers list refurbished pans and pay the manufacturer a commission on each sale. Which description is accurate?

  • A. It is now a platform business rather than a manufacturer, because a platform coordinates others instead of producing anything itself — A platform-based business model does coordinate others rather than providing the product itself, which is why this sounds right. The manufacturer has not stopped making pans, and the chapter’s point is that the two can sit in one business rather than that one replaces the other.
  • B. It is still purely a pipe, because it produces goods and pushes them to customers, and reviews and third-party listings are marketing features rather than parts of a business model — The pipe description is accurate as far as it goes, since products are still produced and pushed to customers. The chapter says explicitly that many pipeline-based businesses now include platform elements such as reviews created by users, and a commissioned third-party marketplace is a good deal more than a marketing feature.
  • C. It has added platform elements to a pipe: the marketplace coordinates others to co-create value, creating a two-sided market whose success depends on network effects — correct. A platform-based business model coordinates others, both businesses and users, to co-create value, and the chapter notes that many pipeline businesses include platform elements and that every business must consider how far its model will include them.
