The restorers produce value that buyers consume, which is the two-sided market the chapter describes.
  • D. It has entered the sharing economy, because assets that already exist are being passed between private individuals rather than newly manufactured — The sharing economy is an economic system in which assets or services are shared between private individuals, free or for a fee, typically over the internet. A refurbished pan sold outright through a commissioned listing is a sale, not shared access to an asset somebody keeps.

12. 2.2 On a hypothetical marketplace for freelance editors, two things are observed over the same quarter. First, as more editors join, each editor faces more competition for the same jobs. Second, as more editors join, the publishers who hire them find the site more useful because more specialists are available. Which classification is correct?

  • A. The first is a cross-side effect and the second a same-side effect, because the harm lands on the editors themselves while the benefit crosses over to the publishers — This has the two labels the wrong way round. A same-side effect is the change in value as additional users join on the same side, and editors crowding other editors is that; a cross-side effect is the change in value for a user when users join on the other side, which is what the publishers experience.
  • B. The first is a same-side effect and the second a cross-side effect, because value falls for users on the same side in one case and rises for users on the other side in the other — correct. Same-side network effects relate to the increase or decrease in value as additional users join on the same side, and the chapter’s own negative example is riders competing for available rides. Cross-side network effects relate to the change in value for a user when users join on the other side, as when an app store becomes more useful to users as more apps are added.
  • C. Both are same-side effects, because in each case the change was caused by editors joining rather than by publishers joining — The cause is the same in both observations, which is what makes this reading tempting. Effects are classified by whose value changes rather than by who joined, so the same arrival of editors produces a same-side effect for editors and a cross-side effect for publishers.
  • D. Neither is a network effect: the first is ordinary competition between sellers and the second is simply a bigger catalogue for buyers to choose from — Competition among sellers and a larger catalogue are exactly what these effects look like from inside; the terms name the mechanism rather than replace the description. A platform only has value if users participate on both sides, which is why the chapter asks platform businesses to evaluate these effects deliberately.

13. 2.2 On a hypothetical grocery-delivery platform, couriers accept jobs one at a time, are not employed by the company, have no protection against discrimination, no social security contributions, and little job security. The company answers criticism by saying it merely removes friction from transactions people were already free to make. How does the chapter frame this?

  • A. This is the gig economy, where workers are hired only for short-term temporary jobs, and the chapter names precisely these losses to workers as a criticism of such business models — correct. In the gig economy workers are not employed by the company but are hired for short-term, temporary jobs, and the chapter lists the consequences directly: rights fought for since the Industrial Revolution neglected, no protection against discrimination, no social security, little job security, and limited income opportunities and social contact.
  • B. This is disintermediation, because the platform has removed the traditional middleman standing between the shopper and the courier — Disintermediation is real here, since many platforms match providers and customers without traditional middlemen, and that is roughly the argument the company is making. It names what happened to the intermediary rather than what happened to the people doing the work.
  • C. This is a same-side network effect, because couriers competing with each other for the same jobs is what determines what the work pays — A same-side effect is a genuine feature of this market, and more couriers competing for the same jobs is one. It describes how value shifts among users of a platform, not the employment arrangement the criticism is about.
  • D. This is unfair competition, which the chapter defines as operating with no employees while established rivals carry the cost of a workforce — The chapter does raise unfair competition, and it defines it as gaining advantage over traditional businesses by breaking or at least bypassing existing laws and regulations. Employing nobody is a feature of the gig arrangement rather than the definition of unfair competition.

14. 2.2 A hypothetical maker of commercial laundry machines is considering a change: instead of selling machines to hotels and then selling spare parts and repairs, it would keep ownership and charge per completed wash cycle. Which consequence does the chapter say follows from a move like this?

  • A. Revenue becomes more predictable and little else changes, because the same machines go to the same hotels under a different payment schedule — Smoother revenue is a fair expectation and one reason firms find these models attractive. The chapter is explicit that a great deal else changes, including pricing models, business processes, service level agreements, capacity management, and the customer segment being sold to.
  • B. The maker should now press harder on minimizing manufacturing cost, since it keeps every machine it builds and margin per unit matters more than it did — Minimizing manufacturing cost is the instinct a pipe-based manufacturer brings with it, which is exactly why the chapter calls it out. Under a service-based model the manufacturer has to focus instead on life span and ease of maintenance and repair, because it now pays for every failure.
  • C. The change is essentially a financing arrangement dressed as a service, so the important new work is assessing each hotel’s credit rather than altering anything about the product or the processes behind it — Money does move differently and credit exposure is real, so this concern belongs somewhere on the list. Treating the change as financing misses the operational half: the maker only earns while the equipment runs, which rewrites what it should design for and monitor.
  • D. The hotel’s fixed costs become variable and the maker earns only while machines run, so its incentive moves to life span and preventive maintenance — correct. The chapter’s jet-engine example has the customer paying for hours of usage rather than buying the engine, transforming fixed costs into variable costs, while the manufacturer earns only for operating equipment and therefore has an incentive to improve design and perform preventive maintenance. It adds that such models are possible only through sensors connected to the internet and advanced analytics that predict failure and schedule maintenance.

15. 2.3 A hypothetical veterinary group made two changes last year. A: it upgraded its booking software to a version that sends automatic reminders, and missed appointments fell. B: it began remote video consultations, which brought in rural clients who had never used any practice regularly, and which are steadily taking over routine follow-up visits. Which change is a radical innovation as the chapter defines it?

  • A. A, because the software version is new to this practice and the change produced a measurable business result, which is the test the chapter applies to anything it is willing to call an innovation — A is an incremental innovation, which the chapter calls the most common form: enhancing or upgrading existing products, services, or processes. Being new to the adopter is not the test, otherwise every purchase a firm had not made before would count as radical.
  • B. Neither, because both run on software the practice bought rather than technology it developed itself — The chapter’s own table of radical innovations lists online retailing, distance education, and online stock brokerage, none of which required the adopting organization to invent the technology. Who built it is a separate question from what it displaced.
  • C. B, because a markedly different technology has reached a customer segment the practice never served and is marginalizing an existing service — correct. Radical innovations use a markedly new or different technology to access new customer segments and/or provide significantly greater benefits to existing customers, and eventually marginalize or replace existing products or services. Both halves are present here: a segment that was never served, and routine visits being displaced.
  • D. Both, because the chapter treats any innovation that returns value to the organization as radical — Returning value to the organization is what separates innovation from mere invention, so both changes qualify as innovations. That test does not distinguish the two sizes, and treating every valuable change as radical empties the word of the meaning the chapter gives it.

16. 2.3 A hypothetical grocery chain stops charging a fee for each home delivery and offers a flat monthly delivery pass instead. The products, the stores, the vans, and the delivery routes are unchanged; what changed is how the customer pays. Which of the ten types of innovation is that?

  • A. Service innovation, because the customer experiences delivery differently now and their experience of the offering is what changed — Service innovations support and enhance the value of an offering, and the chapter’s examples are a retailer’s philosophy of delivering excellent customer service and a clothier offering free lifetime pressing. Nothing about the standard of service changed here, only the basis on which it is billed.
  • B. Profit model innovation, because it is a novel way of generating revenue from an offering that is otherwise the same — correct. Profit model innovation is finding novel ways of generating revenues from offerings, and the chapter’s examples are a storage firm using a freemium approach, a software firm offering its suite on subscription, and an engine maker selling thrust as a service. A pass replacing per-delivery fees is the same kind of change.
  • C. Channel innovation, because delivery is how the offering reaches the customer and delivery is what the change is about — Channel innovations use innovative ways to connect offerings with customers, such as an immersive flagship store or a coffee brand partnering with hotels and airlines. The van reaching the same doorstep is the same channel; what moved is the money.
  • D. Process innovation, because the way the chain plans and staffs its delivery rounds will have to change to serve pass holders — Process innovations change the primary processes used to produce products or services, such as pioneering lean production or moving fashion from design to store in three weeks. Scheduling may well adapt, but adapting to a pricing change is not the same as changing how the work is produced.

17. 2.3 A hypothetical team building scheduling software for salons ships a minimum viable product with six features. Testing shows that owners use only the waitlist feature, will not pay for the other five, and say they would happily pay for a waitlist tool on its own. What does the lean startup methodology say the team should do?

  • A. Persevere and add more features, because a single-feature product cannot support a business and the other five need longer to be understood — Adding features is the inside-out instinct the chapter warns against, and it is what the evidence contradicts. The chapter’s example runs the other way: an app combining check-ins, gaming, and photo sharing was stripped down to the features users valued and became successful afterwards.
  • B. Abandon the venture, because a hypothesis that failed in customer validation shows there is no market for the product — Abandoning is the response to learning nothing, and this test taught the team a great deal. When a hypothesis does not hold the methodology asks for a pivot, a change of direction grounded in what was learned, rather than the end of the venture.
  • C. Move into the execution phase, because customers have said they would pay and willingness to pay is what the search phase exists to settle — Willingness to pay is indeed what customer validation tests, which makes this tempting. What customers said they would pay for is not the product that was built, so the search phase has not yet produced a product/market fit to execute on.
  • D. Pivot: change direction while staying grounded in what was learned, which is what the build-measure-learn cycle exists to produce — correct. If at any stage of the search process a hypothesis does not hold, it is time to pivot, changing direction while remaining grounded in what was learned, and teams typically go through several iterations and pivots before finding product/market fit. The measure step here has produced exactly the learning a pivot is made from.

18. 2.3 A hypothetical equipment-rental firm surveys its regular customers about which emerging technology it should adopt. The customers name one they already encounter elsewhere, and the firm decides to build its differentiation on it. What does the chapter’s account of innovation say about this reasoning?

  • A. It is weak, because customers understand their own problems very well but are not experts in solutions, and a technology they already know is one competitors know as well — correct. The chapter says customers are likely to understand their problems very well but are not experts in solutions and are not likely to know about new technologies, and adds that if they do know about a technology then competitors probably do too, which makes it the wrong one to rest a competitive advantage on.
  • B. It is sound, because the customers are the people who will use it, and outside-in thinking means building what customers ask for — Outside-in thinking is the chapter’s recommendation, so the label is right and the application is not. Outside-in means starting from the customer’s job-to-be-done and the friction points blocking it, which is a question about problems rather than a shopping list of technologies.
  • C. It is sound, because a technology customers already recognise carries less adoption risk than one they have never seen in use — Familiarity does lower adoption risk, and that is a real benefit worth weighing. The chapter’s objection is about advantage rather than adoption: a technology already visible to everyone will not distinguish this firm from the rivals who can see it too.
  • D. It is weak, because customer surveys are inside-out thinking, and outside-in thinking means starting from the firm’s own capabilities and finding a market for them — This reverses the two terms. Inside-out thinking is developing a solution and then trying to find a market for it, while outside-in thinking starts from the customer’s need, so a survey of customers is not itself inside-out.

19. 2.3 A hypothetical logistics firm must choose between two incompatible shipment-tracking standards. One is clearly better engineered; the other is already used by more of the firms it trades with. A manager argues that the choice is obvious, because the better technology will win in the end. What does the chapter’s treatment of innovation support?

  • A. Agree, because the superior technology is the safer investment and markets correct toward quality given enough time — Quality does matter and it often wins, which is why this is the intuitive answer. The chapter’s videocassette example exists precisely to show that most experts agreed one format recorded and played back better and that the other format won the marketplace anyway.
  • B. Agree, because a technically superior system is proprietary technology, which is the kind of resource rivals cannot copy — This misapplies the word proprietary. The chapter says an organization typically cannot patent its use of an information system, particularly one purchased from a vendor: the data in the system may be proprietary, but the system usually is not.
  • C. Disagree: choosing among innovative investments always entails risk, and the technically superior option can still lose the market, as Betamax did to VHS — correct. Choosing among innovative investments always entails risk, and the chapter’s classic example is the videocassette format contest in which the technically superior choice turned out to be the unfortunate one. It adds that for organizations the risk is greater still, given the size and often mission-critical nature of the investment.
  • D. Disagree, and wait until one standard has plainly won before committing anything, because a firm that never moves early can never make the expensive mistake that Betamax turned out to be — Waiting removes one risk and creates another, and the chapter’s account of innovation is that it has to be continuous, with organizations constantly on the lookout and never resting. It also leaves the manager’s reasoning untouched, since the eventual winner is exactly what nobody can read off engineering quality.

20. 2.3 A hypothetical insurer announces it will adopt the lean startup approach for new services. Its funding is approved once a year for a whole project, individual bonuses depend on delivering the plan as written, and a cancelled experiment counts against the person who proposed it. What stands in the way?

  • A. Nothing serious, provided the teams are made cross-functional, because the methodology’s requirements concern how teams are composed rather than how work is funded and rewarded — Cross-functional teams are one of the requirements the chapter names, so this is half right. It stops there, and the chapter also calls for incentives at the team level rather than the individual level and for a startup-like budgeting model, both of which this firm currently contradicts.
  • B. A resource requirement, because what the firm needs is enough people with the knowledge, skills, and time to build a minimum viable product quickly — Having enough people with the relevant knowledge, skills, and time is a genuine resource requirement the chapter lists, and it may well bind here too. Nothing in the situation says the insurer lacks people; what it describes is how money is released and how behavior is rewarded.
  • C. Nothing, because the methodology was developed for startups, so an established insurer adopting it needs no change to how it funds and rewards work — The chapter answers the first half directly, saying the approach does not only work for startups and naming established companies that have used it successfully. The second half is where this fails: the chapter treats process, resource and risk-tolerance requirements as conditions the organization has to meet, not as things a team can work around while funding and rewards stay unchanged.
  • D. Process and risk-tolerance requirements: accountability and incentives need to sit at the team level, funding must be released in stages and be cuttable, and failure has to be tolerable — correct. The chapter’s process requirements call for cross-functional collaboration, incentives and accountability at the team level rather than the individual level, and a startup-like budgeting model where funds are approved as the project moves through stages or cut quickly. Its risk-tolerance requirement adds that members must be willing to test products that may not meet requirements and to fail fast.

21. 2.4 An analyst at a hypothetical distributor asks an AI assistant which competitive force is pressing hardest on the firm. It returns a fluent paragraph naming customers’ bargaining power, citing an industry switching-cost figure and a named competitor’s loyalty program. Neither the figure nor the program can be found anywhere. What is the right next move?

  • A. Keep the diagnosis and drop the two citations, because the force it named is the part the analysis actually needs — This is the tempting shortcut, and it treats the conclusion as separable from the support that came with it. The same process produced both, and the module’s own test for a recommendation is a named force together with the observable evidence that it is the strong one.
  • B. Treat the paragraph as a hypothesis and go and collect the firm’s own evidence, because a confident output can still be invented — correct. A confident, fluent output that turns out to be untrue is the failure this module has been guarding against, and the remedy is a person between the output and the decision. Naming a force is a hypothesis worth testing against renewal history, account concentration, and win-loss records, which are things only this firm holds.
  • C. Ask the assistant to rate its own confidence in each claim and keep only the claims it rates highly — A self-assessment is produced the same way as the rest of the passage, and the paragraph in question already read as confident while being wrong. Asking a text generator to judge its own text adds a second output to verify rather than a check on the first.
  • D. Stop using the assistant for work of this kind altogether, because a tool that can invent a citation and present it in the same tone as a real one cannot safely contribute to a strategy discussion — Refusing the tool entirely is the over-correction, and it gives up real assistance in framing a question and listing candidates. The lesson the module draws is to keep the person in control of the decision, which is a role for the tool inside the work rather than a reason to bar it.

22. 2.4 The strategy team at a hypothetical manufacturer wants a summary of its unreleased pricing model and its supplier contract terms. Someone proposes pasting both documents into a public AI assistant the firm holds no agreement with, whose provider states that submitted content may be retained and used to improve the service. What should be raised first?

  • A. That submitting the documents moves the firm’s own proprietary material outside its control to a provider that says it may keep it — correct. The chapter treats resources such as proprietary technology and accumulated commercial knowledge as the assets an advantage is built from, and unreleased pricing and negotiated supplier terms are exactly that. Once the file is submitted it has left the firm’s control, and the provider has said it may retain the content.
  • B. That the summary may contain an invented figure, so every number in it will have to be checked against the source documents before anyone relies on it — Checking figures against the source is right and would be the first concern if the documents held nothing sensitive. It is a concern about what comes back rather than about what goes out, and the damage in this case is done at the moment of submission.
  • C. That an assistant trained largely on freely available public content is unlikely to have read enough commercial supplier contracts to summarize this firm’s own agreements accurately or safely — How well an assistant reads an unfamiliar commercial document does affect the quality of the summary, so this is a fair question about output. It is a separate question from whether the document should be sent to an outside service at all.
  • D. That summarizing these documents is work the strategy team is there to do, so handing it over makes the team less valuable to the firm — Drafting help is not the same as surrendering the decision, and a summary the team then reads and argues with is assistance of the kind this module endorses. What is wrong here is what the assistant is being handed, not that it is being asked.

23. 2.4 A hypothetical retailer trains a model on eight years of its own promotion results to propose next season’s promotions. The chain now wants to win a customer group it has never served. The model keeps proposing variations of what has worked for the customers it already has and proposes nothing for the new group. Nothing is malfunctioning. What explains the result?

  • A. The output is a hallucination, because the proposals do not correspond to what the chain intends to do next season — A hallucination is a confident statement that is not true, such as a fabricated figure or a citation to something that does not exist. These proposals invent nothing; they repeat faithfully what the chain actually did, which is a different fault needing a different fix.
  • B. The result shows the new customer group is not worth pursuing, since eight years of the chain’s own data turned up nothing that would reach them — This reads silence as evidence, which is the reasoning error the situation is built to expose. Records of customers the chain never sold to do not exist, so the data cannot speak for or against that group and the absence of a proposal says nothing about its value.
  • C. The model reflects the data it was given: the record holds the chain’s history rather than its strategy, so the remedy lies in the inputs rather than in better prompting — correct. Output quality rests on input quality, and a dataset of eight years of one chain’s own promotions describes the customers it had rather than the customers it wants. No amount of phrasing will produce evidence about a group the record never contained, so the work belongs with the analyst and with new data collection.
  • D. The problem is entirely in how the request was phrased, and a prompt naming the new customer group explicitly would have produced a proposal the chain could put into a plan for next season — Sharper requests do produce better responses, and naming the group would certainly change the wording of the answer. It would not change what the model has to draw on, so the reply would be assembled from patterns belonging to the existing customers and presented as though it were about the new ones.

24. 2.4 Four uses of an AI assistant are proposed during a strategy review at a hypothetical wholesaler. Which one fits the discipline this module has been teaching?

  • A. Let it choose which of the three competing proposals to fund, because it can weigh them without the internal politics that distort the room — Hard judgment is where analysis feels most valuable, and the wish to take politics out of a funding decision is a real one. Handing over the decision itself is what the companion rule refuses; having it compare the three proposals against stated criteria while the committee decides would fit.
  • B. Let it write the final recommendation, complete with the measure and the review date, and take that draft to the executive committee as written, since the analyst supplied the evidence it was built from — Supplying the evidence is a real safeguard, and drafting is genuinely the kind of help this module endorses, which is what makes this the hardest of the four to refuse. The verification step belongs after the drafting rather than before it, because a figure, a date or a term can still be restated wrongly in the draft, and whoever carries it into the room is the person who will be asked to defend it.
  • C. Let it generate the evidence for the force we have already agreed is strongest, so that the recommendation reads convincingly when it reaches the committee — This inverts the whole sequence the module teaches, which runs from evidence to a named force to an initiative. Assembling support for a conclusion already reached is the opposite of a diagnosis, and it would survive the meeting only until somebody checked the numbers.
  • D. Let it list candidate substitutes and possible cost drivers for the analyst to test against the firm’s own sales and purchasing records — correct. Candidates and cost drivers are the kind of breadth an assistant supplies well, and every one of them is then checked against records only this firm holds. The analyst keeps control of what the evidence supports, which is the arrangement that makes the person more valuable rather than less.

25. 2.4 For several months a hypothetical wholesaler’s team has received a weekly competitive-scan summary drafted by an AI assistant from public news and vendor sites. Nobody now opens the underlying sources. A manager proposes making the summary the firm’s main strategic input, since it covers more ground than the analysts ever did and arrives days sooner. How should that proposal be judged?

  • A. Sound, because the summary reaches more sources than the analysts could read and speed is what makes a diagnosis useful while a decision is still open — Coverage and speed are genuine gains, and the module does argue that the analyst who closes the gap fastest is the one whose recommendation arrives while the decision is open. Speed does not settle where an advantage comes from, which is the claim this proposal is actually making.
  • B. Weak, because the summary rests on content any rival’s assistant can read too, so it can support parity at best, while the firm’s own records are the input rivals do not have — correct. The chapter’s account of advantage turns on resources and capabilities superior to those of competitors, and on the observation that rivals can copy what they can also obtain. Public sources are available to every competitor, while this firm’s own purchasing, renewal, and margin records are not, which is why the summary belongs alongside the internal evidence rather than in place of it.
  • C. Sound as long as the assistant is required to cite each source, because a summary with citations attached is evidence in the sense this module has been using the word — Citations do make verification possible and they are worth insisting on. A cited public article is still a statement about the industry rather than observable evidence about this firm’s buyers, suppliers, or costs, which is what a named force has to rest on.
  • D. Weak, because the real loss is that nobody on the team reads a source before repeating what the summary says about it — This names a real cost, since a team repeating an unchecked summary cannot say where a claim came from. It is an argument for keeping the reading habit rather than an answer to whether a public-source summary can carry the firm’s strategy.

26. 2.5 An analyst at a hypothetical wholesaler wants a list of departments whose total spending for the year exceeded fifty thousand. Working from a single spending table, she groups the rows by department and totals the amounts, but places the condition on the total in the clause that filters rows before any grouping happens. The query will not give her what she wants. Why?

  • A. The row filter runs before the rows are grouped, so the totals it is being asked to test do not exist yet; a condition on a total belongs in the clause that filters groups — correct. The row filter keeps only the rows that satisfy a condition and it runs before anything is totalled, which is why it quietly determines every number that follows. Filtering on a total requires the clause that filters grouped rows, and that clause exists precisely because the row filter has finished its work by the time totals exist.
  • B. The total was never named among the columns the query returns, and a condition can only test a column that appears in the returned result — This is a common belief and it is worth testing: conditions and returned columns are separate decisions, and a query can perfectly well filter on something it does not display. The trouble here is not visibility but timing, since the total has not been calculated at the moment the row filter runs.
  • C. The result was never sorted, and a condition on a total is applied as the rows are being put into order, so nothing at all is compared until a sort has been added to the end of the query — Sorting arranges the rows that survive; it neither creates nor removes any of them. Adding a sort here would order a result that is still wrong, which is why an ordering clause never repairs a filtering mistake.
  • D. The department names and the amounts have not been brought together, so a join is needed before either column can be used in a condition — Everything the analyst needs sits in one table, so nothing has to be joined before the condition can be written. A join brings related rows from two tables together on a matching column, which would matter if the department names lived somewhere else.

27. 2.5 A hypothetical service desk holds six tickets: A north, 5 days; B north, 2 days; C south, 9 days; D north, 4 days; E east, 3 days; F north, 3 days. An analyst keeps only the tickets from the north region that took more than three days, counts what survives, and reports that the north region resolves most of its tickets slowly. What is wrong with the report?

  • A. Nothing: two of the four northern tickets took more than three days, which is a fair basis for calling the region slow — The arithmetic is nearly right and the conclusion is not: two of four is half rather than most. Even that comparison is unavailable from this result, because the surviving rows no longer include the fast northern tickets the share would be measured against.
  • B. The condition should have read three days or more rather than more than three days, which would have kept ticket F in the result and changed the count the analyst reported to the board — Boundary conditions genuinely matter, and ticket F at exactly three days is excluded by the wording as written. Moving the boundary changes the count by one and leaves the report’s two real problems exactly where they were.
  • C. The filter removed every other region as well as the fast northern tickets, so the result can neither compare north with anywhere else nor give a share — correct. A filter applied before anything is counted decides every number that follows, and this one discarded both halves of the comparison the claim depends on: the northern tickets resolved quickly, and every ticket from the south and east. The result supports only the statement that two northern tickets took more than three days.
  • D. The count is right but the rows should have been grouped by region first, because a count means nothing until the rows are grouped — Grouping would produce a count for each region present in the surviving rows, and only one region survived the filter. The group would therefore be north on its own, which is the same number reported in a different shape.

28. 2.5 A hypothetical retailer is matching a loyalty file against a web-store file on the customer email address. Around forty per cent of the records fail to match even though staff recognise the same customers in both. A spot check shows differences of capitalisation, trailing spaces, and in a few rows an invisible character. What is the right first move?

  • A. Correct the raw values in both files by hand until the two columns agree, since matching them is what the work is for — Editing in place does eventually produce values that agree, and it destroys the originals, so nobody can afterwards show where a matched record came from. It also has to be redone by hand every time either system exports again.
  • B. Build standardised columns beside the raw ones in each file and match on those, leaving the original values in place so anyone can later check where a match came from — correct. A spreadsheet function takes a value and returns a new one without changing the original, which is why cleaning is done in new columns: the raw values stay available when someone asks where a number came from. Removing stray spaces, stripping non-printable characters, and standardising capitalisation is what makes two records for one customer match at all.
  • C. Match on the part of each address after the marker instead, because the domain half is stable, is written the same way in both systems, and does not carry any of the stray spacing — Domains are stable, which is what makes this idea appealing. Matching on the domain merges every customer at the same organization into a single record, which replaces a matching problem with a larger counting problem.
  • D. Ask for fresh exports from both systems, because data with invisible characters in it cannot support a customer analysis — A fresh export is worth asking for when a file is genuinely corrupt, and here the inconsistency is in how the values were entered rather than in the transfer. The same untidy values would arrive again, and the cleaning step would still be waiting.

29. 2.5 An analyst at a hypothetical wholesaler pulls the username out of each email address by taking the first eight characters of the address. It looks right for a few rows and is wrong for many others. What has gone wrong, and what is the rule that fixes it?

  • A. The addresses still carry stray spaces, and once those are removed a fixed count of eight characters will land in the right place — Trimming is a real first step and it does shift every character along by however many spaces came off. A fixed count of eight would still be wrong for every address whose username is not eight characters long, which is most of them.
  • B. The function being used is case sensitive, so every address that happened to contain a capital letter was measured from the wrong place and cut several characters too early — One of the position-finding functions is case sensitive and its companion is not, and that distinction matters when the marker itself is a letter. The marker here is the same character in every row, so capitalisation cannot be what moved it.
  • C. The values vary in length, so the split has to be done by looking each address up against a list of known usernames — Varying length is exactly the problem, and a lookup list is the wrong remedy for it: the list would need maintaining and would fail on the first customer nobody had entered yet. The point of a formula is to state a rule that works on rows nobody has seen.
  • D. The marker sits in a different position in every address, so the rule has to locate the marker first and measure from it rather than count a fixed number of characters — correct. Neither the username nor the domain has a fixed length, so the position of the marker has to be found for each row and the length measured from it. That is why the pattern is find the marker, take everything up to one character before it, and take the remainder by subtracting the marker’s position from the total length.

30. 2.5 A query against a hypothetical wholesaler’s sales table returns revenue by account and shows that four accounts produced roughly two thirds of the year’s revenue. Four sentences are written about it. Which one is the finding — what the numbers mean in the business — rather than the result itself or a recommendation?

  • A. Four accounts produced about two thirds of revenue in the period the query covered — This is the result restated, and it is true and it is where the work starts. It names no consequence for the business, which is why on its own it is a fact nobody has to act on.
  • B. We should build a purchase history for every account and make offers from it, judged by the share of revenue coming from accounts outside the top four at the next review — This is a recommendation, and a well-formed one: it states a concrete initiative and commits to a measure and a date. It is the step after the finding rather than the finding itself, and it only makes sense once the finding has explained why account concentration matters.
  • C. A few buyers hold enough of our revenue to set terms at renewal, which is customers’ bargaining power pressing on us — correct. A finding says what the result means in the business, and this one attaches the concentration of revenue to a named force: buyer power grows when a few accounts hold most of your revenue and can use that leverage at renewal. It is the link between the query result and any initiative anyone might propose.
  • D. We should be spending more time with our largest accounts than we currently do — This is a preference. It offers no evidence, nothing anyone could be assigned to build, and no measure by which it could later be judged to have worked.

31. 2.6 A scoring function for competitive forces returns the single highest-scoring force. Two forces tie at the top and it returns the first one it happened to see. What is the practical consequence?

  • A. None, since either force is equally worth addressing when they score the same — Equal scores do not make the responses interchangeable; relieving buyer power and relieving supplier power call for entirely different systems and budgets.
  • B. Spending is aimed at whichever force the data happened to list first, and the report gives no sign that the evidence never separated them — correct. Right. The ordering of the input decides the recommendation, and nothing in the output warns the reader of that. A confident answer resting on row order is worse than an admitted tie.
  • C. The score itself becomes unreliable and the analysis must be redone from the beginning — A tie does not make the scores wrong. The scoring is fine; the reporting of what it found is what fails.
  • D. The tie will resolve itself as soon as more evidence is gathered, so the output should be read as provisional and the spending decision held until the next round of data arrives — It may well resolve later, but the report as issued presents a winner as settled, and decisions get taken from it now.

32. 2.6 A subscription business calculates that a customer costing 240 to acquire returns 30 a month, and reports a payback of eight months. Customers on that plan churn at 20 percent a month. What has the calculation missed?

  • A. Nothing; eight months is the correct payback period for those figures — The division is right and the conclusion is wrong, which is what makes this the common error. Eight months only matters if the customer is still there in month eight.
  • B. That the expected lifetime is about five months, so the customer leaves roughly three months before the acquisition cost is recovered — correct. Right. A churn rate of twenty percent a month implies an average life near five months, so the eight-month payback never arrives and each acquisition loses money.
  • C. That the monthly return should have been discounted for the time value of money — Discounting would refine the figure slightly and would not change the verdict. The horizon, not the discount rate, is what decides this case.
  • D. That acquisition cost should be spread across the whole customer base rather than charged to one customer — Spreading the cost differently changes the presentation, not the fact that this customer leaves before repaying what winning them cost.

33. 2.6 An analyst needs total revenue per plan and writes a query that filters with WHERE on the summed revenue. The database rejects it. Why?

  • A. Sums cannot be filtered at all; they can only be sorted — Sums are filtered routinely; the question is only where in the statement that filter is allowed to sit.
  • B. WHERE is evaluated before rows are grouped, so no total exists yet for it to test; a condition on an aggregate belongs in HAVING — correct. Right. WHERE decides which rows enter the grouping and has finished before any total is computed. HAVING runs afterwards, which is why the condition belongs there.
  • C. The query is missing an index on the column being summed — An index changes how quickly a query runs, never whether it is a legal statement.
  • D. SUM may appear in the SELECT clause and nowhere else in a query, so a total can never be tested by a condition wherever that condition is written — Aggregates appear in HAVING and ORDER BY as well, which is precisely the point this question turns on.

34. 2.6 A customer's name is stored once in a customer table and joined in wherever it is needed, rather than copied onto each of their subscriptions. Which reason best justifies that design?

  • A. Joining is faster than reading a column that is already on the row — Joining generally costs more at query time than reading a local column. Speed is the argument against this design, not for it.
  • B. The name is a fact about the customer, so keeping one copy means a correction is made once and no two rows can disagree — correct. Right. One fact in one place. Copying the name onto every subscription creates as many chances to disagree as there are rows, and reconciling them later is far more expensive than the join.
  • C. It reduces the total storage the database consumes to a degree that matters once the customer table has grown to several million rows — The saving is real but trivial at this scale, and nobody would restructure a schema for it. Correctness is the reason that holds.
  • D. It is required before a GROUP BY can be used on any of the joined tables — Grouping works perfectly well on duplicated columns. Nothing about GROUP BY requires the data to be split across tables.

35. 2.7 An analyst hands in a study of a hypothetical regional bakery supplier. The forces section names buyer power as the strongest force and evidences it. The value chain section names one activity, outbound logistics, and recommends a delivery-tracking system there with a measure and a date. A reviewer sends it back. What is the defect?

  • A. The recommendation should have been held back until the forces analysis had been accepted — Analysis and recommendation are meant to arrive together; splitting them across two rounds of review would slow the work without improving it.
  • B. One value chain area was named, so nothing shows that the rest of the chain was examined or what the chosen area was preferred over — correct. Right. A single area could be the first idea the writer had. Two areas, each with its own evidence, are what turn a hunch into a scan and give the recommendation an alternative it beat.
  • C. Buyer power cannot be the strongest force in a business whose customers are other businesses — Buyer power is common and often strongest in business-to-business markets, where a handful of large customers can dictate terms. The force is plausible here.
  • D. Delivery tracking belongs to operations rather than to outbound logistics, so the area was misidentified — Tracking what has left the premises sits comfortably in outbound logistics. Even if the placement were arguable, one debatable label is not what makes this study incomplete.

36. 2.7 A study of a hypothetical tool-hire firm closes by recommending a booking portal, a maintenance scheduler and a customer loyalty scheme. All three are costed and each carries a measure. Why is this still weaker than a study recommending one of them?

  • A. Costing three initiatives takes three times as long, which delays the decision the study was commissioned to inform — Thoroughness is not the problem here. A study that costed three options and then chose between them would be stronger, not slower to act on.
  • B. The reader is being asked to approve rather than to choose, and the study never says which of the three it believes in most — correct. Right. Recommending is choosing. Three proposals hand the decision back to the reader, conceal the analyst's own judgement, and guarantee that something on the list can later be called a success.
  • C. A measure attached to three initiatives at once cannot be calculated accurately enough to judge any of them — Each initiative has its own measure and each could be tracked separately. Measurement is not what fails when a recommendation becomes a list.
  • D. Most organizations lack the capacity to run three technology projects within a single year — Capacity varies, and some organizations run several projects comfortably. The limit that matters here is on the argument being made rather than on the firm's throughput.

37. 2.7 A comparison summary about a hypothetical regional print supplier needs a real company to set beside it. Four are proposed: the best-known technology company in the world, whose relevant practice is nowhere described publicly; a competitor two towns away, whose operations nobody outside can observe; a national firm in the same line of business that publishes how its ordering works; and a favourite company from an unrelated industry. Which does the most work in the summary?

  • A. The best-known technology company, because a reader will immediately recognise the comparison — Recognition is not evidence. With nothing published about the practice you need to describe, the summary can admire the company but cannot learn anything specific from it.
  • B. The competitor two towns away, because it is under exactly the same local conditions — Shared conditions would be useful if anything about the firm were visible, but a close competitor publishes nothing about how it schedules or takes orders, so there is nothing to read.
  • C. The national firm in the same line of business, because the practice being compared is documented and the pressure is the same — correct. Right. Same pressure, same kind of value chain, and enough published detail to describe the practice accurately. The difference in size does not matter, because what transfers is a practice rather than a budget.
  • D. The favourite company from an unrelated industry, because a fresh analogy makes the argument more interesting — A distant industry occasionally teaches something, but it makes the transfer much harder to argue and usually produces a summary that explains the other company and never returns.

38. 2.7 Four students each close a comparison summary about a hypothetical regional laundry service with one sentence. Which sentence states a lesson that transfers?

  • A. The larger company spends more on technology in a single month than this firm earns in a year, so nothing in its operation can usefully be carried across to a business of this size — This is a difference rather than a lesson. A gap in spending is the first thing anyone notices about two firms of unequal size and the last thing anyone here can act on.
  • B. This firm should build the same mobile application the larger company built — This copies an artifact rather than a practice, and it commits the firm to a target set by somebody else's balance sheet without saying what the application would be for.
  • C. The practice worth copying is quoting a collection time at the moment of booking rather than promising to call back — correct. Right. It names a practice, explains why the practice survives the difference in scale, and points at data the firm already holds, so somebody could begin doing it on Monday.
  • D. Both firms show that customer expectations are rising across every service industry — A sentence that would fit any two firms in any service industry has compared nothing. It is the most common way a comparison ends without producing anything usable.

39. 2.7 A summary limited to 150 to 200 words arrives at 240. It contains one sentence naming the strongest force with its evidence, two naming value chain areas, one recommending an initiative with a measure and a date, two on the firm's history and reputation, one admiring the comparison company's scale, and one naming the practice that transfers. Which cut brings it into the band without damaging the analysis?

  • A. Drop one of the two value chain areas, since the area that was not built has already served its purpose — The second area is what shows a scan took place, and it is the alternative the recommendation was preferred over. Cutting it removes evidence rather than padding.
  • B. Drop the measure and the date, since both are recorded in the framework analysis anyway — A measure without a date is an aspiration, and a recommendation without either is a preference. These are the words that make the initiative fundable and they earn their place.
  • C. Drop the history and the admiration, which are the three sentences that name nothing anyone could act on — correct. Right. Three sentences of history and admiration are the only ones that leave the reader with nothing to do, and removing them lands the piece inside the band with the argument intact.
  • D. Drop the sentence naming the practice that transfers, since it restates the recommendation in other words — The lesson is what the comparison exists to produce, and it is not the recommendation restated: one says what to build here, the other says which practice carries across.

What to do next. Take one organization you already deal with and run the whole chain on it once: name the force that squeezes it hardest, find the value chain activity where that force lands, say what system would relieve it, and state the number that should move. Then ask what evidence would settle whether you are right, and how you would pull it. That last question is the one that separates an opinion from an analysis.
